with it:** every `create-lumiose` template sets `csp: "strict"` in `vite.config.ts`. The framework
default stays off, so a project set up by hand opts in. With `lumiose({ csp: "strict" })`:

- **Pages rendered per request** (`server` routes, `spa` routes that reach the server) get a new
  random nonce for each response. Every inline `<script>` and `<style>` Lumiose writes carries it:
  the page's stylesheets that are inlined and the script after the linked ones (see
  [Styles](styles.md)), the island loader, the
  streamed `<Suspense>` swaps, the speculation rules, the View Transitions opt-in and module
  preloads. The response gets this header:

  ```
  Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-…' 'strict-dynamic'; style-src 'self' 'nonce-…'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'
  ```

  `'strict-dynamic'` lets the scripts the page loads import their own modules (islands, SPA
  routes). Stylesheets from your own origin are allowed; inline styles need the nonce. These
  responses also get `Cache-Control: private, no-store` unless the page sets its own: a nonce is
  only secret while no shared cache hands the same HTML to someone else.

- **Prerendered pages** (`static` routes, the shells of `spa` pages) are files that every visitor
  gets as they are, so a nonce would be the same for everyone. Each one gets the policy as
  `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">`, first in `<head>`, with the SHA-256 hash of each
  inline script and style that Lumiose or your JSX wrote (the same ones that get a nonce per
  request) and `'self'` for scripts and stylesheets of your origin. It works on any static host.
- **`style` props** render as rules of a nonce'd (or hashed) `<style>` that target a `data-l-v`
  attribute, instead of `style="…"` attributes, which a strict policy refuses. In the browser,
  styles are set through the CSSOM, which the policy allows.
- **Your own inline scripts and styles** written in JSX get the nonce automatically: a
  `<script innerHTML={…}>` in the document, a JSON-LD block, an SVG `<style>`. An explicit `nonce`
  prop wins. Strings rendered as text are escaped and never become elements, and raw HTML strings
  (`innerHTML` of another element) never get a nonce, nor a hash on prerendered pages: a script
  injected through such a string is blocked either way.
- **Static `style="…"` strings** (in JSX, and in `.md`/`.html` imports) are applied like `style`
  props: a nonce'd rule on the server, the CSSOM in the browser.
- **`cspNonce()`** returns the response's nonce during a server render (the document included) and
  in middleware, and `undefined` without strict CSP or while prerendering. Use it for markup you
  build yourself: a third-party snippet as a string, a custom `Content-Security-Policy` header, a
  script you create at runtime. In the browser it reads `<meta property="csp-nonce">`.
- **Your own policy wins.** A `Content-Security-Policy` header from `lumiose({ headers })` for the
  path, or one set with `response().setHeader()` or by middleware, replaces Lumiose's; with `headers`,
  the path's prerendered pages get no `<meta>` policy either. `lumiose dev` puts nonces on the page but sends no policy,
  because Vite injects styles of its own for hot updates.

Elements that the client creates later (a `<style>` inside an `<svg>` rendered after a client
navigation) take the nonce from `<meta property="csp-nonce">`. A prerendered page has no nonce,
so such an element is refused there unless it was in the prerendered HTML: put its rules in the
file's `<style>` block.

**Client navigation.** `navigate()` and the redirects of enhanced form actions only
follow `http:` and `https:` URLs (relative ones included); a `javascript:` or `data:` location
throws a `TypeError` instead of running in the page. Spread props drop lowercase `on*` keys
(`{...{ onclick: "…" }}`): an inline handler attribute is a script sink, so handlers are only
functions in `onClick`.

**Unsafe URLs.** A dynamic value for a URL attribute (`href`, `src`, `action`, `formaction`,
`xlink:href`, `poster`, `data`, …) whose scheme is `javascript:`, `vbscript:` or `data:text/html`
renders as `about:blank#blocked`, on the server and in the browser, with a
[LUM4009](../errors/LUM4009.md) warning in development. Case, leading spaces and control
characters, and tabs or newlines inside the scheme do not get past it. String literals in your JSX
are left as written.

**Error details.** In production server rendering, `<ErrorBoundary>` fallbacks receive a generic
error with a short `digest`, and the original error is logged with the same digest
([ErrorBoundary](../reference/components.md#errorboundary)).

**Redirects.** `redirect()` accepts paths and `http(s)` URLs only; a `javascript:` or `data:`
location throws. For a user-supplied target (`?next=`), accept only same-origin paths, or the user
lands wherever a link sends them:

```ts
// A `next` parameter as a path of this site, else the fallback.
function safeNext(next: string | null, fallback = "/"): string {
  if (next === null || !next.startsWith("/") || next.startsWith("//") || next.startsWith("/\\")) {
    return fallback;
  }
  return next;
}
redirect(safeNext(url.searchParams.get("next")));
```

Trailing-slash redirects (`lumiose({ trailingSlash })`) always stay on your site, also for a
request path such as `//evil.com/`. `href()` refuses `.` and `..` as param values, which a browser
would resolve into another route.

**Files from elsewhere.** Icon sets, Markdown and HTML often come from outside the project. The
compiler treats them as untrusted input:

- **SVG imports** keep an allowlist of SVG elements and attributes: no scripts, handlers,
  `<foreignObject>` HTML, `javascript:` URLs or animations of links, and `<style>` text cannot
  open a tag ([SVG imports](svg.md)).
- **`$` constants** in style blocks cannot end their declaration or the `<style>` element
  ([LUM3021](../errors/LUM3021.md)), so data in a constant cannot add CSS outside its scope.
- **Frontmatter** keys such as `__proto__` stay plain data.
- **Depth limits** turn absurdly nested files into errors instead of crashes or stalls: CSS
  blocks past 64 levels and parentheses past 16 ([LUM3014](../errors/LUM3014.md)), SVG elements past 128,
  Markdown and HTML past 512 ([LUM1009](../errors/LUM1009.md)).

**Cross-site form posts.** Form actions and form-encoded posts to endpoints are checked against
the `Origin` header (on by default, `lumiose({ csrf })`); see [Data and actions](data-and-actions.md).

**Request URLs.** `lumiose dev`, `lumiose preview` and `@lumiose/adapter-node` build each request's URL
from the server's origin (`ORIGIN`, else the socket's protocol and the `Host` header) plus the
request target's path, appended as is: a request for `//attacker.test/reset` stays on your origin
with that path, so `ctx.url`, `url()`, the cross-site check and `fetchJSON()`'s same-origin test
never see another host. Targets that are not a path (`http://other/x`, or `*` other than with
`OPTIONS`) and invalid `Host` headers get `400 Bad Request`. Behind a proxy that rewrites the
host, set `ORIGIN` (or the adapter's `origin`) so a client cannot choose the origin through `Host`.

**Request body limits.** Every request body is bounded (decision-29): URL-encoded forms, JSON and
other bodies at 1 MB, `multipart/form-data` (uploads) at 10 MB. A larger request gets `413 Payload
Too Large`, refused before reading when its `Content-Length` says so, else as soon as the bytes
read pass the limit; nothing buffers an unbounded body. The limits hold for form actions
(`ctx.formData()`), endpoints (`request.formData()`, `json()`, `text()`, `arrayBuffer()` read the
bounded body) and middleware alike, in every deployment. Raise or lower them for the app with
`lumiose({ limits: { body: "2mb", upload: "50mb" } })`, and for one route with
`export const limits = { upload: "200mb" }` in its page or endpoint file.

**Default response headers.** `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (no MIME sniffing of uploads and
JSON) and `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (no full URLs to other sites) go on
every response; override them in `lumiose({ headers })`, or remove one with `""`.

**Server-only code** (`*.server.*` files, `src/server/`) never reaches the browser: imports from
client code fail `lumiose dev`/`lumiose build` (`LUM4003`), `lumiose dev` refuses to serve the files
(`server.fs.deny`), and only `import.meta.env.PUBLIC_*` variables reach client code (`envPrefix`).
See [Server](server.md).

**What the page sends.** Island props, values awaited inside islands and the scoped state islands
use (`defineState`) are serialized into the page as plain data (JSON in
`<script type="application/json">`, escaped so it cannot end the element): anyone who loads the
page can read them. Never pass a secret there; keep it in server-only modules.

**Secrets.** `signedCookie()` needs a secret of at least 32 bytes in production
(`LUMIOSE_SECRET`); a shorter one throws when the cookie is used (in development it warns).
`{ allowWeakSecret: true }` opts out.

**Compression.** `@lumiose/adapter-node` compresses responses; for pages that render a secret next
to reflected input, see BREACH in the [adapter reference](../reference/adapter-node.md).

## API

| Option / export                   | Meaning                                                                     |
| --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `lumiose({ csp: "strict" })`      | Nonces per response, the policy header, hash policies for prerendered pages |
| `cspNonce(): string \| undefined` | The response's nonce (from `lumiose`), for markup the app builds itself     |
| `<meta property="csp-nonce">`     | Written by Lumiose with the nonce; the client's preload helper reads it     |

## Example

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import lumiose from "@lumiose/vite";

export default { plugins: [lumiose({ csp: "strict" })] };
```

```tsx
// src/document.tsx: an inline script that runs before the first paint
import type { DocumentProps } from "lumiose";

const THEME = `document.documentElement.dataset.theme = localStorage.getItem("theme") ?? "auto"`;

export default function Document(props: DocumentProps) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <head>
        <meta charset="utf-8" />
        <script innerHTML={THEME} />
        {props.head}
      </head>
      <body>{props.body}</body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

On a server-rendered page Lumiose gives the script the response's nonce; on a prerendered page the
page's policy lists the script's hash.

## Common mistakes

- **An inline script built as a string** (`<div innerHTML={'<script>…</script>'}>`, a snippet
  added at runtime). Lumiose only nonces elements written in JSX: the browser refuses it and logs a
  CSP violation. Write it as a JSX `<script>`, add `nonce={cspNonce()}` to the markup you build,
  or load the code as a module.
- **A `<style>` inside an `<svg>` that only the client renders, on a prerendered page.** No nonce
  exists there. Put the rules in the file's `<style>` block.
- **Expecting the policy in `lumiose dev`.** Dev sends none; check with `lumiose build` and
  `lumiose preview` or your server.
- **Adding `'unsafe-inline'` to make an error go away.** It disables the protection for every
  inline script. Find the element in the console message and give it the nonce instead.

## Related diagnostics

A CSP violation shows in the browser console, with the refused element. For files:
[LUM1009](../errors/LUM1009.md) (content nested too deeply), [LUM3014](../errors/LUM3014.md) (CSS
nested too deeply), [LUM3021](../errors/LUM3021.md) (a `$` constant that would break out of its
value).

See also: [Head and document](head.md), [Styles](styles.md), [Rendering modes](rendering-modes.md), [reference: `@lumiose/vite`](../reference/vite.md), [reference: app APIs](../reference/app.md).

<!-- source: guides/auth.md -->

# Authentication with Better Auth

> Email and password accounts with Better Auth and Prisma: sign-up, sign-in and sign-out, the session in middleware and protected pages.

Lumiose has no auth module of its own: [Better Auth](https://www.better-auth.com) runs on any
server that hands it a web `Request`, and that is what endpoints, middleware and actions have. This
guide stores accounts with [Prisma](https://www.prisma.io) on a SQLite file. Every piece is in the
[ssr-auth sample](https://github.com/itsjavi/lumiose/tree/main/examples/ssr-auth), with an e2e test.

| File                                    | Role                                                                |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `prisma/schema.prisma`                  | Better Auth's tables.                                               |
| `src/server/db.server.ts`               | The Prisma client. Server-only.                                     |
| `src/server/auth.server.ts`             | The Better Auth instance and helpers for pages and actions.         |
| `src/server/client-address.server.ts`   | The client's address for Better Auth's rate limiter.                |
| `src/routes/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts` | Better Auth's HTTP API, for its browser client.                     |
| `src/middleware.ts`                     | The session on `ctx.locals`.                                        |
| `src/routes/sign-in/page.stsx`, …       | Form actions that post to Better Auth's handler, rate-limited.      |
| `src/islands/AccountMenu.stsx`          | An island that reads the session with Better Auth's browser client. |

## Setup

```sh
pnpm add better-auth @prisma/client @prisma/adapter-libsql @libsql/client
pnpm add -D prisma
```

Prisma 7 talks to the database through a driver adapter; `@prisma/adapter-libsql` opens SQLite
files with prebuilt binaries. For Postgres, swap it for `@prisma/adapter-pg` and the schema's
`provider`. pnpm asks whether `prisma` and `@prisma/engines` may run install scripts:
`allowBuilds` set to `false` for both works, since the CLI downloads its schema engine the first
time it needs it (`prisma migrate`).

`prisma.config.ts`, at the project root:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "prisma/config";

export default defineConfig({
  schema: "prisma/schema.prisma",
  migrations: { path: "prisma/migrations" },
  datasource: { url: process.env.DATABASE_URL ?? "file:./data/auth.db" },
});
```

`prisma/schema.prisma` generates the client into `src/server/`, which makes it server-only, then
lists Better Auth's tables (`npx auth generate` writes them from your Better Auth config):

```prisma
generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client"
  output   = "../src/server/generated/prisma"
}

datasource db {
  provider = "sqlite"
}

model User {
  id            String    @id
  name          String
  email         String
  emailVerified Boolean   @default(false)
  image         String?
  createdAt     DateTime  @default(now())
  updatedAt     DateTime  @updatedAt
  sessions      Session[]
  accounts      Account[]

  @@unique([email])
  @@map("user")
}

// Session, Account and Verification: see the sample's schema.
```

Add `src/server/generated/` to `.gitignore`. `prisma generate` reads `tsconfig.json`, which extends
`.lumiose/tsconfig.generated.json`, so run `lumiose typegen` before it in a fresh checkout. The
sample's scripts do:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "lumiose typegen && prisma generate && prisma migrate deploy && lumiose dev",
    "build": "lumiose typegen && prisma generate && lumiose build",
    "typecheck": "lumiose typegen && prisma generate && lumiose check",
    "db:migrate": "prisma migrate deploy"
  }
}
```

Create the first migration with `prisma migrate dev --name init` and commit `prisma/migrations`.

| Variable             | Value                                                                                                                                          |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` | Signs Better Auth's cookies and tokens. A random value of at least 32 bytes (`openssl rand -base64 32`); a dev-only one in `.env.development`. |
| `BETTER_AUTH_URL`    | The public URL (`https://example.com`), in production. Without it Better Auth takes the origin from each request, which suits dev.             |
| `DATABASE_URL`       | `file:./data/auth.db` by default, relative to the working directory.                                                                           |
| `TRUSTED_PROXIES`    | Behind a proxy: its address (`127.0.0.1` for nginx or Caddy on the same machine), so the rate limiter sees each client's address. See below.   |

## Prisma as a server-only module

```ts
// src/server/db.server.ts
import { PrismaLibSql } from "@prisma/adapter-libsql";
import { env } from "lumiose";
import { PrismaClient } from "./generated/prisma/client.ts";

let client: PrismaClient | undefined;

export function prisma(): PrismaClient {
  client ??= new PrismaClient({
    adapter: new PrismaLibSql({ url: env("DATABASE_URL") ?? "file:./data/auth.db" }),
  });
  return client;
}
```

Files under `src/server/` and named `*.server.ts` are server-only: an island or any other module
that reaches the browser and imports them, directly or through another module, fails
`lumiose dev` and `lumiose build` with [LUM4003](../errors/LUM4003.md), and `lumiose check` reports
it. The client is created on first use rather than at import, so `env()` reads the request's
environment: in dev, that includes the `.env` files.

## The Better Auth instance

```ts
// src/server/auth.server.ts
import { betterAuth } from "better-auth";
import { prismaAdapter } from "better-auth/adapters/prisma";
import { env, href, locals, redirect, url, type RequestContext } from "lumiose";
import { forwardedFor, parseTrustedProxies } from "./client-address.server.ts";
import { prisma } from "./db.server.ts";

function createAuth(trustedProxies: string[]) {
  return betterAuth({
    secret: env("BETTER_AUTH_SECRET"),
    baseURL: env("BETTER_AUTH_URL"),
    database: prismaAdapter(prisma(), { provider: "sqlite" }),
    emailAndPassword: { enabled: true },
    // The rate limiter (on in production) keys requests by client address.
    advanced: { ipAddress: { trustedProxies } },
  });
}

let instance: { auth: ReturnType<typeof createAuth>; trustedProxies: string[] } | undefined;

function setup() {
  if (instance === undefined) {
    const trustedProxies = parseTrustedProxies(env("TRUSTED_PROXIES"));
    instance = { auth: createAuth(trustedProxies), trustedProxies };
  }
  return instance;
}

export function auth(): ReturnType<typeof createAuth> {
  return setup().auth;
}

/** `{ user, session }` of a signed-in request. */
export type AuthSession = ReturnType<typeof createAuth>["$Infer"]["Session"];

declare module "lumiose" {
  interface Locals {
    /** Set by src/middleware.ts: the signed-in user and session, or `null`. */
    session: AuthSession | null;
  }
}

/** The session of a page that needs one; without one, redirects to the sign-in page and back. */
export function requireSession(): AuthSession {
  const session = locals().session;
  if (session === null) {
    const { pathname, search } = url();
    redirect(`${href("/sign-in")}?next=${encodeURIComponent(pathname + search)}`);
  }
  return session;
}

/** `next` when it is a path on this site, else `fallback`: never a redirect to another site. */
export function safeNext(next: string | null, fallback: string = href("/dashboard")): string {
  return next !== null && /^\/(?![/\\])/.test(next) ? next : fallback;
}

// authHandler(), authRequest(), authError() and redirectWithCookies(): below.
```

`auth()` creates the instance inside the first request, for the same reason as `prisma()`. It also
keeps Better Auth from starting while static pages prerender, where there is no secret.

### Client addresses for the rate limiter

In production, Better Auth limits requests per client address: 3 sign-in or sign-up attempts per
10 seconds, 100 requests per 10 seconds elsewhere. It reads the address from `X-Forwarded-For`,
which a request handed to it from Lumiose does not carry by itself. The sample sets it from
`ctx.platform.clientAddress`, the address the host saw:

```ts
// src/server/client-address.server.ts
/** `X-Forwarded-For` to hand to Better Auth, or `undefined` when the host knows no address. */
export function forwardedFor(
  headers: Headers,
  clientAddress: string | undefined,
  trustedProxies: readonly string[],
): string | undefined {
  // Without trusted proxies, the client's own X-Forwarded-For is ignored: it could pick any address.
  const chain = trustedProxies.length > 0 ? headers.get("x-forwarded-for") : null;
  const hops = [chain, clientAddress].filter((hop): hop is string => hop != null && hop !== "");
  return hops.length === 0 ? undefined : hops.join(", ");
}
```

```ts
// src/server/auth.server.ts, continued
type AuthContext = Pick<RequestContext, "request" | "url" | "platform">;

function clientHeaders(ctx: AuthContext, headers: Headers): Headers {
  const { trustedProxies } = setup();
  const forwarded = forwardedFor(ctx.request.headers, ctx.platform.clientAddress, trustedProxies);
  if (forwarded === undefined) headers.delete("x-forwarded-for");
  else headers.set("x-forwarded-for", forwarded);
  return headers;
}

/** Better Auth's HTTP API for a request, with the client's address for its rate limiter. */
export function authHandler(ctx: AuthContext): Promise<Response> {
  const headers = clientHeaders(ctx, new Headers(ctx.request.headers));
  return auth().handler(new Request(ctx.request, { headers }));
}
```

Behind a proxy, the address the host sees is the proxy's, and every visitor would share one
bucket. Set `TRUSTED_PROXIES` to the proxy's address (or CIDR range, comma-separated): the
proxy's `X-Forwarded-For` chain is then kept, and Better Auth, given the same list as
`advanced.ipAddress.trustedProxies`, walks it from the right, skips the trusted hops and takes the
client. On Cloudflare, `clientAddress` is already the visitor's (`CF-Connecting-IP`).

## The handler

Better Auth's HTTP API (sessions, sign-in, sign-out and the rest) goes under `/api/auth/*`, where its
browser client calls it. A catch-all endpoint passes the request through, with the client's
address:

```ts
// src/routes/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts
import type { Endpoint } from "lumiose";
import { authHandler } from "../../../../server/auth.server.ts";

export const GET: Endpoint<"/api/auth/[...all]"> = (ctx) => authHandler(ctx);
export const POST: Endpoint<"/api/auth/[...all]"> = (ctx) => authHandler(ctx);
```

The client posts JSON, which Lumiose's cross-site check leaves to the endpoint; Better Auth checks
the `Origin` of those requests against `BETTER_AUTH_URL` (`403` otherwise).

## The session in middleware

```ts
// src/middleware.ts
import { getSessionCookie } from "better-auth/cookies";
import type { Middleware } from "lumiose";
import { auth } from "./server/auth.server.ts";

const middleware: Middleware = async (ctx, next) => {
  ctx.locals.session = null;
  // Without a session cookie the visitor is signed out: no database query. (This is also the case
  // while prerendering.) Better Auth's own routes read the session themselves.
  if (getSessionCookie(ctx.request) === null || ctx.url.pathname.startsWith("/api/auth/")) {
    return next();
  }
  const { response: session, headers } = await auth().api.getSession({
    headers: ctx.request.headers,
    returnHeaders: true,
  });
  ctx.locals.session = session;
  const response = await next();
  // Better Auth extends a session that passed its update age: send the renewed cookie along.
  const cookies = headers.getSetCookie();
  if (cookies.length === 0) return response;
  const renewed = new Response(response.body, response);
  for (const cookie of cookies) renewed.headers.append("set-cookie", cookie);
  return renewed;
};

export default middleware;
```

Every page, endpoint and action then reads `ctx.locals.session` (`locals().session` in a component).
`getSessionCookie()` only checks that the cookie is there; `getSession()` verifies it against the
database.

## Protected pages

```stsx
// src/routes/dashboard/page.stsx
import { href, response, Title } from "lumiose";
import { requireSession } from "../../server/auth.server.ts";

export default function Dashboard() {
  const { user, session } = requireSession();
  response().setHeader("cache-control", "private, no-store");
  return (
    <main>
      <Title>Dashboard</Title>
      <p>
        Signed in as <strong>{user.name}</strong> ({user.email}).
      </p>
      <p>Your session lasts until {session.expiresAt.toISOString().slice(0, 10)}.</p>
      <form method="post" action={href("/sign-out")}>
        <button>Sign out</button>
      </form>
    </main>
  );
}
```

A visitor without a session gets a `302` to `/sign-in?next=%2Fdashboard`, and signing in brings them
back. Protected pages render per request (`mode = "server"`, the sample's default): a `static` page
cannot read the session ([LUM5001](../errors/LUM5001.md)). To guard a whole section instead, with
its form actions and endpoints, add a `middleware.ts` to its folder that returns a redirect when
`ctx.locals.session` is `null`: it runs after `src/middleware.ts` for every route below the folder
([Server](../concepts/server.md#concept)).

## Forms: sign-up, sign-in and sign-out

The forms post to page actions, so they work without JavaScript, and Lumiose's cross-site check
guards them like any form action. Sign-in and sign-up go on to Better Auth's HTTP handler, as its
browser client would, so its rate limiter counts every attempt: it runs on HTTP requests only,
and calls through `auth.api.signInEmail()` would skip it, leaving passwords open to guessing.

```ts
// src/server/auth.server.ts, continued
/** Posts `body` to a Better Auth endpoint (`/sign-in/email`) through its HTTP handler. */
export function authRequest(
  ctx: AuthContext,
  path: `/${string}`,
  body: unknown,
): Promise<Response> {
  const headers = new Headers({ "content-type": "application/json" });
  for (const name of ["cookie", "origin", "referer", "user-agent"]) {
    const value = ctx.request.headers.get(name);
    if (value !== null) headers.set(name, value);
  }
  const request = new Request(new URL(`/api/auth${path}`, ctx.url), {
    method: "POST",
    headers: clientHeaders(ctx, headers),
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });
  return auth().handler(request);
}

/** The message of a failed Better Auth response: "Invalid email or password", "Too many requests…". */
export async function authError(response: Response): Promise<string> {
  const body = (await response.json().catch(() => null)) as { message?: unknown } | null;
  return typeof body?.message === "string" ? body.message : response.statusText;
}

/** A 303 redirect that sets the cookies of a Better Auth response. */
export function redirectWithCookies(location: string, headers: Headers): Response {
  const response = new Response(null, { status: 303, headers: { location } });
  for (const cookie of headers.getSetCookie()) response.headers.append("set-cookie", cookie);
  return response;
}
```

```stsx
// src/routes/sign-in/page.stsx
import { actionData, fail, Title, type ActionContext, type ActionData } from "lumiose";
import { authError, authRequest, redirectWithCookies, safeNext } from "../../server/auth.server.ts";

export const action = async (ctx: ActionContext<"/sign-in">) => {
  const form = await ctx.formData();
  const email = String(form.get("email") ?? "").trim();
  const password = String(form.get("password") ?? "");
  const response = await authRequest(ctx, "/sign-in/email", { email, password });
  // A wrong password (401) or too many attempts (429): Better Auth's message.
  if (!response.ok) return fail(response.status, { email, message: await authError(response) });
  return redirectWithCookies(safeNext(ctx.url.searchParams.get("next")), response.headers);
};

export default function SignIn() {
  return <SignInForm failed={actionData<typeof action>()} />;
}

function SignInForm(props: { failed: ActionData<typeof action> | undefined }) {
  return (
    <main>
      <Title>Sign in</Title>
      {/* No action attribute: the form posts to this URL, `?next=` included. */}
      <form method="post">
        <input type="email" name="email" value={props.failed?.email ?? ""} required />
        <input type="password" name="password" required />
        <p role="alert">{props.failed?.message}</p>
        <button>Sign in</button>
      </form>
    </main>
  );
}
```

- **Cookies.** Better Auth's response sets the session cookie; the action returns a redirect that
  carries its `Set-Cookie` lines. A plain `redirect()` would drop them, and the visitor would not be
  signed in.
- **Errors.** A wrong password (`401`), a taken email (`422`), a short password (`400`) or too many
  attempts (`429`, "Too many requests. Please try again later.") come back as a status and a
  message, which `fail()` shows on the page.
- **Sign-up** is the same with `authRequest(ctx, "/sign-up/email", { name, email, password })`,
  which signs the new user in.
- **Sign-out** needs no limit, so its action calls the server API, on `/sign-out` so that a form on
  any page can post to it:

```ts
export const action = async (ctx: ActionContext<"/sign-out">) => {
  if (ctx.locals.session === null) return redirectWithCookies(href("/"), new Headers());
  const { headers } = await auth().api.signOut({
    headers: ctx.request.headers,
    returnHeaders: true,
  });
  return redirectWithCookies(href("/"), headers); // the headers clear the cookies
};
```

## Better Auth's client in an island

A prerendered page cannot know who is signed in, and an island can find out in the browser. Better
Auth's browser client has no server imports, so islands can use it:

```ts
// src/lib/auth-client.ts
import { createAuthClient } from "better-auth/client";

export const authClient = createAuthClient(); // calls /api/auth/* on the page's origin
```

```stsx
// src/islands/AccountMenu.stsx (shortened), used as <AccountMenu client:load /> in the layout
import { href, onMount, signal } from "lumiose";
import { authClient } from "../lib/auth-client.ts";

export function AccountMenu() {
  // `undefined` until the session has loaded: no links that may be wrong.
  const account = signal<{ name: string } | null | undefined>(undefined);

  onMount(() =>
    // Called at once with the current value; the returned unsubscribe runs on unmount.
    authClient.useSession.subscribe(({ data, isPending }) => {
      if (!isPending) account.set(data === null ? null : { name: data.user.name });
    }),
  );

  async function signOut() {
    await authClient.signOut();
    location.assign(href("/"));
  }

  return (
    <div class="account">
      {account() === null ? <a href={href("/sign-in")}>Sign in</a> : null}
      {account() ? (
        <button type="button" onClick={signOut}>
          Sign out {account()?.name}
        </button>
      ) : null}
    </div>
  );
}
```

`authClient.useSession` is a nanostores atom: `subscribe` fetches the session and calls back on every
change (after `authClient.signOut()` too), and `onMount` runs only in the browser and disposes the
subscription with the island. Server-rendered pages can pass what they already know as props
instead: `locals().session` is there during their render. With the client, the sample's island
chunk is about 11 kB (brotli); an island that only needs the session can fetch
`/api/auth/get-session` with `fetchJSON` instead.

## Production

- Set `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`, `BETTER_AUTH_URL` (the public `https://` URL: Better Auth then marks its
  cookies `Secure`) and `DATABASE_URL`, plus `ORIGIN` behind a proxy ([Deploy](../deploy/README.md)).
- Apply migrations before starting the new build: `prisma migrate deploy` (the `prisma` CLI is a dev
  dependency, so run it where those are installed, such as CI or a release step).
- Behind a proxy, set `TRUSTED_PROXIES` to its address, or the rate limiter puts every visitor in
  the proxy's bucket. The limiter is off in development (`lumiose dev`).
- **Several instances.** The rate limiter keeps its counts in memory by default, per process: with
  several instances (a cluster, replicas behind a load balancer, serverless functions), each one
  counts on its own, and an attacker gets that many more attempts. Store them where every
  instance sees them, with Better Auth's `rateLimit: { storage: "database" }` (a `rateLimit` table:
  run `npx auth generate` and migrate) or `"secondary-storage"` (Redis or another store, through
  Better Auth's `secondaryStorage` option).

## Common mistakes

- **Importing `auth.server.ts` or the Prisma client into an island.** `LUM4003`. Islands use the
  browser client, or call an endpoint.
- **Calling `betterAuth()` at module scope with `env()` values.** In dev, `.env` values reach
  `env()` only inside a request, and a static page's prerender would start Better Auth without a
  secret. Create it on first use, as `auth()` does.
- **Signing in with `auth.api.signInEmail()` in the action.** It works, but Better Auth's rate
  limiter never sees the attempt. Post to its handler, as `authRequest()` does.
- **Redirecting with `redirect()` after sign-in.** The session cookie is in Better Auth's response
  headers; return a `Response` that sets them.
- **Reading the session in a `static` page.** `locals()` throws `LUM5001` while prerendering; render
  the page per request, or read the session in an island.
- **`prisma generate` failing on a fresh checkout** with "File './.lumiose/tsconfig.generated.json'
  not found". Run `lumiose typegen` first.

See also: [Server](../concepts/server.md), [Data and actions](../concepts/data-and-actions.md),
[Islands](../concepts/islands.md), [Security](../concepts/security.md).

<!-- source: guides/icons.md -->

# Icons with Lucide

> Use Lucide, or any SVG icon set, as inline components compiled at build time, sized and coloured with CSS.

[Lucide](https://lucide.dev) publishes every icon as an SVG file in the
[`lucide-static`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/lucide-static) package. Import a file with
`?component` and it becomes a Lumiose component, the same as an `.svg` file of your own (see
[SVG imports](../concepts/svg.md)): the build optimises and sanitises it, and the icon renders as
inline markup on the server, in the browser and in islands. Only the icons you import end up in
the build.

## Install

```sh
pnpm add -D lucide-static
```

A dev dependency is enough: the build inlines each imported icon, so neither the client nor the
server build loads `lucide-static` at runtime.

## Use an icon

The file name is the icon's name on lucide.dev, in kebab case: `icons/<name>.svg`.

```tsx
// src/components/Nav.stsx
import House from "lucide-static/icons/house.svg?component";
import Search from "lucide-static/icons/search.svg?component";

export function Nav() {
  return (
    <nav>
      <a href="/" class="link">
        <House class="icon" /> Home
      </a>
      <button type="button" class="link">
        <Search class="icon" title="Search" />
      </button>
    </nav>
  );
}

<style>
  .link { color: rebeccapurple; }
  .icon { width: 1.25em; height: 1.25em; stroke-width: 1.5; }
</style>
```

`lumiose/env` types every `*.svg?component` import, from packages too: the props are those of
`<svg>`, plus `title`.

## Size, colour and stroke

Lucide's files are 24 × 24, drawn with `stroke="currentColor"` and `stroke-width="2"` on the root
`<svg>`. Every one of these is a default that CSS or a prop replaces:

- **Size.** Set `width` and `height` in CSS, as `.icon` does above, or pass both props
  (`width={20} height={20}`). Sizing in `em` makes an icon follow the text around it.
- **Colour.** The stroke is `currentColor`, so the icon takes the `color` of its parent: the
  link's `rebeccapurple` above, and any `:hover` colour you give the link.
- **Stroke.** `stroke-width` in CSS or as a prop (`stroke-width={1.5}`). The paths inherit it from
  the root.

`class="icon"` receives the component's scope, so the scoped `.icon` rule applies to the icon's
root `<svg>`.

## Labels

An icon without `title`, `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` is decorative and gets
`aria-hidden="true"`, which is right next to visible text (the "Home" link). An icon-only control
needs a name: `title="Search"` on the icon gives it a `<title>` with `role="img"`, or label the
control itself with `<button aria-label="Search">` and keep the icon decorative.

## Other icon sets

Any package that ships its icons as SVG files works the same way: import the file's path with
`?component`. Monochrome sets drawn with `currentColor` follow `color` as Lucide does. For a set
whose files hard-code a colour (`fill="#000"`), set `lumiose({ svg: { currentColor: true } })` in
`vite.config.ts`, which replaces every colour in `?component` imports with `currentColor`.

## Why not lucide-react or lucide

- **`lucide-react`** (and the other framework packages) export React components. Lumiose's JSX is
  not React's, so they do not render in Lumiose.
- **`lucide`**, the vanilla package, builds the icons in the browser at runtime from JavaScript
  icon data. A `?component` import does that work at build time instead: the server renders the
  icon, and the client ships no icon code beyond the markup it clones.

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting `?component`.** `import House from "lucide-static/icons/house.svg"` is Vite's URL
  string, so `<House />` is a type error. Add `?component`.
- **Styling Lucide's classes.** The files carry `class="lucide lucide-house"`, which a `class` prop
  replaces. Style your own class, as `.icon` above, rather than `.lucide`.
- **Setting only `width`.** The file's `height` of 24 stays and the drawing is centred in that box.
  Set both, in CSS or as props.
- **Labelling an icon next to its text.** A `title` there makes screen readers say the label
  twice. Leave such icons decorative.

See also: [SVG imports](../concepts/svg.md), [Styles](../concepts/styles.md), [Islands](../concepts/islands.md).

<!-- source: guides/i18n.md -->

# i18n with Paraglide JS and i18next

> Translate a site with Paraglide JS or i18next, in server pages and islands, with a language switcher and links search engines understand.

Lumiose routes locales ([Internationalization](../concepts/i18n.md)): it reads the URL prefix,
declares which pages exist in which locale, builds localized links and writes `<html lang>`,
`hreflang` and canonical links. It does not translate or format anything: messages, plurals,
numbers and dates belong to a library. This guide builds the same small site (a bakery in English,
Spanish and French) with the two most used ones:

- **[Paraglide JS](https://paraglidejs.com)** compiles messages into one function per message.
  Pages and islands import the functions they call, so an island's chunk holds only its own
  messages, and keys and parameters are type-checked.
- **[i18next](https://www.i18next.com)** looks keys up in JSON resources at runtime, with
  namespaces, plurals and `Intl` formatting, and a large ecosystem of tools.

Each is a sample with an e2e test on the production build:
[ssr-i18n-paraglide](https://github.com/itsjavi/lumiose/tree/main/examples/ssr-i18n-paraglide) and
[ssr-i18n-i18next](https://github.com/itsjavi/lumiose/tree/main/examples/ssr-i18n-i18next).

| File                              | Role                                                                    |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `vite.config.ts`                  | `lumiose({ i18n, site })`, plus Paraglide's Vite plugin.                |
| `src/routes/page.stsx`            | The home page, in every locale.                                         |
| `src/routes/about/page.stsx`      | A page in English and Spanish only, prerendered per locale.             |
| `src/routes/layout.stsx`          | Navigation and the language switcher, in the page's locale.             |
| `src/routes/not-found.stsx`       | The 404 page, in the locale of the URL.                                 |
| `src/islands/LocaleSwitcher.stsx` | Links to the page in each of its locales; updates the detection cookie. |
| `src/islands/Basket.stsx`         | An island with messages: a plural that changes on click.                |
| `src/lib/i18n.ts`                 | The library's setup, shared by pages and islands.                       |
| `src/server/i18n.server.ts`       | i18next's server instance (i18next sample). Server-only.                |

## The site

The routing is the same with both libraries:

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import lumiose from "@lumiose/vite";

export default {
  plugins: [
    lumiose({
      mode: "server",
      i18n: {
        locales: ["en", "es", "fr"],
        defaultLocale: "en",
        missing: "404", // the i18next sample uses "redirect"
        detect: { cookie: "locale", acceptLanguage: true },
      },
      site: "https://bakery.example",
    }),
  ],
};
```

The home page exists in every locale (`export const locales = "all"`) and renders per request, so
detection can send a Spanish browser from `/` to `/es`. `/about` is translated into English and
Spanish only, and prerendered:

```stsx
// src/routes/about/page.stsx
export const mode = "static";
export const locales = ["en", "es"];
```

So `/es/about` exists, and `/fr/about` is a 404 (or, with `missing: "redirect"`, a redirect to
`/about`). A page without `locales` exists only in English. Translations are a per-page decision,
not a site-wide switch.

### The language switcher

`alternates()` lists the current page in each locale it declares, and the switcher links to them,
named in their own language. It is an island because a click also updates the cookie that detection
reads: without that, a visitor who switched from Spanish to French would land on Spanish again on
their next visit to `/`. The layout renders it with the alternates as a prop (`alternates()` reads the
request, so it only runs on the server):

```stsx
// src/routes/layout.stsx (shortened, Paraglide sample)
<LocaleSwitcher client:load label={m.nav_language()} alternates={alternates()} />
```

```stsx
// src/islands/LocaleSwitcher.stsx
import type { Locale } from "lumiose";
import { Link } from "lumiose/router";

const NAMES: Record<Locale, string> = { en: "English", es: "Español", fr: "Français" };

export function LocaleSwitcher(props: {
  label: string;
  alternates: Array<{ locale: Locale; href: string }>;
}) {
  return (
    <nav class="locales" aria-label={props.label}>
      {props.alternates.map((alternate) => (
        <Link
          href={alternate.href}
          hreflang={alternate.locale}
          lang={alternate.locale}
          onClick={() => rememberLocale(alternate.locale)}
        >
          {NAMES[alternate.locale]}
        </Link>
      ))}
    </nav>
  );
}

/** The cookie of `detect: { cookie: "locale" }`, with the attributes Lumiose uses. */
function rememberLocale(next: Locale) {
  const secure = location.protocol === "https:" ? "; secure" : "";
  document.cookie = `locale=${next}; path=/; max-age=31536000; samesite=lax${secure}`;
}
```

- **Only declared locales.** On `/about` the switcher shows English and Español; there is no
  French link to a page that does not exist.
- **`<Link>`** marks the current locale's link with `aria-current="page"`. The links prefetch like
  any other: with detection on, Lumiose never prefetches `/`, whose answer depends on the cookie
  this click changes ([Internationalization](../concepts/i18n.md)).
- **Without JavaScript** the links still work; only the cookie is not updated. To update it on the
  server instead, make each locale a button of a form that posts to an action, which sets the
  cookie with `cookies().set()` (path `/`, a year) and redirects to the alternate's URL.

### Links to pages that are not translated

`href("/about")` keeps the current locale, so on a French page it is `/fr/about`, which does not
exist. `alternates("/about")` lists the locales the page declares, `[{ locale, href }]`, so link it
in the current locale when it has one, else in another:

```ts
// src/routes/layout.stsx: /about in the current locale when it is translated, else in English.
function aboutHref(): string {
  const translated = alternates("/about").find((each) => each.locale === locale());
  return translated?.href ?? href("/about", { locale: "en" });
}
```

A route with params takes them like `href()`: `alternates("/blog/[slug]", { slug })`. A route whose
locales come from a `locales({ params })` function throws there, since rendering cannot wait for
it: build those links from the translations your content lists.

## Paraglide JS

### Setup

```sh
pnpm add -D @inlang/paraglide-js @inlang/plugin-message-format
```

Paraglide compiles an inlang project: `project.inlang/settings.json` lists the locales and the
plugin that reads the message files. `npx @inlang/paraglide-js init` writes it with the plugin's
CDN URL, which the compiler downloads on every build; the samples load it from `node_modules`
instead, so builds need no network and the version is in the lockfile:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://inlang.com/schema/project-settings",
  "baseLocale": "en",
  "locales": ["en", "es", "fr"],
  "modules": ["./node_modules/@inlang/plugin-message-format/dist/index.js"],
  "plugin.inlang.messageFormat": {
    "pathPattern": "./messages/{locale}.json"
  }
}
```

The locales are the ones in `lumiose({ i18n })`, with the default locale as `baseLocale`. Messages
are one JSON file per locale, with `{placeholders}`, and declarations for plurals and formatting:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://inlang.com/schema/inlang-message-format",
  "home_title": "Fresh bread every morning",
  "home_price": [
    {
      "declarations": [
        "input price",
        "local formattedPrice = price: number style=currency currency=EUR"
      ],
      "match": { "price=*": "A croissant costs {formattedPrice}." }
    }
  ],
  "basket_count": [
    {
      "declarations": ["input count", "local countPlural = count: plural"],
      "selectors": ["countPlural"],
      "match": {
        "countPlural=one": "{count} croissant in your basket",
        "countPlural=other": "{count} croissants in your basket"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

The Vite plugin compiles them into `src/paraglide/` when `lumiose dev` and `lumiose build` start,
and again when a message file changes. Add `src/paraglide/` to `.gitignore`:

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { paraglideVitePlugin } from "@inlang/paraglide-js";
import lumiose from "@lumiose/vite";

export default {
  plugins: [
    paraglideVitePlugin({
      project: "./project.inlang",
      outdir: "./src/paraglide",
      emitTsDeclarations: true,
    }),
    lumiose({
      mode: "server",
      i18n: {
        locales: ["en", "es", "fr"],
        defaultLocale: "en",
        missing: "404",
        detect: { cookie: "locale", acceptLanguage: true },
      },
      site: "https://bakery.example",
    }),
  ],
};
```

`lumiose check` does not run Vite plugins, so a fresh checkout compiles the messages first:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "typecheck": "paraglide-js compile --project ./project.inlang --outdir ./src/paraglide --emit-ts-declarations --silent && lumiose check"
  }
}
```

### The locale

Every message function reads the locale from the runtime's `getLocale()`. Point it at Lumiose's
`locale()`, in the one module that pages and islands import messages from:

```ts
// src/lib/i18n.ts
import { locale } from "lumiose/router";
import { overwriteGetLocale } from "../paraglide/runtime.js";

overwriteGetLocale(() => locale());

export { m } from "../paraglide/messages.js";
```

`locale()` from `lumiose/router` is the request's locale on the server, read from the request's
async context, so concurrent requests in different locales never mix, and prerendering renders
each locale with its own. In the browser it is the page's locale (reactive in `spa` routes). Leave
the rest of Paraglide's locale handling unused: Lumiose already routes the prefix, detects on entry
and writes `<html lang>`, so Paraglide's `url` strategy, `paraglideMiddleware()`,
`localizeHref()` and `setLocale()` would do the same work a second time, with their own cookie.

### Messages in pages

```stsx
// src/routes/page.stsx
import { Title } from "lumiose";
import { Basket } from "../islands/Basket.stsx";
import { m } from "../lib/i18n.ts";

export const locales = "all";

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <main>
      <Title>{m.site_name()}</Title>
      <h1>{m.home_title()}</h1>
      <p>{m.home_price({ price: 1.2 })}</p>
      <Basket client:visible />
    </main>
  );
}
```

`m.home_price({ price: 1.2 })` is "A croissant costs €1.20." on `/` and "Un croissant coûte
1,20 €." on `/fr`: Paraglide formats with `Intl` for the locale. A message missing in a locale falls
back to the base locale's. The `not-found` page uses the same calls, so `/fr/about` says "Page
introuvable".

### Messages in islands

Islands import the same functions:

```stsx
// src/islands/Basket.stsx
import { signal } from "lumiose";
import { m } from "../lib/i18n.ts";

export function Basket() {
  const count = signal(0);
  return (
    <div class="basket">
      <p aria-live="polite">{m.basket_count({ count: count() })}</p>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => count.update((n) => n + 1)}>
        {m.basket_add()}
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

The island renders on the server in the request's locale and runs again in the browser in the
page's locale, so hydration finds the same text. Its chunk holds the two messages it calls, in the
three locales, and none of the others: 1.8 kB with brotli in the sample, Paraglide's runtime
included.

## i18next

### Setup

```sh
pnpm add i18next
```

The sample keeps one JSON file per locale and namespace: `site` for the pages, `basket` for the
island.

`src/locales/en/basket.json`:

```json
{
  "add": "Add a croissant",
  "count_one": "{{count}} croissant in your basket",
  "count_other": "{{count}} croissants in your basket"
}
```

`src/locales/en/site.json` (shortened):

```json
{
  "name": "Sunrise Bakery",
  "home": {
    "title": "Fresh bread every morning",
    "price": "A croissant costs {{price, currency(EUR)}}."
  }
}
```

The options and the key types live in a module that the server and islands share:

```ts
// src/lib/i18n.ts
import i18next, { type TFunction } from "i18next";
import type basket from "../locales/en/basket.json";
import type site from "../locales/en/site.json";

export interface Namespaces {
  site: typeof site;
  basket: typeof basket;
}

declare module "i18next" {
  interface CustomTypeOptions {
    defaultNS: "site";
    resources: Namespaces;
  }
}

export const options = {
  fallbackLng: "en",
  // Synchronous init: resources are inline, so `t` works right after init().
  initAsync: false,
  // Lumiose escapes text when it renders it; escaping values here too would show `&amp;`.
  interpolation: { escapeValue: false },
} as const;
```

With `CustomTypeOptions`, `lumiose check` reports a key that does not exist (`t("home.titel")`)
and suggests the right one.

### A `t` per request

The server has one instance with every locale's resources, created once and never switched to a
language. Each request asks for a `t` fixed to its locale:

```ts
// src/server/i18n.server.ts
import i18next, { type TFunction } from "i18next";
import { locale } from "lumiose";
import { options, type Namespaces } from "../lib/i18n.ts";
import enBasket from "../locales/en/basket.json" with { type: "json" };
import enSite from "../locales/en/site.json" with { type: "json" };
// … es and fr

const i18n = i18next.createInstance({
  ...options,
  supportedLngs: ["en", "es", "fr"],
  ns: ["site", "basket"],
  defaultNS: "site",
  resources: {
    en: { site: enSite, basket: enBasket },
    es: { site: esSite, basket: esBasket },
    fr: { site: frSite, basket: frBasket },
  },
});
void i18n.init();

/** `t` in the request's locale. */
export function getT(): TFunction<"site"> {
  return i18n.getFixedT(locale());
}

/** One namespace in the request's locale, for an island's props. */
export function messages<NS extends keyof Namespaces>(ns: NS): Namespaces[NS] {
  return i18n.getResourceBundle(locale(), ns) as Namespaces[NS];
}
```

`getFixedT()` returns a function bound to a language without changing the instance, so two
requests in different locales can render at the same time. `i18n.changeLanguage()` per request
would not be safe: the instance is shared, and a request that awaits would continue in the language
of whichever request changed it last. The module is server-only (`*.server.ts`): islands cannot
import it ([LUM4003](../errors/LUM4003.md)), and the browser never downloads every locale. In a
component, take a `t` and use it:

```stsx
// src/routes/page.stsx
import { Title } from "lumiose";
import { Basket } from "../islands/Basket.stsx";
import { getT, messages } from "../server/i18n.server.ts";

export const locales = "all";

export default function Home() {
  const t = getT();
  return (
    <main>
      <Title>{t("name")}</Title>
      <h1>{t("home.title")}</h1>
      <p>{t("home.price", { price: 1.2 })}</p>
      <Basket client:visible messages={messages("basket")} />
    </main>
  );
}
```

`getT()` also works in middleware, actions and endpoints, which run in the request too
(`locale()` is `ctx.locale` there).

### Islands receive their resources

An island gets the namespace it needs, in the page's locale, as a prop (serialized into the page),
and creates a small instance from it:

```ts
// src/lib/i18n.ts (continued)
export function islandT<NS extends keyof Namespaces>(
  locale: string,
  ns: NS,
  messages: Namespaces[NS],
): TFunction<NS> {
  const instance = i18next.createInstance({
    ...options,
    lng: locale,
    ns: [ns],
    defaultNS: ns,
    resources: { [locale]: { [ns]: messages } },
  });
  void instance.init();
  return instance.getFixedT(locale, ns);
}
```

```stsx
// src/islands/Basket.stsx
import { signal } from "lumiose";
import { locale } from "lumiose/router";
import { islandT, type Namespaces } from "../lib/i18n.ts";

export function Basket(props: { messages: Namespaces["basket"] }) {
  const t = islandT(locale(), "basket", props.messages);
  const count = signal(0);
  return (
    <div class="basket">
      <p aria-live="polite">{t("count", { count: count() })}</p>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => count.update((n) => n + 1)}>
        {t("add")}
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

The component runs once per island, so the instance is created once. The island's chunk carries
i18next itself, about 12.5 kB with brotli in the sample, and no translations: those arrive as props,
only the namespace this island uses and only in the page's locale.

## Search engines

- **`hreflang` and canonical links** come from the locales a page declares: `/es/about` links to
  `/about` and itself, and not to a French page that does not exist. Each locale is canonical for
  itself. A `<link rel="canonical">` the page renders with `<Head>` replaces Lumiose's.
- **Absolute URLs.** Pages rendered per request use the request's origin (set `ORIGIN` behind a
  proxy, see [Deploy](../deploy/README.md)); prerendered pages use `lumiose({ site })`. Without
  `site`, a prerendered page's links are root-relative, which search engines ignore, and
  `lumiose build` warns.
- **Translate the head too.** `<Title>` and `<Meta name="description">` take messages like any
  text. `<html lang>` follows the URL's locale.
- **Translating some pages.** Declare `locales` per page or per layout. Choose `missing: "404"`
  when an untranslated URL should not exist, or `"redirect"` when visitors who guess or keep an old
  URL should land on the default locale's page; neither serves an untranslated duplicate.
- **Detection** only redirects on `/` and first visits, with `Vary: Cookie, Accept-Language` and
  `Cache-Control: private, no-store`. Crawlers keep no cookies and usually send no
  `Accept-Language`, so they get each URL in its own locale and follow the `hreflang` links.
  Prerendered pages are files and never redirect.

## Testing

Playwright's `locale` option sets the browser's `Accept-Language`, and the context's cookies show
the detection cookie:

```ts
test.describe("a first visit from a Spanish browser", () => {
  test.use({ locale: "es-ES" });

  test("is redirected from / to /es", async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto("/");
    await expect(page).toHaveURL("/es");
    const cookies = await page.context().cookies();
    expect(cookies.find((cookie) => cookie.name === "locale")?.value).toBe("es");
  });
});
```

The samples' tests also check `<html lang>`, the `hreflang` and canonical URLs, the 404 or redirect
of `/fr/about`, the switcher and its cookie, and the island's plural after a click.

## Common mistakes

- **Changing a shared instance's language per request** (`i18next.changeLanguage()`, Paraglide's
  `setLocale()` on the server). Concurrent requests overwrite each other's locale. Use
  `getFixedT(locale())`, and `overwriteGetLocale(() => locale())` for Paraglide.
- **Paraglide's own routing next to Lumiose's** (`url` strategy, `paraglideMiddleware()`,
  `localizeHref()`). Lumiose already does it; `href()` and `alternates()` build the links.
- **`escapeValue: true` (i18next's default).** Lumiose escapes text, so an interpolated `&` would
  show as `&amp;`.
- **Importing `m` from `src/paraglide/messages.js` directly.** An island whose chunk never loads
  `src/lib/i18n.ts` keeps Paraglide's own `getLocale()`, which knows nothing of the URL's locale.
  Import messages from the module that calls `overwriteGetLocale()`.
- **All locales in an island.** Importing every resource file into client code ships every
  translation. Pass the namespace in the page's locale as a prop, or let Paraglide tree-shake.
- **A switcher that does not update the detection cookie**: the next visit to `/` goes back to the
  old locale.
- **Linking an untranslated page in the current locale.** `href("/about")` on a French page is
  `/fr/about`, a 404; pick a locale from `alternates("/about")`.
- **Hard-coded prefixes** (`"/es" + path`). They break for the default locale, which has none, and
  below a `base`; use `href(pattern, { locale })`.

See also: [Internationalization](../concepts/i18n.md), [Islands](../concepts/islands.md),
[Head and document](../concepts/head.md), [`lumiose/router`](../reference/router.md).

<!-- source: guides/realtime.md -->

# Realtime: server-sent events and WebSockets

> Push live updates to the browser with server-sent events or WebSockets, with proxy configs and notes per platform.

**Server-sent events** (SSE) are a streamed `GET` response: the server pushes, the browser's
`EventSource` reads and reconnects by itself, and they pass through proxies and CDNs as plain HTTP.
Use them when updates flow from the server to the page (feeds, notifications, progress).
**WebSockets** carry messages both ways, and need a server that keeps connections open:
`@lumiose/adapter-node` on a VPS, in Docker or on Coolify.

Both are in the [ssr-realtime sample](https://github.com/itsjavi/lumiose/tree/main/examples/ssr-realtime),
with unit and e2e tests.

## Server-sent events

### The stream

An endpoint returns a `Response` whose body is a `ReadableStream` in the `text/event-stream` format.
This helper writes the events, sends a comment every 15 s so proxies keep an idle connection open,
and runs a cleanup exactly once when the stream ends:

```ts
// src/server/event-stream.server.ts
export type Send = (event: string, data: unknown, id?: string | number) => void;

export function eventStream(
  request: Request,
  start: (send: Send, close: () => void) => () => void,
  options: { keepAliveMs?: number; retryMs?: number } = {},
): Response {
  const encoder = new TextEncoder();
  let stopped = false;
  let cleanup: (() => void) | undefined;
  let keepAlive: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | undefined;
  let controller!: ReadableStreamDefaultController<Uint8Array>;

  const write = (text: string) => {
    if (!stopped) controller.enqueue(encoder.encode(text));
  };
  const stop = () => {
    if (stopped) return;
    stopped = true;
    clearInterval(keepAlive);
    request.signal.removeEventListener("abort", onAbort);
    cleanup?.();
  };
  const close = () => {
    if (stopped) return;
    stop();
    controller.close();
  };
  const onAbort = () => close();

  const body = new ReadableStream<Uint8Array>({
    start(streamController) {
      controller = streamController;
      write(`retry: ${options.retryMs ?? 3000}\n\n`); // the browser's reconnection delay
      keepAlive = setInterval(() => write(": keep-alive\n\n"), options.keepAliveMs ?? 15_000);
      const send: Send = (event, data, id) => {
        const lines = [`event: ${event}`];
        if (id !== undefined) lines.push(`id: ${id}`);
        lines.push(`data: ${JSON.stringify(data)}`); // JSON has no raw newlines: one data line
        write(`${lines.join("\n")}\n\n`);
      };
      cleanup = start(send, close);
      if (stopped) cleanup(); // closed by `start` itself
      else if (request.signal.aborted) close();
      else request.signal.addEventListener("abort", onAbort, { once: true });
    },
    cancel() {
      stop();
    },
  });

  return new Response(body, {
    headers: { "content-type": "text/event-stream; charset=utf-8", "cache-control": "no-cache" },
  });
}
```

**Disconnects.** When the browser closes the connection (the tab closes, `EventSource.close()`),
the adapter aborts `request.signal` and cancels the body; either one runs the cleanup. Without
it, a closed tab would leave its subscription, timers and database listeners behind for good.

### The endpoint

```ts
// src/routes/api/events/route.ts
import type { Endpoint } from "lumiose";
import { subscribe } from "../../../server/bus.server.ts";
import { eventStream } from "../../../server/event-stream.server.ts";

export const mode = "server";

export const GET: Endpoint<"/api/events"> = ({ request }) =>
  eventStream(request, (send) =>
    // The unsubscribe is the stream's cleanup: it runs when the client goes away.
    subscribe((message) => send("message", message, message.id)),
  );
```

`subscribe` is the sample's in-process bus: a `Set` of listeners that a form action publishes to
(`publish(text)` calls each one). It reaches the clients of one process. With several (a cluster,
several containers, serverless instances), publish through a shared channel instead: Redis
pub/sub, Postgres `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` or a hosted service.

### The island

```stsx
// src/islands/LiveFeed.stsx (shortened), used as <LiveFeed client:load />
import { onCleanup, onMount, signal } from "lumiose";
import type { Message } from "../lib/messages.ts";

export function LiveFeed() {
  const messages = signal<Message[]>([]);
  const state = signal<"connecting" | "open" | "reconnecting">("connecting");

  onMount(() => {
    const source = new EventSource("/api/events");
    source.addEventListener("open", () => state.set("open"));
    // EventSource reconnects by itself, after the stream's `retry:` delay.
    source.addEventListener("error", () => state.set("reconnecting"));
    source.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
      const message = JSON.parse(event.data) as Message;
      messages.update((list) => [...list.slice(-49), message]);
    });
    // Closing the source ends the request, and the server's cleanup unsubscribes.
    onCleanup(() => source.close());
  });

  return (
    <ol>
      {messages().map((message) => (
        <li key={message.id}>{message.text}</li>
      ))}
    </ol>
  );
}
```

`onMount` runs only in the browser, so the server render shows an empty list. The sample's island
also has a form that posts to the page's action with `submit()`: the page does not reload, so
the stream stays open.

**After a reconnect**, the browser sends the last `id:` it received as the `Last-Event-ID` request
header; an endpoint that keeps recent events can send the missed ones first. The sample does not.

**Compression.** The Node adapter compresses `text/event-stream` like any text response and
flushes the compressor whenever the stream pauses, so every event reaches the browser at once
(checked with brotli and gzip).

## WebSockets

Lumiose has no WebSocket API of its own. On Node, `createServer()` returns the `node:http` server,
and a WebSocket library attaches to its `upgrade` event. With [`ws`](https://github.com/websockets/ws):

```ts
// src/server/chat-socket.server.ts (shortened)
import type { IncomingMessage } from "node:http";
import type { Duplex } from "node:stream";
import { WebSocket, WebSocketServer } from "ws";

const sockets = new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true, maxPayload: 2048 });

sockets.on("connection", (socket) => {
  socket.on("message", (data, isBinary) => {
    if (isBinary) return;
    const payload = JSON.stringify({ text: data.toString().slice(0, 500), at: new Date() });
    for (const client of sockets.clients) {
      if (client.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) client.send(payload);
    }
  });
});

/** Upgrades requests to /ws and returns true; returns false for any other path. */
export function handleUpgrade(
  request: IncomingMessage,
  socket: Duplex,
  head: Buffer,
  origin: string | undefined = process.env.ORIGIN,
): boolean {
  const { pathname } = new URL(request.url ?? "/", "http://localhost");
  if (pathname !== "/ws") return false;
  // Browsers send the page's origin with the handshake, and the same-origin policy does not apply
  // to WebSockets: refuse other sites (cross-site WebSocket hijacking).
  if (!sameSite(request, origin)) {
    socket.end("HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden\r\nConnection: close\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n");
    return true;
  }
  sockets.handleUpgrade(request, socket, head, (ws) => sockets.emit("connection", ws, request));
  return true;
}

function sameSite(request: IncomingMessage, origin: string | undefined): boolean {
  const from = request.headers.origin;
  if (from === undefined) return true; // not a browser
  try {
    const host = origin === undefined ? request.headers.host : new URL(origin).host;
    return new URL(from).host === host;
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}
```

One `server.ts` serves the app in dev and in production: [`createDevHandler()`](../reference/vite.md#createdevhandler)
mounts `lumiose dev` in it (HMR and the error overlay included), and `@lumiose/adapter-node`'s
`createHandler()` serves the build. The chat's upgrades attach to the same server in both:

```ts
// server.ts: `node server.ts --dev` in dev, `node server.ts` after `lumiose build`
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { createHandler } from "@lumiose/adapter-node";
import { handleUpgrade } from "./src/server/chat-socket.server.ts";

const dev = process.argv.includes("--dev");
const server = createServer();
// @lumiose/vite is a dev dependency: production never loads it.
const handler = dev
  ? await (await import("@lumiose/vite/dev")).createDevHandler({ server })
  : await createHandler({ dir: new URL("dist", import.meta.url) });
server.on("request", handler);

server.on("upgrade", (request, socket, head) => {
  if (handleUpgrade(request, socket, head)) return;
  // Not the chat's path. In dev, Vite's hot reload upgrades on this server too: leave it alone.
  if (!dev) socket.destroy();
});
server.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000));
```

In the browser, an island opens `new WebSocket(url)` in `onMount` (with `wss:` on an `https:` page)
and closes it in `onCleanup`, like the `EventSource` above.

**In dev**, run `node server.ts --dev` instead of `lumiose dev`: the WebSockets work as in
production, with no Vite plugin. `lumiose dev` and `lumiose preview` do not run `server.ts`, so
they have no WebSockets.

**Signing in.** The browser sends its cookies with the handshake: read the session from
`request.headers.cookie` before calling `handleUpgrade`, and refuse with `401` when it is missing.
Upgrades bypass Lumiose's middleware, which runs for HTTP requests only.

**Several processes** do not share `sockets.clients`: broadcast through a shared channel (Redis
pub/sub, for example), as with SSE. On `SIGTERM`, close the sockets (`client.close(1001)`) before
the server, as the sample's `server.ts` does.

## Behind a proxy

**Caddy** passes WebSocket upgrades and flushes streamed responses with the
[VPS guide's](../deploy/vps.md#caddy) `reverse_proxy` alone.

**nginx** needs a location that passes the upgrade on, next to the
[VPS guide's](../deploy/vps.md#nginx) `location /`, whose `proxy_buffering off` already sends each
event at once:

```nginx
    location /ws {
        proxy_pass http://my_app;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        # nginx closes a connection that stays quiet for proxy_read_timeout (60 s by default).
        proxy_read_timeout 1h;
    }
```

An event stream stays open past nginx's 60 s `proxy_read_timeout` thanks to the keep-alive
comments (checked for 75 s through nginx and Caddy). A WebSocket that may stay quiet longer needs the longer timeout above, or pings.

## Platforms

| Target                                                                                                | Server-sent events                                                                                                                                                                         | WebSockets                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Node adapter: [VPS](../deploy/vps.md), [Docker](../deploy/docker.md), [Coolify](../deploy/coolify.md) | Tested (the sample's e2e).                                                                                                                                                                 | Tested: `ws` on `createServer().server`'s `upgrade` event.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| [Cloudflare Workers](../deploy/cloudflare.md)                                                         | A Worker can stream a response. Requests may run in different isolates, so to reach every client, publish through a Durable Object. Not tested with Lumiose.                               | Workers accept WebSockets with `WebSocketPair`; a Durable Object holds them for a room (with the WebSocket Hibernation API, idle sockets do not keep it running). Bind it in `wrangler.jsonc` and reach it through `ctx.platform.env`, or route `/ws` to its own Worker. Not tested with Lumiose. |
| [Vercel](../deploy/vercel.md), [Netlify](../deploy/netlify.md)                                        | A streaming function holds the connection until its maximum duration, then `EventSource` reconnects. Instances share no memory: publish through a hosted channel. Not tested with Lumiose. | Serverless functions cannot keep a WebSocket open. Use a hosted realtime service (Ably, Pusher, PartyKit, Supabase Realtime, Liveblocks, …) and connect islands to it directly.                                                                                                                   |

## Common mistakes

- **No cleanup on disconnect.** A stream that ignores `request.signal` and `cancel()` keeps its
  subscription and timers after the tab closes, for every visitor who ever came.
- **Reloading the page to post.** A plain form post reloads the page and reopens the stream; post
  with `submit()` from the island.
- **Opening the `EventSource` or `WebSocket` during render.** Islands also render on the server; open
  them in `onMount`.
- **Accepting any `Origin` on the WebSocket handshake.** Another site's page could open a socket
  with your visitor's cookies. Compare the origin, as `handleUpgrade` does.
- **Expecting `lumiose dev` or `lumiose preview` to serve WebSockets.** They do not run
  `server.ts`: run `node server.ts --dev`, or `node server.ts` after a build.
- **Destroying unknown upgrades in dev.** Vite's hot reload upgrades on the same server; destroy
  only in production, or leave upgrades you do not handle alone.
- **An in-memory bus with several processes.** Each process only reaches its own clients.

See also: [Data and actions](../concepts/data-and-actions.md) (endpoints, `submit()`),
[Islands](../concepts/islands.md), [`@lumiose/adapter-node`](../reference/adapter-node.md),
[Deploy](../deploy/README.md).

<!-- source: guides/stripe.md -->

# Payments with Stripe Checkout

> Start Stripe Checkout from a form action, fulfill orders in a `route.ts` endpoint that verifies Stripe's webhook signature, and show the result on a return page.

Lumiose has no payments module: the `stripe` package runs in server code, and that is where form
actions and endpoints run. This guide uses Stripe's hosted Checkout page, so the browser loads no
Stripe script and the forms work without JavaScript.

| File                                     | Role                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/server/stripe.server.ts`            | The Stripe client and the products on sale. Server-only.                |
| `src/routes/pricing/page.stsx`           | A form whose action creates a Checkout Session and redirects to it.     |
| `src/routes/checkout/success/page.tsx`   | The return page: what the customer sees after paying.                   |
| `src/routes/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts` | Stripe's events, with the signature verified: fulfillment happens here. |

> **Status:** written against Stripe's API reference and the `stripe` package 23 (its types check
> every example on this page); not run against a Stripe account.

## Setup

```sh
pnpm add stripe
```

The server needs two secrets, never `PUBLIC_*` variables:

| Variable                | Where it comes from                                                                           |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`     | The dashboard's API keys (`sk_test_…` while testing).                                         |
| `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | The webhook endpoint's signing secret (`whsec_…`), or the one `stripe listen` prints locally. |

The pages and the endpoint below render per request (`export const mode = "server"`), or the
whole project does with `lumiose({ mode: "server" })`: a `static` endpoint can only answer `GET`
([LUM5005](../errors/LUM5005.md)), and a form action needs a server anyway.

## The client

The client and the price list live in a `*.server.ts` module, so neither the secret key nor the
prices can reach browser code ([LUM4003](../errors/LUM4003.md)). It is created on first use: `env()`
reads the adapter's environment, which is only there during a request on some hosts.

```ts check file=server/stripe.server.ts
// src/server/stripe.server.ts
import { env } from "lumiose";
import Stripe from "stripe";

let client: Stripe | undefined;

export function stripe(): Stripe {
  const key = env("STRIPE_SECRET_KEY");
  if (key === undefined) throw new Error("STRIPE_SECRET_KEY is not set.");
  return (client ??= new Stripe(key));
}

/** What the store sells: the form posts a plan name, never a price. */
export const PLANS = {
  starter: { name: "Starter", price: "price_starter_monthly" },
  team: { name: "Team", price: "price_team_monthly" },
} as const;

export type Plan = keyof typeof PLANS;

export function isPlan(value: unknown): value is Plan {
  return typeof value === "string" && Object.hasOwn(PLANS, value);
}
```

## Checkout from a form action

The form posts the plan to the page's `checkout` action. The action checks it against `PLANS`,
creates a Checkout Session and redirects (303) to the URL Stripe returns. Stripe sends the customer
back to `success_url`, with `{CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID}` replaced by the session's id, or to `cancel_url`.

```stsx check file=routes/pricing/page.stsx
// src/routes/pricing/page.stsx
import { Title, actionData, fail, redirect, type ActionContext } from "lumiose";
import { PLANS, isPlan, stripe } from "../../server/stripe.server.ts";

export const mode = "server";

export const actions = {
  async checkout(ctx: ActionContext<"/pricing">) {
    const plan = (await ctx.formData()).get("plan");
    if (!isPlan(plan)) return fail(400, { error: "Pick a plan." });

    const session = await stripe().checkout.sessions.create({
      mode: "subscription",
      line_items: [{ price: PLANS[plan].price, quantity: 1 }],
      success_url: new URL("/checkout/success?session_id={CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID}", ctx.url).href,
      cancel_url: new URL("/pricing", ctx.url).href,
      // Ties the payment to your user in the webhook.
      client_reference_id: ctx.locals.userId ?? undefined,
      metadata: { plan },
    });
    if (session.url === null) return fail(502, { error: "Checkout is not available." });
    redirect(session.url, 303);
  },
};

export default function Pricing() {
  return (
    <main>
      <Title>Pricing</Title>
      <h1>Pricing</h1>
      <form method="post" action="?/checkout">
        {Object.entries(PLANS).map(([id, plan]) => (
          <button name="plan" value={id}>
            Subscribe to {plan.name}
          </button>
        ))}
      </form>
      <p class="error">{actionData<typeof actions>()?.error}</p>
    </main>
  );
}
```

`ctx.locals.userId` is whatever your middleware puts on `locals` (here the `Locals` of the
[Server](../concepts/server.md) page); pass `customer` or `customer_email` instead when you keep
Stripe customers. `mode: "payment"` sells one-off items; `"subscription"` needs recurring prices.

To post without a page load, put the form in an island with `onSubmit={submit}`: `submit()` follows
the redirect to Stripe like the plain form. The form above needs no JavaScript at all.

## The return page

The return page shows the result. It does not fulfill the order: the customer may close the tab
before it loads, and anyone can open the URL. Fulfillment happens in the webhook.

```tsx check file=routes/checkout/success/page.tsx
// src/routes/checkout/success/page.tsx
import { Title, notFound, url } from "lumiose";
```
