```tsx check file=routes/checkout/success/page.tsx
import { stripe } from "../../../server/stripe.server.ts";

export const mode = "server";

export default async function CheckoutSuccess() {
  const id = url().searchParams.get("session_id") ?? notFound();
  const session = await stripe().checkout.sessions.retrieve(id);
  const paid =
    session.payment_status === "paid" || session.payment_status === "no_payment_required";
  return (
    <main>
      <Title>{paid ? "Thank you" : "Payment pending"}</Title>
      <h1>{paid ? "Thank you!" : "Your payment is being processed"}</h1>
      <p>A receipt is on its way to {session.customer_details?.email ?? "your email"}.</p>
    </main>
  );
}
```

## Webhooks in an endpoint

Stripe posts events to a `route.ts` endpoint. The signature covers the exact bytes of the body, so
read it with `request.text()` (never parse and re-serialize it), and verify it with
`constructEventAsync`, which uses the Web Crypto API and runs on every host Lumiose deploys to.
Answer quickly with a 2xx: Stripe retries failed deliveries, and the same event may arrive twice,
so make fulfillment idempotent.

```ts check file=routes/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts
// src/routes/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts
import { env, type Endpoint } from "lumiose";
import type Stripe from "stripe";
import { stripe } from "../../../../server/stripe.server.ts";

export const mode = "server";

export const POST: Endpoint<"/api/stripe/webhook"> = async ({ request, platform }) => {
  const signature = request.headers.get("stripe-signature");
  const secret = env("STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET");
  if (signature === null || secret === undefined) return new Response(null, { status: 400 });

  let event: Stripe.Event;
  try {
    event = await stripe().webhooks.constructEventAsync(await request.text(), signature, secret);
  } catch {
    return new Response("Invalid signature", { status: 400 });
  }

  switch (event.type) {
    case "checkout.session.completed":
    case "checkout.session.async_payment_succeeded": {
      const session = event.data.object;
      if (session.payment_status !== "unpaid") {
        // Slow work (emails, provisioning) may finish after the response.
        platform.waitUntil(fulfill(event.id, session));
      }
      break;
    }
    case "checkout.session.async_payment_failed":
      // Tell the customer the delayed payment failed.
      break;
  }
  return new Response(null, { status: 200 });
};

/** Grants what was bought, once per event id. */
async function fulfill(eventId: string, session: Stripe.Checkout.Session): Promise<void> {
  // if (await db.events.seen(eventId)) return;
  // await db.subscriptions.activate(session.client_reference_id, session.metadata?.plan);
  void [eventId, session];
}
```

Lumiose's cross-site check covers page form posts and form-encoded endpoint requests; Stripe posts
JSON, so the endpoint answers it and the signature is the check. Keep the endpoint out of any
middleware that requires a session.

In the dashboard, add the endpoint's URL (`https://example.com/api/stripe/webhook`) with the events
it handles. Locally, the Stripe CLI forwards them and prints the signing secret for
`STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`:

```sh
stripe listen --forward-to localhost:5173/api/stripe/webhook
stripe trigger checkout.session.completed
```

## Production

- Set `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` and `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` on the host, with live keys for production and
  a webhook endpoint per environment (each has its own signing secret).
- Behind a proxy, set `ORIGIN` so `ctx.url` (and with it `success_url` and `cancel_url`) has the
  public origin ([Deploy](../deploy/README.md)).
- Hosted Checkout is a redirect, so a strict CSP (`lumiose({ csp: "strict" })`) needs no change.
  Stripe.js (embedded Checkout, Elements) is a third-party script: allow its origins in your own
  policy ([Security](../concepts/security.md)).

## Common mistakes

- **Fulfilling on the return page.** It may never load, and anyone can open it. Fulfill in the
  webhook, and use the return page to show the status.
- **Trusting a price from the form.** Post a plan or product id and look its price up on the
  server, as `PLANS` does.
- **Parsing the webhook body before verifying it.** `request.json()` and `JSON.stringify` change the
  bytes, and the signature check fails. Pass `await request.text()`.
- **A static webhook endpoint.** Without `mode = "server"` (here or for the project), a `POST`
  export is [LUM5005](../errors/LUM5005.md).
- **Importing the Stripe client into an island.** The secret key would ship to the browser;
  `*.server.ts` makes it [LUM4003](../errors/LUM4003.md).
- **Doing slow work before answering the webhook.** Stripe waits a few seconds, then retries. Answer
  first and hand the rest to `platform.waitUntil()`, or queue it.

<!-- source: guides/sanity.md -->

# Content from Sanity

> Read Sanity content in async components and prerender it, preview drafts on server-rendered routes behind a secret, and rebuild the static pages when editors publish.

[Sanity](https://www.sanity.io) keeps the content and its editing studio; Lumiose reads it with
`@sanity/client`, which runs in server code. Published content is read at build time, so the
pages are static files; drafts are read per request on a separate, server-rendered preview route.

| File                                          | Role                                                                      |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/server/sanity.server.ts`                 | The Sanity clients, the queries and the preview cookie. Server-only.      |
| `src/components/Story.stsx`                   | A story, rendered the same way for published content and drafts.          |
| `src/routes/stories/page.stsx`                | The list of stories, prerendered.                                         |
| `src/routes/stories/[slug]/page.stsx`         | One page per published story, prerendered with `staticPaths()`.           |
| `src/routes/api/preview/route.ts`             | Turns preview on (a signed cookie) when the secret matches.               |
| `src/routes/preview/stories/[slug]/page.stsx` | The draft of a story, rendered per request for previewers.                |
| `src/routes/api/sanity/webhook/route.ts`      | Optional: Sanity's publish webhook, verified, then the host's build hook. |

> **Status:** written against Sanity's documentation and the `@sanity/client` 8 and
> `@sanity/webhook` 4 packages (their types check every example on this page); not run against a
> Sanity project.

## Setup

```sh
pnpm add @sanity/client
pnpm add @sanity/webhook   # only for the webhook endpoint
```

| Variable                | Use                                                                            |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `SANITY_PROJECT_ID`     | The project id, from the Sanity dashboard.                                     |
| `SANITY_DATASET`        | Usually `production`.                                                          |
| `SANITY_READ_TOKEN`     | A token with read access to drafts, for previews only. Never in browser code.  |
| `SANITY_PREVIEW_SECRET` | A random string the studio's preview link carries (`openssl rand -base64 32`). |
| `LUMIOSE_SECRET`        | Signs the preview cookie ([Server](../concepts/server.md)).                    |

The pages here are `static` (the project default) except the preview route and the endpoints,
which say `export const mode = "server"`. A site with no server at all can skip previews and the
webhook endpoint, and point Sanity's webhook straight at the host's build hook
([below](#rebuilding-when-content-changes)).

## The clients and queries

One client reads published content through Sanity's CDN. The preview client reads drafts with a
token, without the CDN. Both live in a `*.server.ts` module, so the token never reaches browser code
([LUM4003](../errors/LUM4003.md)), and are created on first use, when `env()` has the host's
variables.

```ts check file=server/sanity.server.ts
// src/server/sanity.server.ts
import { createClient, type SanityClient } from "@sanity/client";
import { env, signedCookie } from "lumiose";

/** Set by /api/preview; the preview route renders drafts only while it is valid. */
export const previewCookie = signedCookie("sanity-preview", { maxAge: 60 * 60 });

export interface Story {
  title: string;
  slug: string;
  summary: string;
  publishedAt: string | null;
}

let published: SanityClient | undefined;

function required(name: string): string {
  const value = env(name);
  if (value === undefined) throw new Error(`${name} is not set.`);
  return value;
}

/** Published content, through the CDN. With `preview`, drafts, with the read token. */
function sanity(preview = false): SanityClient {
  published ??= createClient({
    projectId: required("SANITY_PROJECT_ID"),
    dataset: required("SANITY_DATASET"),
    apiVersion: "2026-10-01",
    useCdn: true,
    perspective: "published",
  });
  return preview
    ? published.withConfig({
        token: required("SANITY_READ_TOKEN"),
        useCdn: false,
        perspective: "drafts",
      })
    : published;
}

const STORY = `{ title, "slug": slug.current, summary, publishedAt }`;

export function listStories(): Promise<Story[]> {
  return sanity().fetch(
    `*[_type == "story" && defined(slug.current)] | order(publishedAt desc) ${STORY}`,
  );
}

export function getStory(slug: string, preview = false): Promise<Story | null> {
  return sanity(preview).fetch(`*[_type == "story" && slug.current == $slug][0] ${STORY}`, {
    slug,
  });
}
```

Rich text (Portable Text) renders to HTML with a framework-agnostic library such as
`@portabletext/to-html`, written with `innerHTML`; this guide keeps a plain `summary` field.

## Reading content

Pages await their content in async components. `query()` caches each result for the request (or
the build), so a layout and a page that need the same story share one fetch
([Async components](../concepts/async.md)).

```stsx check file=components/Story.stsx
// src/components/Story.stsx
import type { Story as StoryData } from "../server/sanity.server.ts";

export function Story({ story }: { story: StoryData }) {
  return (
    <article class="story">
      <h1>{story.title}</h1>
      {story.publishedAt && <time datetime={story.publishedAt}>{story.publishedAt.slice(0, 10)}</time>}
      <p>{story.summary}</p>
    </article>
  );
}

<style>
  .story time { color: gray; }
</style>
```

```stsx check file=routes/stories/page.stsx
// src/routes/stories/page.stsx: built once per deploy
import { Title, href, query } from "lumiose";
import { listStories } from "../../server/sanity.server.ts";

export default async function Stories() {
  const stories = await query(["stories"], listStories);
  return (
    <main>
      <Title>Stories</Title>
      <ul>
        {stories.map((story) => (
          <li key={story.slug}>
            <a href={href("/stories/[slug]", { slug: story.slug })}>{story.title}</a>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </main>
  );
}
```

```stsx check file=routes/stories/[slug]/page.stsx
// src/routes/stories/[slug]/page.stsx: one file per published story
import { Meta, Title, notFound, query, type PageProps } from "lumiose";
import { Story } from "../../../components/Story.stsx";
import { getStory, listStories } from "../../../server/sanity.server.ts";

export async function staticPaths() {
  return (await listStories()).map((story) => ({ params: { slug: story.slug } }));
}

export default async function StoryPage({ params }: PageProps<"/stories/[slug]">) {
  const story = (await query(["story", params.slug], () => getStory(params.slug))) ?? notFound();
  return (
    <main>
      <Title>{story.title}</Title>
      <Meta name="description" content={story.summary} />
      <Story story={story} />
    </main>
  );
}
```

## Previewing drafts

Drafts change on every keystroke and need a token, so they cannot be prerendered. A preview route
renders them per request, for people who opened the studio's preview link. The link carries the
secret; the endpoint checks it, sets a signed cookie and redirects to the preview page, which reads
the cookie on every request.

```ts check file=routes/api/preview/route.ts
// src/routes/api/preview/route.ts: GET /api/preview?secret=…&slug=…
import { env, href, type Endpoint } from "lumiose";
import { previewCookie } from "../../../server/sanity.server.ts";

export const mode = "server";

export const GET: Endpoint<"/api/preview"> = async ({ url, cookies }) => {
  const secret = env("SANITY_PREVIEW_SECRET");
  const slug = url.searchParams.get("slug");
  if (secret === undefined || url.searchParams.get("secret") !== secret || slug === null) {
    return new Response("Invalid preview link", { status: 401 });
  }
  await previewCookie.set(cookies, "1");
  return Response.redirect(new URL(href("/preview/stories/[slug]", { slug }), url), 307);
};
```

```stsx check file=routes/preview/stories/[slug]/page.stsx
// src/routes/preview/stories/[slug]/page.stsx: the draft, rendered per request
import { Meta, Title, cookies, notFound, query, response, type PageProps } from "lumiose";
import { Story } from "../../../../components/Story.stsx";
import { getStory, previewCookie } from "../../../../server/sanity.server.ts";

export const mode = "server";

export default async function StoryPreview({ params }: PageProps<"/preview/stories/[slug]">) {
  if ((await previewCookie.get(cookies())) !== "1") notFound();
  response().setHeader("cache-control", "private, no-store");
  const story =
    (await query(["story", params.slug, "drafts"], () => getStory(params.slug, true))) ?? notFound();
  return (
    <main>
      <Title>{`Preview: ${story.title}`}</Title>
      <Meta name="robots" content="noindex" />
      <p role="status">Preview of the latest draft.</p>
      <Story story={story} />
    </main>
  );
}
```

In the studio, point the preview link (the Presentation tool's preview URL, or a document action)
at `https://example.com/api/preview?secret=<SANITY_PREVIEW_SECRET>&slug=<slug>`. To refresh the
preview while an editor types, reload the page, or poll from an island that calls
`invalidate()` on an interval.

## Rebuilding when content changes

Published pages are files, so new content needs a new build. Most hosts give a build hook: a URL
that starts a deploy when something posts to it (Netlify build hooks, Vercel deploy hooks,
Cloudflare Pages deploy hooks, a CI workflow dispatch).

**Without a server:** in Sanity's dashboard, create a webhook that posts to the build hook on
create, update and delete, with the filter `_type == "story"`. No code runs in the app.

**With a server:** point the webhook at an endpoint instead. It verifies Sanity's signature (set a
secret on the webhook), so nobody else can trigger builds, keeps the build hook's URL off Sanity,
and can skip changes that do not affect the site:

```ts check file=routes/api/sanity/webhook/route.ts
// src/routes/api/sanity/webhook/route.ts
import { SIGNATURE_HEADER_NAME, isValidSignature } from "@sanity/webhook";
import { env, type Endpoint } from "lumiose";

export const mode = "server";

export const POST: Endpoint<"/api/sanity/webhook"> = async ({ request, platform }) => {
  const secret = env("SANITY_WEBHOOK_SECRET");
  const hook = env("BUILD_HOOK_URL");
  const signature = request.headers.get(SIGNATURE_HEADER_NAME);
  const body = await request.text(); // the exact bytes Sanity signed
  if (secret === undefined || hook === undefined || signature === null) {
    return new Response(null, { status: 400 });
  }
  if (!(await isValidSignature(body, signature, secret))) {
    return new Response("Invalid signature", { status: 401 });
  }
  const { _type } = JSON.parse(body) as { _type?: string };
  if (_type === "story") platform.waitUntil(fetch(hook, { method: "POST" }));
  return new Response(null, { status: 202 });
};
```

The webhook posts JSON, which Lumiose's cross-site check leaves to the endpoint: the signature is
the check. Set the webhook's projection to `{_type}` (or more) so the body carries what the
endpoint reads.

## Common mistakes

- **Reading drafts on a static page.** A prerendered page cannot read cookies
  ([LUM5001](../errors/LUM5001.md)) and would bake one moment's draft into a public file. Keep
  drafts on the `server` preview route.
- **The read token in browser code.** It reads every draft; keep it in `*.server.ts`, and fetch in
  server components or endpoints.
- **Expecting published edits to appear without a build.** The pages are files: trigger a build
  from the webhook, or make the route `server` and read through the CDN on every request.
- **Verifying the webhook against re-serialized JSON.** Pass `await request.text()` to
  `isValidSignature`, then parse.
- **A preview page without `noindex` and `no-store`.** Search engines and shared caches would keep
  a draft. The preview page sets both.

<!-- source: guides/opentelemetry.md -->

# Tracing with OpenTelemetry

> Trace requests, their phases and the browser's navigations with OpenTelemetry from `src/instrumentation.server.ts` and `src/instrumentation.client.ts`, and send them to OpenObserve, SigNoz or Datadog.

Lumiose has no tracing of its own: its instrumentation files hand every phase of a request, and
every client navigation, submission, fetch and hydration, to observers you write
([Server](../concepts/server.md#instrumentation), [Islands](../concepts/islands.md#concept)). This
guide makes those observers OpenTelemetry spans and exports them over OTLP, which every backend
below accepts.

| File                                     | Role                                                                         |
| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/instrumentation.server.ts`          | Starts the Node SDK; a span per request and per phase; errors as spans.      |
| `src/instrumentation.client.ts`          | A browser tracer; spans for navigations, submissions, fetches and hydration. |
| `src/routes/api/otel/v1/traces/route.ts` | Relays the browser's spans to the backend with the server's credentials.     |

> **Status:** checked end to end on 2026-10-15 with a Lumiose app built with `lumiose build` and
> served by `lumiose preview`, against OpenObserve and self-hosted SigNoz 0.129 (its last Docker Compose release) in Docker (server spans
> nested by phase, failed requests, a continued `traceparent`, and browser navigation and
> hydration spans through the relay). The Datadog setup follows Datadog's documentation; it was not
> run. Packages: `@opentelemetry/api` 1.9, `@opentelemetry/sdk-node` and
> `@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http` 0.223, `@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-web` 2.12.

## Setup

```sh
pnpm add @opentelemetry/api @opentelemetry/sdk-node @opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http
pnpm add @opentelemetry/sdk-trace-web @opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base @opentelemetry/resources @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions
```

The Node SDK runs where the server runs on Node: `lumiose dev`, `lumiose preview`,
`@lumiose/adapter-node` and the Docker and VPS targets. On Cloudflare Workers or Vercel's Edge
runtime, start that platform's OpenTelemetry integration in `register()` instead; the wrappers
below stay the same.

## Server spans

`register()` starts the SDK once per server instance, before the first request. The
`instrumentations` wrappers open a span per request (`SERVER` kind, named after the route
pattern, as OpenTelemetry's HTTP conventions ask) and a child span per phase: each middleware file,
the action, the endpoint, the render until the shell is ready, and each streamed boundary. The
SDK's context manager makes each phase's span a child of the one around it, so a trace shows the
request, then its middleware, then its render, then its streamed parts. A `traceparent` header
from a proxy or another service continues its trace. `onRequestError` records unexpected errors
with the phase and the `digest` that an `<ErrorBoundary>` fallback shows.

```ts check
// src/instrumentation.server.ts
import {
  ROOT_CONTEXT,
  SpanKind,
  SpanStatusCode,
  propagation,
  trace,
  type Span,
  type TextMapGetter,
} from "@opentelemetry/api";
import type { RequestErrorInfo, ServerInstrumentation } from "lumiose";

export async function register() {
  const { NodeSDK } = await import("@opentelemetry/sdk-node");
  const { OTLPTraceExporter } = await import("@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http");
  // The endpoint and headers come from the OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* variables (see the backends).
  new NodeSDK({ serviceName: "my-app", traceExporter: new OTLPTraceExporter() }).start();
}

const tracer = trace.getTracer("lumiose");

/** Reads a `traceparent` header, so a trace started by a proxy or another service continues. */
const headers: TextMapGetter<Headers> = {
  get: (carrier, key) => carrier.get(key) ?? undefined,
  keys: (carrier) => [...carrier.keys()],
};

type Result = { status: "success" } | { status: "error"; error: unknown };

/** Ends a phase's span: failed, with the exception, when the phase failed. */
function end(span: Span, result: Result): void {
  if (result.status === "error") {
    span.recordException(result.error instanceof Error ? result.error : String(result.error));
    span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR });
  }
  span.end();
}

/** The endpoint that relays the browser's spans (below): no spans for the relay itself. */
const RELAY = "/api/otel/v1/traces";

/** A child span around one phase: `call()` runs it, inside the span. */
function phase(
  name: string,
  info: { route: string | undefined },
  attributes: Record<string, string>,
  call: () => Promise<Result>,
) {
  if (info.route === RELAY) return call();
  return tracer.startActiveSpan(name, { attributes }, async (span) => end(span, await call()));
}

export const instrumentations: ServerInstrumentation[] = [
  {
    request: (call, info) => {
      if (info.route === RELAY) return call();
      const parent = propagation.extract(ROOT_CONTEXT, info.request.headers, headers);
      const method = info.request.method;
      const name = info.route === undefined ? method : `${method} ${info.route}`;
      const attributes = {
        "http.request.method": method,
        "url.path": new URL(info.request.url).pathname,
        ...(info.route === undefined ? {} : { "http.route": info.route }),
      };
      return tracer.startActiveSpan(
        name,
        { kind: SpanKind.SERVER, attributes },
        parent,
        async (span) => {
          const result = await call();
          const status = result.status === "success" ? result.response?.status : undefined;
          if (status !== undefined) span.setAttribute("http.response.status_code", status);
          if (status !== undefined && status >= 500) span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR });
          end(span, result);
        },
      );
    },
    middleware: (call, info) => phase("middleware", info, { "code.file.path": info.file }, call),
    action: (call, info) => phase(`action ${info.name}`, info, {}, call),
    endpoint: (call, info) => phase(`${info.method} handler`, info, {}, call),
    render: (call, info) => phase("render", info, {}, call),
    stream: (call, info) => phase("stream", info, {}, call),
  },
];

/** Unexpected errors, as spans of their own with the phase and the digest users see. */
export function onRequestError(error: unknown, info: RequestErrorInfo) {
  const span = tracer.startSpan(`error ${info.phase}`, {
    attributes: {
      "http.route": info.route ?? "",
      "lumiose.phase": info.phase,
      "lumiose.digest": info.digest ?? "",
    },
  });
  end(span, { status: "error", error });
}
```

## Client spans

`src/instrumentation.client.ts` runs on every page before islands hydrate and before the SPA
router starts, so its tracer sees the first hydration. The `navigate` wrapper covers a client
navigation of an SPA until the new page is on screen; `submit`, `fetch` and `hydrate` cover form
submissions, `fetchJSON()` and `query()` requests, and each island. MPA pages have no client
navigations: their page loads are the server's `request` spans.

```ts check
// src/instrumentation.client.ts
import { SpanStatusCode, trace, type Span } from "@opentelemetry/api";
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from "@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http";
import { resourceFromAttributes } from "@opentelemetry/resources";
import { BatchSpanProcessor } from "@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base";
import { WebTracerProvider } from "@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-web";
import { ATTR_SERVICE_NAME } from "@opentelemetry/semantic-conventions";
import type { ClientErrorInfo, ClientInstrumentation } from "lumiose";

const provider = new WebTracerProvider({
  resource: resourceFromAttributes({ [ATTR_SERVICE_NAME]: "my-app-browser" }),
  // The app's own endpoint forwards the spans with the server's credentials (below).
  spanProcessors: [new BatchSpanProcessor(new OTLPTraceExporter({ url: "/api/otel/v1/traces" }))],
});
provider.register();

const tracer = trace.getTracer("lumiose");

type Result = { status: "success" } | { status: "error"; error: unknown };

function end(span: Span, result: Result): void {
  if (result.status === "error") {
    span.recordException(result.error instanceof Error ? result.error : String(result.error));
    span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR });
  }
  span.end();
}

function phase(name: string, attributes: Record<string, string>, call: () => Promise<Result>) {
  return tracer.startActiveSpan(name, { attributes }, async (span) => end(span, await call()));
}

export const instrumentations: ClientInstrumentation[] = [
  {
    // A client navigation of an SPA, until the new page is on screen.
    navigate: (call, info) =>
      phase(
        `navigate ${info.to?.route ?? info.to?.url.pathname ?? ""}`,
        { "lumiose.navigation": info.type, "url.path": info.to?.url.pathname ?? "" },
        call,
      ),
    submit: (call, info) => phase(`submit ${info.action}`, { "url.full": info.url }, call),
    fetch: (call, info) =>
      phase(
        "fetch",
        "url" in info ? { "url.full": info.url } : { "lumiose.query": JSON.stringify(info.key) },
        call,
      ),
    hydrate: (call, info) => phase(`hydrate ${info.island}`, {}, call),
  },
];

export function onError(error: unknown, info: ClientErrorInfo) {
  const span = tracer.startSpan(`error ${info.phase}`, {
    attributes: { "lumiose.phase": info.phase, "lumiose.island": info.island ?? "" },
  });
  end(span, { status: "error", error });
}

// Spans are batched: send the last ones when the page goes away.
addEventListener("pagehide", () => void provider.forceFlush());
```

The web SDK adds about 58 kB of JavaScript (16 kB brotli) to every page, since every page loads
the file. The `@opentelemetry/api` calls in the wrappers do nothing until a provider is registered,
so a site that only needs a sample can load the SDK with `import()` for some page loads and leave
the rest without it.

## The relay endpoint

Backends need credentials that must not ship to the browser, and most do not accept cross-origin
requests. The browser exporter posts to the app instead, and this endpoint forwards the spans with
the same `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*` settings the server uses. The server instrumentation above skips
it, so relaying spans creates none. The body limit keeps it from relaying anything larger than a
batch of spans.

```ts check file=routes/api/otel/v1/traces/route.ts
// src/routes/api/otel/v1/traces/route.ts: the browser's spans, forwarded with the server's settings
import { env, type Endpoint } from "lumiose";

export const mode = "server";
// Spans come in batches; anything larger is not a span batch.
export const limits = { body: "256kb" };

/** `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` (`key=value,…`, values URL-encoded), as OpenTelemetry reads it. */
function otlpHeaders(): Record<string, string> {
  const pairs = (env("OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS") ?? "")
    .split(",")
    .filter((pair) => pair.includes("="));
  return Object.fromEntries(
    pairs.map((pair) => {
      const at = pair.indexOf("=");
      return [pair.slice(0, at).trim(), decodeURIComponent(pair.slice(at + 1).trim())];
    }),
  );
}

export const POST: Endpoint<"/api/otel/v1/traces"> = async ({ request }) => {
  const url =
    env("OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT") ??
    `${env("OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT") ?? "http://localhost:4318"}/v1/traces`;
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      ...otlpHeaders(),
      "content-type": request.headers.get("content-type") ?? "application/json",
    },
    body: await request.arrayBuffer(),
  });
  return new Response(null, { status: response.ok ? 204 : 502 });
};
```

## Backends

The server exporter and the relay read OpenTelemetry's standard variables:

| Variable                             | Use                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`        | The backend's OTLP/HTTP base URL; traces go to `<url>/v1/traces`.           |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT` | The full traces URL, when it is not `<base>/v1/traces`.                     |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`         | `key=value` pairs, comma-separated, values URL-encoded (`%20` for a space). |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME`                  | Overrides `serviceName`.                                                    |

### OpenObserve

OpenObserve takes OTLP/HTTP at `/api/<organization>/v1/traces`, with HTTP Basic authentication
(the user's email and password, or an ingestion token from the UI):

```sh
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT=https://openobserve.example.com/api/default/v1/traces
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Basic%20Og=="
```

Locally, OpenObserve runs in one container; its UI is at `http://localhost:5080`:

```sh
docker run -d -p 5080:5080 -e ZO_ROOT_USER_EMAIL=root@example.com -e ZO_ROOT_USER_PASSWORD=change-me \
  public.ecr.aws/zinclabs/openobserve:latest
```

### SigNoz

Self-hosted SigNoz receives OTLP/HTTP on port 4318, without authentication: keep that port on a
private network.

```sh
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://signoz-otel-collector:4318
```

SigNoz Cloud takes the region's ingestion URL and the ingestion key as a header:

```sh
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://ingest.<region>.signoz.cloud:443
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS=signoz-ingestion-key=<your-ingestion-key>
```

SigNoz installs with its `foundryctl` tool ([SigNoz docs](https://signoz.io/docs/install/docker/));
the UI is at `http://localhost:8080`. On a fresh install the collector starts receiving once the
first user has signed up in the UI, which creates the organization.

### Datadog

The Datadog Agent receives OTLP once its receiver is enabled, and forwards to Datadog with the
Agent's API key, so the app needs no Datadog credentials. Enable the HTTP receiver on the Agent
(`DD_OTLP_CONFIG_RECEIVER_PROTOCOLS_HTTP_ENDPOINT=0.0.0.0:4318`, and expose the port), then point
the app at it:

```sh
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://datadog-agent:4318
```

The spans appear in Datadog APM under the service name. For the browser, Datadog's own RUM SDK
started in `src/instrumentation.client.ts` is the usual choice; the relay above works too, through
the Agent.

## Common mistakes

- **Starting the SDK at module scope.** Start it in `register()`, which the server awaits before the
  first request; module code also runs while `lumiose build` loads the server.
- **Exporting from the browser straight to the backend.** The credentials would ship in the bundle,
  and the backend must allow the page's origin. Relay through the app.
- **High-cardinality span names.** Name spans after the route pattern (`GET /stories/[slug]`), not
  the URL; the URL goes in `url.path`.
- **Expecting spans for static files.** The server serves them before the app, so no wrapper sees
  them; prerendered pages are static files.
- **Changing the request in a wrapper.** Wrappers observe: they cannot change arguments, results or
  the response. Use middleware for that.

<!-- source: guides/sentry.md -->

# Error reporting with Sentry

> Report server errors from `onRequestError` and browser errors from `onError` to Sentry, with source maps for the client and the server bundles.

Sentry has no Lumiose SDK, and needs none: `@sentry/node` starts in
`src/instrumentation.server.ts` and receives every unexpected error of a request, and
`@sentry/browser` starts in `src/instrumentation.client.ts`, before any island hydrates, and
receives the errors of islands, the SPA router and `submit()`
([Server](../concepts/server.md#instrumentation), [Islands](../concepts/islands.md#concept)).
Sentry's Vite plugin uploads the source maps of both builds.

| File                            | Role                                                                   |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `vite.config.ts`                | Hidden source maps, uploaded to Sentry after each build, then deleted. |
| `src/instrumentation.server.ts` | Starts `@sentry/node`; reports request errors with their phase.        |
| `src/instrumentation.client.ts` | Starts `@sentry/browser`; reports island, router and submit errors.    |

> **Status:** checked on 2026-10-15 with a Lumiose app built with `lumiose build` and served by
> `lumiose preview`, against a local stand-in for Sentry's ingest endpoint: a server render error
> and an island error each arrived as one event with the tags below and debug IDs for the source
> maps, and the build wrote hidden source maps for the client and the server. Not run against a
> Sentry account (no upload of the maps). Packages: `@sentry/node` and `@sentry/browser` 10.76,
> `@sentry/vite-plugin` 5.4.

## Setup

```sh
pnpm add @sentry/node @sentry/browser
pnpm add -D @sentry/vite-plugin
```

| Variable                       | Where                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `SENTRY_DSN`                   | The server, at run time.                                                              |
| `PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN`            | The build, for the browser bundle (`import.meta.env` only sees `PUBLIC_*` variables). |
| `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN`            | The build, to upload source maps. A secret: never a `PUBLIC_*` variable.              |
| `SENTRY_ORG`, `SENTRY_PROJECT` | The build, with the token.                                                            |

A DSN is not a secret (it only lets clients send events), so the same one may serve both sides.

## Source maps

`build.sourcemap: "hidden"` writes a map next to every bundle of both builds without the
`//# sourceMappingURL` comment, so browsers do not fetch them. The plugin, last in the list, runs
after the client build and after the server build: it adds a debug ID to each bundle and its map,
uploads the maps, and deletes them so they are not deployed. Without `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` (on a
laptop) it builds as usual, warns, and uploads nothing.

```ts check
// vite.config.ts
import lumiose from "@lumiose/vite";
import { sentryVitePlugin } from "@sentry/vite-plugin";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  // Source maps for Sentry only: "hidden" leaves out the //# sourceMappingURL comment.
  build: { sourcemap: "hidden" },
  plugins: [
    lumiose({ mode: "server" }),
    // Last: uploads the client's and the server's source maps after each build, then deletes them.
    sentryVitePlugin({
      org: process.env.SENTRY_ORG,
      project: process.env.SENTRY_PROJECT,
      authToken: process.env.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN,
      sourcemaps: { filesToDeleteAfterUpload: ["dist/**/*.map"] },
    }),
  ],
});
```

## Server errors

`register()` starts the SDK once per server instance, before the first request.
`onRequestError` receives what the request handler catches and Sentry's own Node integrations do
not see: errors that render the `error` page or answer 500, errors of streamed `<Suspense>`
boundaries, rejected `waitUntil()` work and errors an `<ErrorBoundary>` caught, each with the
phase it happened in. `redirect()`, `notFound()` and `error(status)` are not reported.

```ts check
// src/instrumentation.server.ts
import * as Sentry from "@sentry/node";
import { env, type RequestErrorInfo } from "lumiose";

export function register() {
  Sentry.init({
    dsn: env("SENTRY_DSN"),
    environment: env("SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT") ?? "production",
    // Errors only; tracing is in the OpenTelemetry guide.
    tracesSampleRate: 0,
  });
}

export function onRequestError(error: unknown, info: RequestErrorInfo) {
  Sentry.captureException(error, {
    tags: { phase: info.phase, route: info.route ?? "(none)" },
    extra: { url: info.request.url, method: info.request.method, digest: info.digest },
  });
}
```

The `digest` is what an `<ErrorBoundary>` fallback shows in production: a user who quotes it
leads you to the event. Sentry's Node SDK also sets up OpenTelemetry for its own tracing; to keep
the [OpenTelemetry guide](opentelemetry.md)'s setup as well, follow Sentry's instructions for an
existing OpenTelemetry setup (`skipOpenTelemetrySetup`).

## Browser errors

The file's top-level code runs before any island hydrates, so the SDK is ready for hydration
errors. `onError` receives what Lumiose catches: an island that fails to load or hydrate
(`"hydrate"`), an async component or an `<ErrorBoundary>` (`"render"`), an effect or binding
(`"effect"`), the SPA router (`"navigate"`) and `submit()` (`"submit"`), with the island's
module and export. Sentry's own handlers still catch everything else on the page.

```ts check
// src/instrumentation.client.ts
import * as Sentry from "@sentry/browser";
import type { ClientErrorInfo } from "lumiose";

Sentry.init({
  dsn: import.meta.env.PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN,
  environment: import.meta.env.PROD ? "production" : "development",
});

export function onError(error: unknown, info: ClientErrorInfo) {
  Sentry.captureException(error, {
    tags: { phase: info.phase, route: info.route ?? "(mpa)", island: info.island ?? "(none)" },
  });
}
```

## Production

- On serverless hosts the function may stop before the SDK sends: call
  `ctx.platform.waitUntil(Sentry.flush(2000))` after reporting, or follow Sentry's guide for the
  platform.
- With `lumiose({ csp: "strict" })`, the browser SDK posts events with `fetch`, which the
  strict policy does not restrict (it sets `script-src` and `style-src`, not `connect-src`).
- Set `release` in both `init` calls, or let the plugin inject it from the Git commit, so
  events and source maps match.

## Common mistakes

- **Starting the server SDK at module scope.** Start it in `register()`, which the server awaits
  before the first request.
- **Reporting from middleware with `try`/`catch` around `next()`.** Render errors, streamed
  boundaries and endpoint 500s never reach it; `onRequestError` gets them.
- **`SENTRY_DSN` in browser code.** It is undefined there; the browser bundle reads
  `import.meta.env.PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN` at build time.
- **Deploying the source maps.** Keep `filesToDeleteAfterUpload`, or anyone can read the original
  source.
- **The plugin before `lumiose()`.** Put it last, so it sees the final bundles.

<!-- source: guides/posthog.md -->

# Product analytics with PostHog

> Start PostHog in `src/instrumentation.client.ts`, count page views on MPA pages and SPA navigations (`afterNavigate`), send events from islands, and evaluate feature flags on the server.

PostHog's browser SDK starts in `src/instrumentation.client.ts`, the one file every page loads,
also pages without islands. A page view is a document load there, and an SPA's client navigation
in `afterNavigate` ([`lumiose/router`](../reference/router.md#afternavigate)). Islands send events,
and `posthog-node` evaluates feature flags while the server renders, so a page shows the right
variant without a flicker.

| File                            | Role                                                                     |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `src/instrumentation.client.ts` | Loads and starts `posthog-js`; counts each document load as a page view. |
| `src/components/PageViews.tsx`  | In the outermost `spa` layout: counts client navigations.                |
| `src/components/PlanButton.tsx` | An island that sends an event.                                           |
| `src/server/posthog.server.ts`  | The `posthog-node` client. Server-only.                                  |
| `src/routes/plans/page.stsx`    | A server page that renders a feature flag's variant.                     |

> **Status:** checked on 2026-10-15 with a Lumiose app built with `lumiose build` and served by
> `lumiose preview`, against a local stand-in for PostHog's API: one `$pageview` per MPA page
> load, per SPA document load and per SPA navigation, the island's event, and the server's flag
> evaluation. Not run against a PostHog project. Packages: `posthog-js` 1.438, `posthog-node` 5.55.

## Setup

```sh
pnpm add posthog-js posthog-node
```

| Variable                      | Where                                                                       |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY`          | The build, for the browser (`phc_…`, the project API key: not a secret).    |
| `PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST`         | The build: `https://us.i.posthog.com`, `https://eu.i.posthog.com` or yours. |
| `POSTHOG_KEY`, `POSTHOG_HOST` | The server, for `posthog-node` (the same key).                              |

## Page views

`posthog-js` is about 300 kB of JavaScript (85 kB brotli), so the file loads it with `import()`
instead of a static import, which would hold back hydration on every page until it ran. Automatic
page views are off: the file counts each document load (an MPA page, or the first page of an SPA)
once.

```ts check
// src/instrumentation.client.ts
// posthog-js is large (about 85 kB brotli): load it without holding back hydration.
void import("posthog-js").then(({ default: posthog }) => {
  posthog.init(import.meta.env.PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY, {
    api_host: import.meta.env.PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST ?? "https://us.i.posthog.com",
    // Page views are counted here and in <PageViews>, the same way on MPA and SPA pages.
    capture_pageview: false,
    person_profiles: "identified_only",
  });
  // Every document load: an MPA page, or the first page of an SPA.
  posthog.capture("$pageview");
});
```

An SPA navigates on the client, so no document loads: `afterNavigate` counts those navigations.
Render this component once, in the outermost `spa` layout, where it stays mounted across
navigations. Its `"enter"` call is the document load the file above already counted.

```tsx check file=components/PageViews.tsx
// src/components/PageViews.tsx: in the outermost spa layout
import posthog from "posthog-js";
import { afterNavigate } from "lumiose/router";

export function PageViews() {
  afterNavigate((navigation) => {
    // "enter" is the document load, which instrumentation.client.ts already counted.
    if (navigation.type === "enter" || navigation.to === null) return;
    posthog.capture("$pageview", { $current_url: navigation.to.url.href });
  });
  return null;
}
```

```stsx check file=routes/workspace/layout.stsx
// src/routes/workspace/layout.stsx
import type { LayoutProps } from "lumiose";
import { PageViews } from "../../components/PageViews.tsx";

export const mode = "spa";

export default function Workspace(props: LayoutProps<"/workspace">) {
  return (
    <div class="workspace">
      <PageViews />
      {props.children}
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Events

Islands import `posthog` and send events from handlers. They share the instance the
instrumentation file starts, which is ready long before a person clicks.

```tsx check file=components/PlanButton.tsx
// src/components/PlanButton.tsx: an island
import posthog from "posthog-js";

export function PlanButton(props: { plan: string }) {
  return (
    <button onClick={() => posthog.capture("plan_selected", { plan: props.plan })}>
      Choose {props.plan}
    </button>
  );
}
```

To tie events to your users, call `posthog.identify(userId)` in an island once the person is
signed in, and `posthog.reset()` on sign-out.

## Feature flags

A flag read in the browser arrives after the page shows, so the page would switch variants in
front of the reader. Evaluate it on the server instead, while the page renders, with the same
distinct id the browser uses (your user id once identified):

```ts check file=server/posthog.server.ts
// src/server/posthog.server.ts
import { env } from "lumiose";
import { PostHog } from "posthog-node";

let client: PostHog | undefined;

export function posthog(): PostHog {
  const key = env("POSTHOG_KEY");
  if (key === undefined) throw new Error("POSTHOG_KEY is not set.");
  return (client ??= new PostHog(key, { host: env("POSTHOG_HOST") ?? "https://us.i.posthog.com" }));
}
```

```stsx check file=routes/plans/page.stsx
// src/routes/plans/page.stsx
import { Title, locals } from "lumiose";
import { PlanButton } from "../../components/PlanButton.tsx";
import { posthog } from "../../server/posthog.server.ts";

export const mode = "server";

export default async function Pricing() {
  const user = locals().userId ?? "anonymous";
  // Evaluated on the server, so the page renders the right variant without a flicker.
  const annual = await posthog().isFeatureEnabled("annual-pricing", user);
  return (
    <main>
      <Title>Plans</Title>
      <h1>{annual ? "Pay yearly, save 20%" : "Plans"}</h1>
      <PlanButton client:load plan={annual ? "team-yearly" : "team"} />
    </main>
  );
}
```

`locals().userId` is whatever your middleware stores ([Server](../concepts/server.md)). The page is a
`server` route, since a flag depends on the reader. `posthog-node` batches its own events (such as
`$feature_flag_called`); on a serverless host, flush before the function ends with
`ctx.platform.waitUntil(posthog().flush())`.

## Production

- With `lumiose({ csp: "strict" })`, `posthog-js` is bundled with your code, so the policy allows
  it. Its extensions (surveys, session recording) load further scripts from PostHog's host, which a
  strict policy refuses: keep them off, or set your own policy for them
  ([Security](../concepts/security.md)).
- Ad blockers often block PostHog's hosts: PostHog documents a reverse proxy, which in Lumiose can
  be middleware or an endpoint that forwards `/ingest/*` to PostHog.
- Ask for consent where the law requires it before `posthog.init()` (or start with
  `opt_out_capturing_by_default: true` and call `posthog.opt_in_capturing()`).

## Common mistakes

- **Leaving automatic page views on.** PostHog's history-based page views and the ones above would
  count SPA navigations twice; keep `capture_pageview: false`.
- **`afterNavigate` in a page instead of the layout.** A page is replaced on navigation, so its
  hook would see only its own `"enter"`. Put the component in the outermost `spa` layout.
- **A static `import posthog from "posthog-js"` in the instrumentation file.** Every page then waits
  for 300 kB of JavaScript before its islands hydrate.
- **Reading flags in the browser for content above the fold.** Evaluate them on the server.
- **The server key in browser code.** Only `PUBLIC_*` variables reach `import.meta.env`; keep
  `posthog-node` in `*.server.ts` modules.

<!-- source: guides/editors.md -->

# Editors: Neovim, Helix and Zed

> Run the Lumiose language server in Neovim and Helix (file type, root markers, the server command), what works in Zed today, and how GitHub highlights `.stsx` files.

VS Code has the Lumiose extension, which bundles the language server
([Getting started](../getting-started.md#editor)). Other editors start the same server over the
Language Server Protocol. It gives them everything the extension shows: TypeScript for `.ts`,
`.tsx` and `.stsx` files, CSS features in `<style>` blocks, class and custom property completion,
the compiler's `LUMxxxx` diagnostics and hovers that explain how each JSX expression runs.

## Set up the server

Install it in the project, so it matches your `lumiose` version:

```sh
pnpm add -D @lumiose/language-server
```

Every editor needs the same four things:

| Setting      | Value                                                                                         |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Command      | `npx --no-install lumiose-language-server --stdio`, run in the project (Node.js 24 or later). |
| Files        | `.stsx` (a file type of its own), `.ts` and `.tsx`.                                           |
| Root markers | `vite.config.ts`, then `package.json`.                                                        |
| Highlighting | The TSX grammar for `.stsx`: the editor colors the TSX, and the server adds the rest.         |

The server proxies TypeScript 7 for `.ts` and `.tsx` files too ("takeover"), so types, renames and
go-to-definition flow between them and `.stsx` files. Disable the editor's own TypeScript server
(`ts_ls`, `vtsls`, `typescript-language-server`) for Lumiose projects; with two servers, `.tsx`
files would get every diagnostic twice.

## Neovim

Neovim 0.11 or later, with the built-in LSP client. In `init.lua` (or a file under `plugin/`):

```lua
-- .stsx files: TSX with <style> blocks.
vim.filetype.add({ extension = { stsx = "stsx" } })
-- Color them with the TSX tree-sitter parser (nvim-treesitter's "tsx").
vim.treesitter.language.register("tsx", "stsx")

vim.lsp.config("lumiose", {
  -- The project's own server, started in the project root.
  cmd = function(dispatchers, config)
    return vim.lsp.rpc.start(
      { "npx", "--no-install", "lumiose-language-server", "--stdio" },
      dispatchers,
      { cwd = config.root_dir }
    )
  end,
  filetypes = { "typescript", "typescriptreact", "stsx" },
  root_markers = { "vite.config.ts", "package.json" },
})
vim.lsp.enable("lumiose")
```

Do not enable `ts_ls` or `vtsls` for the same projects (with nvim-lspconfig, leave them out of
`vim.lsp.enable`). `:checkhealth vim.lsp` shows the attached client.

## Helix

In `~/.config/helix/languages.toml`:

```toml
[language-server.lumiose]
command = "npx"
args = ["--no-install", "lumiose-language-server", "--stdio"]

# .stsx files: TSX plus <style> blocks, colored with the TSX grammar.
[[language]]
name = "stsx"
scope = "source.stsx"
file-types = ["stsx"]
roots = ["vite.config.ts", "package.json"]
grammar = "tsx"
comment-tokens = "//"
block-comment-tokens = { start = "/*", end = "*/" }
indent = { tab-width = 2, unit = "  " }
language-servers = ["lumiose"]

# Takeover: one TypeScript server, through Lumiose, for .ts and .tsx files too.
[[language]]
name = "typescript"
roots = ["vite.config.ts", "package.json"]
language-servers = ["lumiose"]

[[language]]
name = "tsx"
roots = ["vite.config.ts", "package.json"]
language-servers = ["lumiose"]
```

The `stsx` language reuses the TSX grammar, and its queries come from TSX: create
`~/.config/helix/runtime/queries/stsx/highlights.scm` with the single line `; inherits: tsx`, and
the same for `indents.scm`, `injections.scm`, `locals.scm` and `textobjects.scm`. To keep the
TypeScript override to Lumiose projects, put the `language-server` and `typescript`/`tsx` entries
in the project's `.helix/languages.toml` instead. `hx --health stsx` checks the setup.

## Zed

Zed runs language servers only through its extensions, and this version of Lumiose has no Zed
extension, so the server's features are not available in Zed. Mapping `.stsx` to Zed's TSX
language (`"file_types": { "TSX": ["stsx"] }`) colors the files, but Zed's TypeScript server then
reports the CSS of every `<style>` block as TSX syntax errors. Use VS Code, Neovim or Helix for
`.stsx` files, and run `lumiose check` for the diagnostics.

## Other editors

Any editor with an LSP client works with the settings in [Set up the server](#set-up-the-server).
JetBrains IDEs have no Lumiose plugin.

## GitHub

GitHub highlights `.stsx` files as TSX through `.gitattributes`:

```
*.stsx linguist-language=TSX
```

`create-lumiose` writes this file, and `lumiose agents init` adds the line to an existing project.

<!-- source: guides/web-components.md -->

# Web components

> Use custom elements and web-component libraries in Lumiose: define them in the browser, type them in JSX, pass properties and attributes, listen to their events with `on:`, and render them on the server. Lumiose scores 100 on Custom Elements Everywhere.

Web components are how Lumiose works with UI libraries that are not written for it (decision-54):
anything built as custom elements, by hand or with Lit, Stencil, FAST or Web Awesome, runs in
Lumiose pages and islands without an adapter.

## Custom Elements Everywhere

[Custom Elements Everywhere](https://custom-elements-everywhere.com) tests how a framework passes
data to custom elements and listens to their events. Lumiose runs its suites in
`benchmarks/custom-elements-everywhere`, with upstream's tests, weights and scoring:

| Engines                     | Score | Basic | Advanced |
| --------------------------- | ----- | ----- | -------- |
| Chrome and Firefox (scored) | 100   | 16/16 | 16/16    |
| WebKit                      | 100   | 8/8   | 8/8      |

Basic support: elements with and without children in a shadow root, booleans, numbers and strings,
and events listened to imperatively. Advanced support: arrays and objects (camelCase names too) as
properties, and events with lowercase, kebab-case, camelCase, CAPS and PascalCase names, listened
to in JSX. Run it with `pnpm --filter @lumiose/bench-cee test:e2e`. The site does not list Lumiose
yet.

## Define the elements in the browser

A custom element must be defined before the component that renders it runs, so that it is already
upgraded when Lumiose passes it properties. `customElements` exists only in the browser, and
components are also imported on the server, so load the definitions with a guarded import at the
top of the island's module. The island then hydrates once the elements exist, and the server
renders the tags with their attributes:

```ts check file=elements/star-rating.ts
// src/elements/star-rating.ts: a custom element of your own, or a library's entry point
export class StarRating extends HTMLElement {
  #value = 0;
  labels: string[] = [];

  get value(): number {
    return this.#value;
  }
  set value(next: number) {
    this.#value = next;
    this.render();
  }

  connectedCallback(): void {
    // Before an island sets the property, the server's attribute.
    this.#value ||= Number(this.getAttribute("value") ?? 0);
    this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" });
    this.render();
  }

  render(): void {
    if (!this.shadowRoot) return;
    const max = Number(this.getAttribute("max") ?? 5);
    this.shadowRoot.innerHTML = "";
    for (let star = 1; star <= max; star++) {
      const button = document.createElement("button");
      button.textContent = star <= this.#value ? "★" : "☆";
      button.title = this.labels[star - 1] ?? String(star);
      button.onclick = () => {
        this.value = star;
        this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("rating-change", { detail: star }));
      };
      this.shadowRoot.append(button);
    }
  }
}

customElements.define("star-rating", StarRating);
```

## Type it in JSX

Undeclared custom elements accept any attribute. Declare an element to type-check its props, in
any `.d.ts` or module of the project ([JSX types](../reference/jsx.md#custom-elements)):

```tsx check file=components/Review.tsx
// src/components/Review.tsx
import { signal } from "lumiose";

declare module "lumiose/jsx-runtime" {
  namespace JSX {
    interface IntrinsicElements {
      "star-rating": JSX.HTMLProps<HTMLElement> & {
        /** A property: the element defines `value`. */
        value?: number;
        /** An attribute: the element reads `max` with `getAttribute()`. */
        max?: number;
        /** A property holding an array. */
        labels?: string[];
      };
    }
  }
}

// Defines <star-rating> in the browser before the island hydrates; the server skips it.
if (typeof customElements !== "undefined") await import("../elements/star-rating.ts");

export function Review(props: { rating: number }) {
  const rating = signal(props.rating);
  return (
    <figure>
      <star-rating
        value={rating()}
        max={5}
        labels={["Bad", "Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Great"]}
        on:rating-change={(event: CustomEvent<number>) => rating.set(event.detail)}
      />
      <figcaption>{rating()} of 5</figcaption>
    </figure>
  );
}
```

Render it as an island: `<Review client:visible rating={4} />` ([Islands](../concepts/islands.md)).

## Properties and attributes

Lumiose follows React 19's rule. On a custom element (a tag with a dash), each prop goes to:

- **the property of that name, as it is**, when the element defines one (`name in element`, and not
  a property that every element has, such as `id` or `title`): `value={rating()}` sets
  `element.value`, and arrays, objects, booleans and camelCase names (`labels`, `camelCaseObj`)
  arrive unchanged;
- **the attribute** otherwise: `max={5}` writes `max="5"`, and `true`, `false` and `null` add or
  remove it, as on built-in elements.

Strings set as properties keep the URL check of attributes (a `javascript:` URL becomes a
placeholder). An element that is not defined yet when the component runs gets attributes for
everything, so load its definition first (above). `class`, `style`, `ref`, `attach` and
`innerHTML` work as on any element, and a spread (`{...props}`) follows the same rule.

## Events

`on:name` adds a native listener for the event of that exact name, so any casing works:
`on:rating-change`, `on:sl-change`, `on:valueChanged`, `on:PascalEvent`. Type the handler's event
yourself, as above. `onClick` and the other camelCase handlers are for the standard DOM events,
lowercased and delegated: use `on:` for a component's own events.

## Server rendering

On the server a custom element renders as its tag with the attributes Lumiose can write:
strings, numbers and `true` (`<star-rating max="5" value="4">`), and its light-DOM children. Its
shadow root and properties exist only once the browser defines the element; when the island
hydrates, Lumiose sets the properties on the upgraded element. Arrays and objects are not
attributes: the server leaves them out of the HTML, as React 19 does (`labels` above), and the
island sets them as properties when it hydrates; functions are left out too. Elements outside
islands stay server HTML: they upgrade when their definition loads, and read what they need from
attributes.

To show the element before its definition loads, style it with `:not(:defined)`:

```css
star-rating:not(:defined) {
  display: inline-block;
  inline-size: 7.5em;
  block-size: 1.5em;
}
```

## Related

- [JSX](../concepts/jsx.md): element props and `on:` events.
- [JSX types](../reference/jsx.md#custom-elements): declaring custom elements.
- [Islands](../concepts/islands.md): hydration and directives.

<!-- source: deploy/README.md -->

# Deploy

> Run a Lumiose build in production: what the build writes, the settings a server needs, and a guide for each hosting target.

## What to deploy

`lumiose build` writes `dist/` ([Rendering modes](../concepts/rendering-modes.md)):

- `dist/client`: the browser assets (content-hashed, under `assets/`), the files of `public/`, and
  the prerendered pages, with `.br` and `.gz` copies of every text file of 1 kB or more.
- `dist/server/entry.js`: the request handler for server-rendered pages, endpoints and form
  actions. It bundles your server code and the Lumiose runtime; other npm packages stay imports,
  so production needs the app's `dependencies` installed.

A site whose every route is prerendered builds no `dist/server`: any static host serves
`dist/client`. Anything else needs a runtime for `dist/server/entry.js`. On Node,
`@lumiose/adapter-node` serves both directories, from the `server.ts` that
`create-lumiose --template ssr` writes ([reference](../reference/adapter-node.md)); the guides
below run it on Docker, a VPS, Coolify, Fly.io, Render and Railway. `dist/server/entry.js` exports
a web-standard `{ fetch }` ([the server build](../reference/server-entry.md)), which Bun and Deno
serve as it is.

For Cloudflare, Vercel and Netlify, a deploy adapter in the Vite config writes the platform's
output after the build: `lumiose({ adapter: cloudflare() })`, `vercel()` or `netlify()`. Those
platforms serve `dist/client` themselves and compress on their own, so the build then writes no
`.br`/`.gz` copies.

## Production settings

The Node adapter and the request handler read these environment variables:

| Variable         | Set it to                                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NODE_ENV`       | `production`. The adapter sets it when it is unset, before the build loads.                                                                                     |
| `PORT`           | The port to listen on. Default: `3000`.                                                                                                                         |
| `HOST`           | The address to listen on. Default: every address, which a container needs. Behind a proxy on the same machine, `127.0.0.1`.                                     |
| `ORIGIN`         | The public origin, such as `https://example.com`, behind a proxy that terminates TLS or rewrites the host. Request URLs (`url()`, `ctx.url`) are built from it. |
| `LUMIOSE_SECRET` | When the app signs cookies (`signedCookie()`): a random secret of at least 32 bytes (`openssl rand -base64 32`). Never commit it or bake it into an image.      |

## Guides

- [Docker](docker.md): A multi-stage Dockerfile: `node:24-alpine`, production dependencies only, a non-root user and a health check.
- [VPS](vps.md): The Node adapter under systemd or pm2, behind Caddy or nginx, and what the adapter already does for compression and caching.
- [Coolify](coolify.md): Deploy from the Dockerfile with Coolify's Dockerfile build pack.
- [Cloudflare Workers](cloudflare.md): `@lumiose/adapter-cloudflare`: the Worker, static assets, bindings as `ctx.platform.env`.
- [Vercel](vercel.md): `@lumiose/adapter-vercel`: the Build Output API, with a Node.js or Edge function.
- [Netlify](netlify.md): `@lumiose/adapter-netlify`: the site and a Netlify Function.
- [Bun](bun.md): `bun dist/server/entry.js`, static files included.
- [Deno](deno.md): `deno serve dist/server/entry.js`, static files included.
- [Fly.io](fly.md), [Render](render.md), [Railway](railway.md): The Node adapter on container and Node hosts.
- [Static hosts](static.md): A fully prerendered site on Cloudflare, Netlify, GitHub Pages, S3 with CloudFront or any file server.
- [AWS Lambda](aws-lambda.md): A handler from Lambda's events to the server build's `fetch`.

## Verification

Each target's status says how far its guide has been checked:

- **Verified on the platform**: deployed to the real service by hand, on the date given.
- **Tested locally**: run on a development machine in the target's own runtime (a container, the
  platform's emulator), by the script named or by hand; not on the real service.
- **Not tested**: written from the platform's documentation only.
- **Planned**: no guide yet.

# Docker

> A multi-stage Dockerfile for a Lumiose app: production dependencies only, a non-root user and a health check.

This page is for an app with server routes and the `server.ts` that `create-lumiose --template ssr`
writes (`@lumiose/adapter-node`'s `createServer()`). The same image runs on any host that runs
containers: a [VPS](vps.md) with Docker, [Coolify](coolify.md), Kubernetes, a container platform.

## The Dockerfile

Put it at the root of the project, next to `package.json` and `pnpm-lock.yaml`:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
ARG NODE_VERSION=24

# Build: all dependencies, then `lumiose build`. Debian (glibc): the compiler ships native
# binaries for Linux x64 and arm64 on glibc, and up to 0.2.0 for x64 only on musl (Alpine).
FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-slim AS build
ENV PNPM_HOME=/pnpm CI=true
RUN npm install --global pnpm@11
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml pnpm-workspace.yaml* ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,id=pnpm,target=/pnpm/store pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
COPY . .
RUN pnpm build

# Production dependencies only, on the runtime's base image (native packages match its C library).
FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-alpine AS prod-deps
ENV PNPM_HOME=/pnpm CI=true
RUN npm install --global pnpm@11
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml pnpm-workspace.yaml* ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,id=pnpm,target=/pnpm/store pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --prod

# Runtime: Node, the build output and production dependencies, as the unprivileged `node` user.
FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-alpine
# tini passes `docker stop`'s SIGTERM on to Node, which ignores it as PID 1.
RUN apk add --no-cache tini
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 HEALTHCHECK_PATH=/
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=prod-deps /app/node_modules node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist dist
COPY package.json server.ts ./
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=30s --start-interval=2s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["node", "-e", "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:' + process.env.PORT + process.env.HEALTHCHECK_PATH).then((r) => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1), () => process.exit(1))"]
ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini", "--"]
CMD ["node", "server.ts"]
```

And a `.dockerignore`, so the build context leaves out what the image builds itself:

```text
node_modules
dist
.lumiose
.git
.env*
*.log
```

Build and run it:

```sh
docker build -t my-app .
docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 -e LUMIOSE_SECRET="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" my-app
```

`LUMIOSE_SECRET` is only needed when the app signs cookies (`signedCookie()`); pass every secret
at run time like this, never as a build argument or an `ENV` line, which stay in the image. The
other settings (`ORIGIN` behind a proxy, `PORT`, `HOST`) are in
[Production settings](README.md#production-settings).

## How it works

- **Three stages.** `build` installs everything and runs `lumiose build`. `prod-deps` installs only
  `dependencies`, so Vite, the compiler and the CLI never reach the image. The last stage copies
  `dist/`, those `node_modules` and `server.ts` onto a fresh `node:24-alpine`. The server build
  bundles your server code and the Lumiose runtime; other npm packages stay imports, which is why
  production dependencies are installed.
- **Debian to build, Alpine to run.** `lumiose build` loads the compiler's native binary, published
  for Linux x64 and arm64 on glibc but only x64 on musl, so the build stage is `node:24-slim`,
  which builds on both architectures (an arm64 laptop or server included). The build output is
  JavaScript and static files, so it runs on Alpine. `prod-deps` uses the runtime's image so that a
  dependency with a native addon is built for musl. The release after 0.2.0 also publishes the
  arm64 musl binary (`@lumiose/compiler-linux-arm64-musl`); from that version on, the build stage
  can be `node:24-alpine` as well, and this Debian stage becomes optional.
- **Non-root.** The app runs as `node` (uid 1000), and the files it runs are owned by root, so it
  cannot change them. A directory it writes to, such as a SQLite database's, must be created for
  it before `USER node` and mounted as a volume:
  `RUN mkdir /data && chown node:node /data`, then `docker run -v my-app-data:/data …`.
- **Health check.** `HEALTHCHECK` fetches `HEALTHCHECK_PATH` (default `/`) with Node, since Alpine
  has no curl; any `2xx` answer is healthy. Point it at a cheap URL, such as a `GET` endpoint
  that returns `ok` without rendering a page: `docker run -e HEALTHCHECK_PATH=/healthz …`.
  `--start-interval` (Docker Engine 25 or later) checks every 2 s while the container starts.
- **Signals.** Node as PID 1 ignores `SIGTERM`, so `docker stop` would wait 10 s and kill it.
  [tini](https://github.com/krallin/tini) passes the signal on, and Node exits at once.
- **pnpm.** `npm install --global pnpm@11` installs pnpm; when `package.json` has a
  `packageManager` field (`pnpm@11.x.y`), pnpm switches to that version. The cache mounts keep
  the package store between builds. `pnpm-workspace.yaml*` copies the file when it exists
  (pnpm 11 keeps settings there).

**With npm** instead of pnpm: drop the `npm install --global pnpm@11` lines, the `PNPM_HOME`
variable and the cache mounts, copy `package-lock.json` instead of `pnpm-lock.yaml`, and run
`npm ci`, `npm run build` and `npm ci --omit=dev`. This variant has not been tested.

## The bookshelf sample

The repository's [bookshelf sample](https://github.com/itsjavi/lumiose/tree/main/examples/ssr-bookshelf)
has a Dockerfile of the same shape, built from the monorepo instead of from npm:

- The build context is the repository root (`docker build -f examples/ssr-bookshelf/Dockerfile .`).
  Its ignore file is `examples/ssr-bookshelf/Dockerfile.dockerignore`: BuildKit reads the ignore
  file named after the Dockerfile before the one at the context root. It allows only the
  workspace packages the sample uses.
- A first stage compiles the compiler's native binary from the Rust sources, because the
  monorepo has no Linux binaries (npm installs them as `@lumiose/compiler-linux-*`).
- pnpm installs with `--filter "@lumiose-examples/ssr-bookshelf..."`, and the production install
  with `--filter-prod`, which leaves out the workspace's dev dependencies.
- The build seeds a throwaway database, because the genre pages are prerendered from it. The
  container seeds `/data/bookshelf.db` on its first start, and the health check calls `/api/me`.

```sh
docker build -f examples/ssr-bookshelf/Dockerfile -t lumiose-bookshelf .
docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 -e LUMIOSE_SECRET="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  -v bookshelf-data:/data lumiose-bookshelf
```

`node examples/ssr-bookshelf/e2e/docker-smoke.ts` builds the image and checks a running container:
health, a server-rendered page compressed with brotli, a database query, a sign-in, prerendered pages, the
`immutable` caching of hashed assets and their precompressed copies, the `node` user, no dev
dependency in the image, and a prompt stop. It needs Docker, skips itself in CI, and is never run
by CI: a cold build compiles the Rust compiler (about 1 minute on an 8-core arm64 machine).

<!-- source: deploy/vps.md -->

# VPS

> Run a Lumiose app on your own server with the Node adapter under systemd or pm2, behind Caddy or nginx for TLS.

This page covers an app with server routes and the `server.ts` that `create-lumiose --template ssr`
writes. The examples call the app `my-app`, serve it as `example.com`, and keep it in
`/srv/my-app`. To run it in Docker on the server instead, see [Docker](docker.md).

## Build and install

The server needs Node 24 or later. Build on the server, or in CI and copy the output. The build
loads the compiler's native binary, published for Linux x64 and arm64 on glibc and for x64 on
musl (Alpine; arm64 too from the release after 0.2.0); on another platform, build in CI.

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm build
```

To ship production dependencies only, build in CI (or with the [Docker](docker.md) image's
`build` stage), copy `dist/`, `server.ts`, `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml` and
`pnpm-workspace.yaml` (if any) to `/srv/my-app`, and run
`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --prod` there. Then start it with `node server.ts`, which serves
`dist/` on `PORT` (3000).

## What the adapter already does

`createServer()` serves `dist/client` first, then the app ([`@lumiose/adapter-node`](../reference/adapter-node.md)):

- **Compression.** Static files are sent from the `.br` and `.gz` copies that `lumiose build`
  writes next to every text file of 1 kB or more (brotli 11, gzip 9), at no CPU cost per request.
  Pages and endpoints with a text content type are compressed as they stream: brotli quality 4,
  else gzip 6. Every compressible response gets `Vary: Accept-Encoding`.
- **Caching.** Content-hashed files under `assets/` (`loader-BzIcWyn5.js`) get
  `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`; a new build changes their names. Every
  other file, prerendered pages included, gets `public, max-age=0, must-revalidate` with an `ETag`
  and `Last-Modified`, answered with `304` when unchanged. Pages rendered per request send what
  the app sets (`response().setHeader("cache-control", …)`).
- **Headers.** `lumiose({ headers })` and the default `X-Content-Type-Options` and
  `Referrer-Policy` go on static files and pages alike.

So the proxy only adds TLS, HTTP/2 and connection limits. Proxy every request to Node: a proxy
that serves `dist/client` itself would have to repeat the caching rules and the headers above.
With compression on in both, the proxy leaves the already encoded responses alone; or pass
`compress: false` to `createServer()` and let the proxy compress.

## The process

### systemd

Create a system user that owns nothing it runs:

```sh
sudo useradd --system --home-dir /srv/my-app --shell /usr/sbin/nologin my-app
```

Put the secrets in `/etc/my-app.env`, one `KEY=value` per line, readable by root only
(`sudo chmod 600 /etc/my-app.env`):

```sh
LUMIOSE_SECRET=paste-the-output-of-openssl-rand-base64-32
```

`/etc/systemd/system/my-app.service`:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=my-app (Lumiose)
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=my-app
Group=my-app
WorkingDirectory=/srv/my-app
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node server.ts
Environment=NODE_ENV=production HOST=127.0.0.1 PORT=3000 ORIGIN=https://example.com
# Secrets as KEY=value lines (LUMIOSE_SECRET=…), readable by root only.
EnvironmentFile=/etc/my-app.env
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
# The app can read /srv/my-app and write only its state directory, /var/lib/my-app.
StateDirectory=my-app
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true
PrivateDevices=true

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

```sh
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now my-app
journalctl -u my-app -f                # logs
sudo systemctl restart my-app          # after deploying a new build
```

Set `ExecStart` to the path `command -v node` prints. `HOST=127.0.0.1` keeps the app off the
public network: only the proxy reaches it. Point file databases and uploads at `/var/lib/my-app`
(the `StateDirectory`): with `ProtectSystem=strict`, it and a private `/tmp` are the only places
the app can write.

### pm2

`ecosystem.config.cjs`, next to `server.ts`:

```js
module.exports = {
  apps: [
    {
      name: "my-app",
      cwd: "/srv/my-app",
      script: "server.ts",
      // Node runs server.ts itself; pm2 6 would start .ts files with Bun.
      interpreter: "node",
      env: {
        NODE_ENV: "production",
        HOST: "127.0.0.1",
        PORT: "3000",
        ORIGIN: "https://example.com",
      },
    },
  ],
};
```

```sh
LUMIOSE_SECRET=… pm2 start ecosystem.config.cjs   # the app inherits this shell's variables
pm2 save && pm2 startup                           # restart it on boot
pm2 logs my-app
```

`pm2 save` writes the process list with its environment, the secret included, to
`~/.pm2/dump.pm2`, which `pm2 resurrect` (run at boot by the script `pm2 startup` installs)
restores. This runs one process (pm2's fork mode); pm2's cluster mode has not been tested with
Lumiose.

## The proxy

Set `ORIGIN` to the public origin (`https://example.com`), as in the configs above. The app
then builds request URLs (`url()`, `ctx.url`) with `https:` and your host, not the `http:` it
receives from the proxy. Without `ORIGIN`, the URL comes from the `Host` header, which the proxy
must pass through. The cross-site check of form posts compares the browser's `Origin` host with
that URL's host. Behind a proxy, the app's `clientAddress` is the proxy's: read
`X-Forwarded-For`, which both configs set, in middleware.

### Caddy

`/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`:

```caddy
example.com {
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}
```

Caddy gets and renews the certificate, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, passes `Host` and sets
`X-Forwarded-For`/`X-Forwarded-Proto`. It flushes streamed responses as they arrive, so
`<Suspense>` chunks are not held back. It needs no `encode` directive: responses arrive
compressed.

### nginx

`/etc/nginx/sites-available/my-app` (linked into `sites-enabled`), with a certificate from
certbot:

```nginx
upstream my_app {
    server 127.0.0.1:3000;
    keepalive 16;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name example.com;
    return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name example.com;

    ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;

    # The app accepts uploads up to 10 MB (lumiose({ limits })); nginx's default is 1 MB.
    client_max_body_size 10m;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://my_app;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        # Send each streamed chunk (a <Suspense> boundary) to the browser as it arrives.
        proxy_buffering off;
    }
}
```

`proxy_set_header Host $host` matters: nginx sends the upstream's name (`my_app`) as `Host`
otherwise. `http2 on` needs nginx 1.25.1 or later; on older versions, write `listen 443 ssl http2`.
`proxy_http_version 1.1` with an empty `Connection` header reuses connections to Node
(`keepalive`). For WebSockets, add the `/ws` location from the [realtime guide](../guides/realtime.md#behind-a-proxy).
`client_max_body_size` should match the largest body the app accepts
([Security](../concepts/security.md)), or nginx answers `413` first.

<!-- source: deploy/coolify.md -->

# Coolify

> Deploy to Coolify with its Dockerfile build pack: the port, a domain, secrets, the health check and a volume for data.

[Coolify](https://coolify.io) builds the app's Dockerfile on your server and runs the image behind
its proxy, which terminates TLS for the domain. Lumiose needs nothing Coolify-specific: the image
is the one from [Docker](docker.md). The field names below follow Coolify v4's documentation; this
guide has not been run on a Coolify instance yet (see the [verification table](README.md#verification)).

## 1. Add the Dockerfile

Commit the [Dockerfile and `.dockerignore`](docker.md#the-dockerfile) at the root of the
repository. Check that it builds locally (`docker build -t my-app .`): Coolify runs the same build.

## 2. Create the application
