In Coolify, **+ New**, pick the project and environment, connect the repository (a public URL, a
Git App or a deploy key) and choose the **Dockerfile** build pack. Then, under **General**:

| Field                   | Value                                                           |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Base Directory**      | `/`, the build context (the directory with `package.json`)      |
| **Dockerfile Location** | `/Dockerfile`, relative to the base directory                   |
| **Ports Exposes**       | `3000`, the image's `PORT`                                      |
| **Domains**             | `https://example.com`; Coolify's proxy gets the TLS certificate |

Coolify sets `PORT` to the first exposed port and `HOST` to `0.0.0.0` when they are not set,
which is what `createServer()` reads.

## 3. Environment variables

Under **Environment Variables**:

| Variable         | Value                                                                                                               |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ORIGIN`         | The domain, `https://example.com`. The proxy speaks plain HTTP to the container, so request URLs (`url()`) need it. |
| `LUMIOSE_SECRET` | When the app signs cookies: `openssl rand -base64 32`. Set **Build time** to **Not available during build**.        |
| Your own secrets | Database URLs, API keys: also **Not available during build**, since only the running server reads them.             |

New variables are available during the build by default; a secret that reaches the build can end
up in the image's layers. Restart or redeploy after changing them.

## 4. Health check

The image's `HEALTHCHECK` fetches `HEALTHCHECK_PATH` (`/` by default) inside the container. For a
Dockerfile application, Coolify uses an image's `HEALTHCHECK` instead of the one in its
**Healthcheck** settings, waits for the new container to be healthy before it replaces the old
one, and its default proxy (Traefik) stops routing to a container that turns unhealthy. To check a cheaper URL than the home
page, add a `GET` endpoint such as `/healthz` and set `HEALTHCHECK_PATH=/healthz` as a variable.
A health check configured in Coolify's dashboard instead runs `curl` or `wget` in the container;
Alpine has `wget`.

## 5. Persistent storage

Files the app writes at run time (a SQLite database, uploads) are lost when Coolify replaces the
container, unless they live on a volume. Create the directory for the `node` user in the
Dockerfile, before `USER node`:

```dockerfile
RUN mkdir /data && chown node:node /data
```

Then **Configuration**, **Persistent Storage**, **Add**, **Volume Mount**, with `/data` as the
**Destination Path**, and point the app at it (`DATABASE_PATH=/data/app.db`, or whatever your app
reads). Redeploy, and back the volume up outside the server.

## 6. Deploy

**Deploy**, then read the build log (the three Dockerfile stages) and the runtime logs (the
`Listening on …` line of `server.ts`). Pushes to the branch redeploy when automatic deployments
are on.

## A monorepo

Set **Base Directory** to the directory the Dockerfile's `COPY` lines are relative to, and
**Dockerfile Location** to the Dockerfile's path from there. The bookshelf sample, for example,
builds from the repository root with `/examples/ssr-bookshelf/Dockerfile`
([its notes](docker.md#the-bookshelf-sample)).

<!-- source: deploy/cloudflare.md -->

# Cloudflare Workers

> Deploy to Cloudflare Workers with `@lumiose/adapter-cloudflare`: the app runs as a Worker, the static files as assets.

Tested locally in `wrangler dev` (workerd), not yet on Cloudflare itself: see the
[verification table](README.md#verification).

## Set it up

```sh
pnpm add -D @lumiose/adapter-cloudflare wrangler
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { cloudflare } from "@lumiose/adapter-cloudflare";
import lumiose from "@lumiose/vite";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [lumiose({ adapter: cloudflare() })],
});
```

```jsonc
// wrangler.jsonc, next to package.json
{
  "name": "my-app",
  "main": "dist/_worker.js",
  "compatibility_date": "2026-09-01",
  // AsyncLocalStorage, which Lumiose's request APIs use, and process.env for your variables.
  "compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"],
  "assets": { "directory": "dist/client" },
}
```

Then build and deploy:

```sh
pnpm lumiose build
pnpm wrangler deploy      # or `wrangler dev` to try the build locally first
```

`lumiose build` warns, with a config to copy, when the project has no `wrangler.jsonc`,
`wrangler.json` or `wrangler.toml`. A site whose every route is prerendered builds no Worker: drop
`main`, and Cloudflare serves the assets alone.

## What the build writes

| File                        | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dist/_worker.js`           | The Worker: `dist/server/entry.js`'s `fetch`, called with `ctx.platform` (below). Wrangler bundles it, with the npm packages your server code imports, when it deploys.                                                                                                                              |
| `dist/client`               | The static assets. Cloudflare serves a request that matches a file without running the Worker.                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `dist/client/_headers`      | `lumiose({ headers })` and Lumiose's default headers for the static files, plus a year of caching (`immutable`) for `/assets/*`, whose files Vite names by content hash, except files you put in `public/assets/` (`! cache-control`). The Worker's responses get the same headers from the handler. |
| `dist/client/.assetsignore` | Only when prerendered pages have form actions: their HTML is left out of the assets, because Cloudflare answers a `POST` to a static file itself (`405`). The Worker renders those pages, fully resolved, and runs their actions.                                                                    |

Cloudflare compresses responses itself, so the build writes no `.br`/`.gz` copies, and the server
build leaves out its own static file layer (no `node:fs`).

## The platform in your code

Middleware, endpoints and actions get Cloudflare's arguments as `ctx.platform`:

- `ctx.platform.env`: the Worker's bindings (KV, D1, R2, Durable Objects, variables, secrets).
- `ctx.platform.waitUntil(promise)`: `ctx.waitUntil()`, for work after the response.
- `ctx.platform.clientAddress`: the `CF-Connecting-IP` header.

Type your bindings by augmenting `PlatformEnv` (with `@cloudflare/workers-types` or the types
`wrangler types` generates):

```ts
// src/routes/api/notes/route.ts
import type { Endpoint } from "lumiose";

declare module "lumiose" {
  interface PlatformEnv {
    DB: D1Database;
  }
}

export const mode = "server";

export const GET: Endpoint<"/api/notes"> = async (ctx) => {
  const { results } = await ctx.platform.env.DB.prepare("select * from notes").all();
  return Response.json(results);
};
```

Server components read them through middleware: copy what they need to `ctx.locals`.
Variables and secrets are also in `process.env` with `nodejs_compat` (compatibility dates from
2025-04-01), so `env("NAME")` and `ctx.env.NAME` work as on Node.

## Trailing slashes

Cloudflare's assets follow `assets.html_handling`. Match it to `lumiose({ trailingSlash })`:

| `trailingSlash`      | `html_handling`                   | `/about`                       |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `"ignore"` (default) | `"auto-trailing-slash"` (default) | redirects to `/about/` (`307`) |
| `"always"`           | `"force-trailing-slash"`          | redirects to `/about/`         |
| `"never"`            | `"drop-trailing-slash"`           | serves `about.html`            |

With `"ignore"`, Lumiose serves both forms itself, but Cloudflare redirects `/about` before the
Worker runs.

## Good to know

- Static files skip the Worker, so middleware does not run for them. Headers they need belong in
  `lumiose({ headers })`.
- Streaming works: the shell of a page is sent first, `<Suspense>` content follows.
- Unknown URLs reach the Worker, which renders your `not-found` page. Without a Worker (a static
  site), set `"not_found_handling": "404-page"` in `assets` to serve `404.html`.
- The Worker's npm packages must run on Workers: with `nodejs_compat`, many Node.js APIs do, but
  not everything (native modules, the file system of a server).

## API

```ts
import { cloudflare } from "@lumiose/adapter-cloudflare";

function cloudflare(): Adapter; // for lumiose({ adapter })
```

<!-- source: deploy/vercel.md -->

# Vercel

> Deploy to Vercel with `@lumiose/adapter-vercel`: the static files plus the app as a Node.js or Edge function.

Tested locally with a harness for the Build Output API, not yet on Vercel itself: Vercel has no
local runner for `.vercel/output`. See the [verification table](README.md#verification).

## Set it up

```sh
pnpm add -D @lumiose/adapter-vercel
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { vercel } from "@lumiose/adapter-vercel";
import lumiose from "@lumiose/vite";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [lumiose({ adapter: vercel() })], // or vercel({ runtime: "edge" })
});
```

In the Vercel project, set the **Framework Preset** to "Other" and the **Build Command** to
`lumiose build` (or `pnpm build`). Vercel deploys the `.vercel/output` directory that the build
writes. From the command line, build and deploy the output as it is:

```sh
pnpm lumiose build
pnpm dlx vercel deploy --prebuilt
```

Add `.vercel/` to `.gitignore`.

## What the build writes

| Path                                      | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.vercel/output/static/`                  | `dist/client` (below Vite's `base`), without `_headers`. Served first.                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `.vercel/output/functions/__lumiose.func` | The server, for every path no static file answers. Not written when every route is prerendered.                                                                                                                                                     |
| `.vercel/output/config.json`              | The routes: `lumiose({ headers })` and Lumiose's default headers, a year of caching (`immutable`) for the files the build named by content hash (not `public/assets/` files), form posts to prerendered pages, the static files, then the function. |

Prerendered pages also answer at their URL without the trailing slash (`/about` serves
`about/index.html` with `trailingSlash: "ignore"`, `about.html` with `"never"`), so the usual links
hit the static files. Vercel compresses responses itself: the build writes no `.br`/`.gz` copies.

## Node.js or Edge

`vercel({ runtime })` picks where the function runs:

- `"nodejs"` (default): a Node.js function (the build's Node.js major version, 22 at least),
  with response streaming. The function directory holds the server build and the npm packages it
  imports, found with `@vercel/nft`; native modules are copied as they are, so build on Linux
  (Vercel's build does) when your dependencies have native binaries. The project and its
  `node_modules` must be on one drive: the build stops with an error when the traced files share
  no common directory.
- `"edge"`: one bundled module for Vercel's Edge runtime. npm packages are bundled with their
  `edge-light` and `worker` builds. The Edge runtime has no file system and only some Node.js
  modules (`async_hooks`, `buffer`, `events`, `util`, `assert`): the build stops with an error
  naming any other module your server code imports.

## The platform in your code

- `ctx.platform.clientAddress`: the `X-Real-IP` header that Vercel sets.
- `ctx.platform.waitUntil(promise)`: Vercel's `waitUntil` (the Edge function's context, or the
  request context of a Node.js function), for work after the response.
- `ctx.platform.env` is empty: variables are in `process.env`, `env("NAME")` and `ctx.env`.

Request URLs use the public origin from `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host`, which
Vercel's proxy sets, so the cross-site check of form posts compares the right origins.

## Good to know

- Static files skip the function, so middleware does not run for them. Headers they need belong in
  `lumiose({ headers })`.
- Vercel applies the header routes to the function's responses too. When the app sets a header
  that `lumiose({ headers })` also sets for that path, which value wins on Vercel is not verified
  yet; the handler itself keeps the app's.
- A `""` value, which removes a header in `lumiose({ headers })`, can only remove it everywhere
  (`/**`) on Vercel: routes cannot unset headers for some paths.

## API

```ts
import { vercel } from "@lumiose/adapter-vercel";

function vercel(options?: { runtime?: "nodejs" | "edge" }): Adapter; // default "nodejs"
```

<!-- source: deploy/netlify.md -->

# Netlify

> Deploy to Netlify with `@lumiose/adapter-netlify`: the static files are the site, the app runs as a Netlify Function.

Tested locally with `netlify serve`, not yet on Netlify itself: see the
[verification table](README.md#verification).

## Set it up

```sh
pnpm add -D @lumiose/adapter-netlify
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { netlify } from "@lumiose/adapter-netlify";
import lumiose from "@lumiose/vite";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [lumiose({ adapter: netlify() })],
});
```

```toml
# netlify.toml, next to package.json
[build]
  command = "lumiose build"
  publish = "dist/client"
```

Push to a site connected to the repository, or deploy from the command line with
`pnpm dlx netlify-cli deploy --build`. `netlify serve` runs the build and serves it locally.
`lumiose build` warns when the project has no `netlify.toml`.

**In a monorepo**, set the site's package directory to the app's directory: Netlify then runs the
command from the repository root, so name the package and the full publish path:

```toml
[build]
  command = "pnpm --filter my-app build"
  publish = "apps/my-app/dist/client"
```

## What the build writes

| Path                                        | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dist/client`                               | The site (`publish`). Netlify serves it first.                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `dist/client/_headers`                      | `lumiose({ headers })` and Lumiose's default headers for the static files, plus a year of caching (`immutable`) for the files Vite names by content hash: `/assets/*`, or each of them when `public/assets/` has files of its own. |
| `.netlify/v1/functions/lumiose-server.mjs`  | The server: a Netlify Function (web `Request`/`Response`) for every path below Vite's `base` that no static file answers (`preferStatic`). Netlify bundles it with its npm packages when it deploys.                               |
| `.netlify/v1/functions/lumiose-actions.mjs` | Only when prerendered pages have form actions: the same server for their `POST`s, which Netlify would otherwise answer from the static file (`405`).                                                                               |

Netlify compresses responses itself: the build writes no `.br`/`.gz` copies. Add `.netlify/` to
`.gitignore`.

## The platform in your code

- `ctx.platform.clientAddress`: the function context's `ip`.
- `ctx.platform.waitUntil(promise)`: the context's `waitUntil`, for work after the response.
- `ctx.platform.env` is empty: variables are in `process.env`, `env("NAME")` and `ctx.env`.

## Good to know

- Static files skip the function, so middleware does not run for them. Headers they need belong in
  `lumiose({ headers })`.
- Streaming works: the shell of a page is sent first, `<Suspense>` content follows.
- `netlify serve` sends `cache-control: public, max-age=0` for static files whatever `_headers`
  says. On Netlify itself, `_headers` sets it, as Netlify documents (not verified yet).
- A site whose every route is prerendered needs no function: the build writes none, and Netlify
  serves `404.html` for unknown URLs.

## API

```ts
import { netlify } from "@lumiose/adapter-netlify";

function netlify(): Adapter; // for lumiose({ adapter })
```

<!-- source: deploy/bun.md -->

# Bun

> Run a Lumiose build with Bun, which serves the server build's fetch handler and the static files as they are.

Tested locally with Bun 1.4.2: see the [verification table](README.md#verification).

## Run it

Build with Node or Bun, then start the server build from the project directory, so that the npm
packages it imports resolve from `node_modules`:

```sh
pnpm lumiose build
NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 bun dist/server/entry.js
```

Bun starts a server for a module whose default export has a `fetch` method, on `PORT` (default
3000). The handler serves the static files of `dist/client` (with their `.br`/`.gz` copies,
`ETag`s and a year of caching for content-hashed assets), then the app, with
`lumiose({ headers })`. `ctx.platform.clientAddress` is Bun's `server.requestIP(request)`.

Bun does not compress responses on the fly: put a proxy or CDN that does in front for
server-rendered pages ([VPS](vps.md#the-proxy)).

## In a container

```dockerfile
FROM oven/bun:1.4 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json bun.lock ./
RUN bun install --frozen-lockfile
COPY . .
RUN bun run build

FROM oven/bun:1.4
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000
COPY --from=build /app/package.json /app/bun.lock ./
RUN bun install --frozen-lockfile --production
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER bun
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["bun", "dist/server/entry.js"]
```

The image is not tested; the [Docker](docker.md) guide's Node image is.

See also: [the server build](../reference/server-entry.md).

<!-- source: deploy/deno.md -->

# Deno

> Run a Lumiose build with Deno: `deno serve` runs the server build's fetch handler and serves the static files as they are.

Tested locally with Deno 2.9.6: see the [verification table](README.md#verification).

## Run it

Build with Node (Deno reads the project's `package.json` and `node_modules`), then serve the server
build from the project directory:

```sh
pnpm lumiose build
deno serve --allow-net --allow-read --allow-env --port 3000 dist/server/entry.js
```

`--allow-read` covers `dist/client` and `node_modules`, `--allow-env` the environment that
`env()` and `ctx.env` read. The handler serves the static files of `dist/client` (with their
`.br`/`.gz` copies, `ETag`s and a year of caching for content-hashed assets), then the app, with
`lumiose({ headers })`. `ctx.platform.clientAddress` is the handler info's
`remoteAddr.hostname`. The app's responses were not compressed in the local tests (streamed pages
included): put a proxy or CDN that compresses in front ([VPS](vps.md#the-proxy)).

**Deno Deploy** runs modules that export `{ fetch }`, but it is not tested: the server build
imports npm packages from `node_modules` and reads `dist/client` from disk, which a deployment must
include.

See also: [the server build](../reference/server-entry.md).

<!-- source: deploy/fly.md -->

# Fly.io

> Run a Lumiose app on Fly.io from the Docker guide's image, behind Fly's proxy.

Not tested on Fly.io yet: the image is (see the [verification table](README.md#verification)).

Add the Dockerfile and `.dockerignore` from [Docker](docker.md), then create the app with
`fly launch` (it finds the Dockerfile; decline the database offers you do not need) and adjust the
generated `fly.toml`:

```toml
# fly.toml
app = "my-app"
primary_region = "ams"

[env]
  NODE_ENV = "production"
  PORT = "3000"

[http_service]
  internal_port = 3000
  force_https = true
  auto_stop_machines = "stop"
  auto_start_machines = true
  min_machines_running = 0

[[http_service.checks]]
  grace_period = "10s"
  interval = "30s"
  method = "GET"
  timeout = "5s"
  path = "/"
```

Secrets go in with `fly secrets set LUMIOSE_SECRET="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"`, then
`fly deploy`. Fly's proxy terminates TLS and forwards the `Host` header, so request URLs are
right without `ORIGIN`; `ctx.platform.clientAddress` is the proxy's address, and the client's is
in the `Fly-Client-IP` header.

The adapter compresses responses itself; Fly's proxy passes them through.

<!-- source: deploy/render.md -->

# Render

> Run a Lumiose app on Render as a Node web service, with the Node adapter or the Docker guide's image.

Not tested on Render yet: see the [verification table](README.md#verification).

Create a **Web Service** from the repository with the Node runtime:

| Setting       | Value                                                             |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Build command | `corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build` |
| Start command | `node server.ts`                                                  |
| Health check  | `/` (or a cheap endpoint such as `/healthz`)                      |

Set the environment variable `NODE_VERSION` to `24` (Lumiose needs Node 24 or later), and
`LUMIOSE_SECRET` when the app signs cookies. Render sets `PORT`, which `createServer()` reads; its
proxy terminates TLS and forwards the `Host` header, so `ORIGIN` is not needed.

Or as a blueprint:

```yaml
# render.yaml
services:
  - type: web
    name: my-app
    runtime: node
    buildCommand: corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build
    startCommand: node server.ts
    healthCheckPath: /
    envVars:
      - key: NODE_VERSION
        value: "24"
      - key: LUMIOSE_SECRET
        generateValue: true
```

With the Docker runtime instead, Render builds the Dockerfile from [Docker](docker.md) and runs it
as is.

A site whose every route is prerendered can be a **Static Site** instead: build command as above,
publish directory `dist/client` (see [Static hosts](static.md)).

<!-- source: deploy/railway.md -->

# Railway

> Run a Lumiose app on Railway with the Node adapter and Railway's Node builder, or from the Docker guide's image.

Not tested on Railway yet: see the [verification table](README.md#verification).

Create a service from the repository. Railway uses the `Dockerfile` when the repository has one
([Docker](docker.md)); otherwise it builds with Node and runs the `build` and `start` scripts of
`package.json`:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "lumiose build",
    "start": "node server.ts"
  },
  "engines": { "node": ">=24" }
}
```

Or pin the commands in `railway.json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://railway.com/railway.schema.json",
  "build": { "buildCommand": "pnpm build" },
  "deploy": { "startCommand": "node server.ts", "healthcheckPath": "/" }
}
```

Railway sets `PORT`, which `createServer()` reads. Add `LUMIOSE_SECRET` in the service's
variables when the app signs cookies, then generate a domain in the service's networking settings.

<!-- source: deploy/static.md -->

# Static hosts

> Deploy a fully prerendered site to GitHub Pages, Cloudflare, Netlify, S3 or any file server: `dist/client` is the whole site.

`lumiose build` writes no `dist/server` when no route renders per request (no `server` route, no
`spa` route rendered on the server per request, no form action): see
[Rendering modes](../concepts/rendering-modes.md). What `dist/client` holds:

- the pages as `path/index.html` (`path.html` with `lumiose({ trailingSlash: "never" })`), and
  `404.html`, rendered from your root `not-found` page;
- `assets/`, named by content hash: cache them for a year (files you put in `public/assets/` are
  not hashed: keep them elsewhere in `public/`, or out of the long cache);
- `_headers`: Lumiose's default headers and `lumiose({ headers })` in the format Netlify and
  Cloudflare read;
- a `.br` and a `.gz` copy of every text file of 1 kB or more, for servers that serve
  precompressed files. Hosts that compress on their own serve them as plain files; leave them out of
  the upload there.

Set Vite's `base` when the site is served below a path (`base: "/my-repo/"` for a GitHub Pages
project site): links built with `href()` follow it.

How far each host's steps were checked is in the [verification table](README.md#verification).

## Cloudflare

Use the [Cloudflare adapter](cloudflare.md) even for a static site: it skips the precompressed
copies and adds a year of caching for the hashed files of `/assets/` to `_headers`. Without a server, the build writes
no Worker, and the wrangler config has assets only:

```jsonc
// wrangler.jsonc
{
  "name": "my-site",
  "compatibility_date": "2026-09-01",
  "assets": { "directory": "dist/client", "not_found_handling": "404-page" },
}
```

`pnpm wrangler deploy` uploads it. `not_found_handling: "404-page"` serves `404.html` with status
404 for unknown URLs. On Cloudflare Pages, `pnpm wrangler pages deploy dist/client` deploys the
same directory (Pages reads `_headers` and serves `404.html` by itself); add a
`dist/client/.assetsignore` with `*.br` and `*.gz` there, or build with the adapter.

## Netlify

Use the [Netlify adapter](netlify.md) and the same `netlify.toml`: for a static site the build
writes no function, and Netlify serves `404.html` and applies `_headers` by itself.

## GitHub Pages

Deploy `dist/client` with GitHub's Pages actions (set the repository's Pages source to "GitHub
Actions"). GitHub Pages serves `404.html` for unknown URLs and ignores `_headers`; it compresses
on its own.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/pages.yml
name: Pages
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm lumiose build
      - run: find dist/client -name "*.br" -o -name "*.gz" | xargs rm -f
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: dist/client
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
```

For a project site (`https://<user>.github.io/<repo>/`), build with `base: "/<repo>/"` in
`vite.config.ts`.

## S3 and CloudFront

Upload `dist/client` to the bucket with a long cache for the hashed assets and revalidation for the
rest, then let CloudFront compress (enable "Compress objects automatically") and answer unknown URLs
with `404.html` (a custom error response for 403 and 404, status 404):

```sh
aws s3 sync dist/client s3://my-bucket --delete \
  --exclude "*.br" --exclude "*.gz" --exclude "_headers" \
  --exclude "assets/*" --cache-control "public, max-age=0, must-revalidate"
aws s3 sync dist/client/assets s3://my-bucket/assets --delete \
  --exclude "*.br" --exclude "*.gz" --cache-control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"
```

S3 serves `about/index.html` for `/about/` only from its website endpoint (or with a CloudFront
function that appends `index.html`). Headers from `lumiose({ headers })` go into a CloudFront
response headers policy.

## Any file server

nginx, Caddy or another server can serve `dist/client` as it is, `.br`/`.gz` copies included
(nginx's `brotli_static`/`gzip_static`, Caddy's `precompressed`). `lumiose preview` serves it
locally the way static hosts do.

<!-- source: deploy/aws-lambda.md -->

# AWS Lambda

> Run the server build on AWS Lambda behind a Function URL or API Gateway, through a small adapter from Lambda events to its fetch handler.

Not tested on AWS yet: see the [verification table](README.md#verification). There is no
`@lumiose/adapter-lambda`; this page shows the handler to write.

The Lambda runs `dist/server/entry.js`'s `fetch`, which serves the static files of `dist/client`
when the deployment package includes them, then the app, with `lumiose({ headers })`. A CDN in
front serves them better: put `dist/client` on S3 behind CloudFront
([Static hosts](static.md#s3-and-cloudfront)), with a behavior that sends the other paths to the
function.

```ts
// lambda.ts: deploy it with dist/ and the production node_modules (Node.js 24 runtime)
import app from "./dist/server/entry.js";

interface FunctionUrlEvent {
  rawPath: string;
  rawQueryString: string;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
  cookies?: string[];
  body?: string;
  isBase64Encoded: boolean;
  requestContext: { http: { method: string; sourceIp: string } };
}

export async function handler(event: FunctionUrlEvent) {
  const { method, sourceIp } = event.requestContext.http;
  const headers = new Headers(event.headers);
  if (event.cookies?.length) headers.set("cookie", event.cookies.join("; "));
  const url = `https://${event.headers.host}${event.rawPath}${event.rawQueryString ? `?${event.rawQueryString}` : ""}`;
  const body =
    event.body === undefined || method === "GET" || method === "HEAD"
      ? undefined
      : Buffer.from(event.body, event.isBase64Encoded ? "base64" : "utf8");
  const response = await app.fetch(new Request(url, { method, headers, body }), {
    clientAddress: sourceIp,
  });
  const bytes = Buffer.from(await response.arrayBuffer());
  return {
    statusCode: response.status,
    headers: Object.fromEntries([...response.headers].filter(([name]) => name !== "set-cookie")),
    cookies: response.headers.getSetCookie(),
    body: bytes.toString("base64"),
    isBase64Encoded: true,
  };
}
```

This buffers each response: pages arrive whole, after their `<Suspense>` content resolves. Lambda's
response streaming (`awslambda.streamifyResponse`, Function URLs only) can send the stream
instead. `ctx.platform.waitUntil` falls back to letting the promise run, which Lambda may freeze
once the response is returned: await such work in the handler instead.

<!-- source: reference/reactivity.md -->

# `lumiose`: reactivity

> Signatures of the reactive core: signals, computeds, effects, stores, context, ids and scoped state.

All of these are exported by `lumiose` in the browser and on the server. On the server (the `node`
entry) signals are plain cells, computeds evaluate once per request, and `effect`/`onMount` never
run. Concepts: [Signals and reactivity](../concepts/signals.md).

## signal

```ts
function signal<T>(value: T, options?: SignalOptions<T>): Signal<T>;

interface Signal<T> {
  (): T; // read (tracked)
  set(value: T): void;
  update(fn: (value: T) => T): void;
  peek(): T; // read without tracking
}
interface SignalOptions<T> {
  /** When a write counts as a change. Default Object.is; false: every write is a change. */
  equals?: false | ((a: T, b: T) => boolean);
}
```

## computed

```ts
function computed<T>(fn: (previous: T | undefined) => T, options?: SignalOptions<T>): Computed<T>;
type Computed<T> = () => T;
```

Lazy (runs on first read), cached, glitch-free. `fn` must be pure: no signal writes (`LUM2002`).
An unobserved computed unlinks itself from its sources.

## effect

```ts
function effect(fn: EffectFn): () => void;
type EffectFn = () => void | (() => void);
```

Runs `fn` after the DOM updates, then again whenever a signal it read changes. A returned function
is a cleanup, run before the next run and on disposal. Returns a disposer. Owned by the current
owner, so it is disposed with the component.

## onMount

```ts
function onMount(fn: EffectFn): void;
```

Runs `fn` once, untracked, after the current owner's DOM is mounted. It may return a cleanup.

## onCleanup

```ts
function onCleanup(fn: () => void): void;
```

Registers `fn` on the current owner: it runs when the owner is disposed (or, for an effect, before
its next run).

## getAbortSignal

```ts
function getAbortSignal(): AbortSignal;
```

An `AbortSignal` for the current owner. Aborted when the owner is disposed, when an effect re-runs,
or when an async component run is superseded. On the server it is the request's signal. Throws
outside an owner (with a message in development). Svelte has the same function.

## untrack

```ts
function untrack<T>(fn: () => T): T;
```

Runs `fn` without subscribing the current scope to the signals it reads.

## batch

```ts
function batch<T>(fn: () => T): T;
```

Defers dependents until `fn` returns, so they run once. Delegated event handlers are batched
automatically.

## flush

```ts
function flush(): void;
```

Runs pending computeds, DOM bindings and effects now, instead of in the next microtask.

## store

```ts
function store<T extends object>(value: T): T;
```

Wraps a plain object or array in a deep, **mutable** reactive proxy, like Valtio's `proxy`, Vue's
`reactive` or Solid's `createMutable`: you write to it directly (`state.count++`,
`state.items.push(item)`), with no setter. Reads track per property, writes notify only on change,
array methods work. Class instances, `Map`s, `Set`s and frozen objects are returned as is.

## snapshot

```ts
function snapshot<T>(value: T): T;
```

A deep plain copy of a store, of a value inside one (`snapshot(state.items)`), or of plain data
that holds stores. Plain objects and arrays are copied; other values (`Date`s, `Map`s, class
instances) are kept as they are, and shared or circular references stay shared. Use it where a
proxy does not work: `structuredClone()` and `postMessage()` (to a worker or an AudioWorklet)
throw on proxies, and a copy does not change when the store does (saving, undo history). Reads
are not tracked: in an effect, read the properties it should react to. On the server it copies the
plain object.

```ts
const song = store({ title: "Demo", rows: [] as number[][] });
worker.postMessage({ type: "song", song: snapshot(song) });
```

## reconcile

```ts
function reconcile<T extends object>(target: T, data: T, options?: ReconcileOptions): void;

interface ReconcileOptions {
  key?: string; // identifies array items, default "id"
}
```

Patches fresh `data` (a fetch result, a server payload) into a store, or into an object or array
inside one (`reconcile(state.books, fresh)`), in place, with Solid's `reconcile` semantics:

- Array items are matched by reference, or by `key` when the new item has it. Items without the
  key are merged into the item at the same index when that item has no key either; unmatched
  items are inserted as new values, and leftovers are removed. Keys should be unique: new items
  that share a key end up as the same store item.
- Matched objects are merged deeply; an object whose `key` differs from the old one is replaced.
- Keys missing from `data` are deleted. Primitives and other values (`Date`s, `Map`s, class
  instances) are replaced.

Unchanged items keep their identity, so keyed list rows, their DOM and their local state survive,
and only properties whose value changed notify, all in one batch. Reads are not tracked, so it is
safe in an effect. `target` and `data` must be the same kind (both arrays or both plain objects),
otherwise it throws a `TypeError` in development. Pass the store, not plain data: a plain object is patched
without notifying anything (that is what happens on the server, where stores are plain objects).

```ts
const books = store<Book[]>([]);
reconcile(books, (await (await fetch("/api/books")).json()) as Book[]);

const page = store({ rows: [{ slug: "intro", views: 1 }] });
reconcile(page.rows, [{ slug: "intro", views: 2 }], { key: "slug" });
```

## createContext, useContext

```ts
function createContext<T>(defaultValue: T): Context<T>;
function createContext<T>(): Context<T | undefined>;
function useContext<T>(context: Context<T>): T;
interface Context<T> {
  (props: { value: T; children?: JSX.Element }): JSX.Element; // the provider component
  readonly id: symbol;
  readonly defaultValue: T;
}
```

A context is also its provider component, as in React 19 and Solid 2: `<Theme value="dark">…</Theme>`
provides `value` to everything rendered inside it, including content rendered later (conditionals,
lists). `useContext` returns the value of the nearest provider above, or the default. A nested
provider of the same context shadows the outer one for its subtree. Context survives `await` in
async components. Islands start a new root ([LUM4010](../errors/LUM4010.md)).

The provider reads `value` once, when it renders, like Solid's provider and like every component
prop read in a component body: components run once. To share state that changes, provide a signal,
a store or an object with getters, and read it where it is used.

```tsx
const Theme = createContext("light");
const Count = createContext(signal(0));

<Theme value="dark">
  <Count value={signal(5)}>
    <Toolbar /> {/* useContext(Theme) is "dark"; useContext(Count)() is reactive */}
  </Count>
</Theme>;
```

## useId

```ts
function useId(): string;
```

Returns an id that is unique in the page, for `id`/`for`, `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`,
`aria-controls` and the like. Call it in a component's setup, once per id you need; each call returns
the instance's next id. The id is a valid HTML id and CSS identifier (`l0-0-1-0`, `ls3`, `lc7`), so
it also works in selectors and as a `view-transition-name`. Do not parse it: the format may change.

- **Server and hydration.** Inside an island (and an SPA, which is one), the server builds the id
  from the island's id and the component instance's position in it, and hydration computes the same
  id, so the server's `for`/`id` pairs stay as they are. Outside islands, server ids follow the
  render tree, so the same page renders the same ids whatever order its async content resolves in.
- **Browser only.** Content rendered in the browser after hydration, or by
  [`render()`](dom.md#render), gets ids from a counter.
- **Several apps on one page.** Give each a prefix: `render(code, container, { idPrefix: "cart-" })`,
  or `renderToStream(root, { idPrefix })` on the server, which the page's islands reuse when they
  hydrate. Ids then start with the prefix.
- **Async components.** Each run of an async component runs its body again, so a re-run after a
  signal it read changed gets new ids, as its other locals are new too.

```tsx check
import { useId } from "lumiose";

export function EmailField(props: { label: string; hint: string }) {
  const id = useId();
  const hintId = useId();
  return (
    <p>
      <label for={id}>{props.label}</label>
      <input id={id} type="email" aria-describedby={hintId} />
      <small id={hintId}>{props.hint}</small>
    </p>
  );
}

export function SignUp() {
  const title = useId();
  return (
    <form aria-labelledby={title}>
      <h2 id={title}>Sign up</h2>
      <EmailField label="Email" hint="We never share it." />
      <EmailField label="Backup email" hint="Optional." />
    </form>
  );
}
```

## defineState

```ts
function defineState<T>(factory: () => T): () => T;
```

Scoped state: returns an accessor whose `factory` runs on the first call, once per scope, and
returns the same instance after that.

| Scope          | One instance per                                                                       |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Browser        | page: shared by every island and the SPA tree                                          |
| Server         | request: middleware, endpoints, actions and the render share it; never across requests |
| Tests (Vitest) | test: `@lumiose/vite` resets scoped state before each test                             |

The factory runs outside the component tree: it sees no context and its reads are not tracked; in
the browser its effects live as long as the page. On the server it may read request APIs
(`cookies()`, `locals()`, …), which do not exist in the browser: guard them with
[`isServer`](#isserver). Calling an accessor on the server outside a request or render (at module
scope) throws.

**Sent to the browser.** When islands or SPA routes import the state, a page that created it
sends what the factory returned that the browser cannot rebuild: the returned signal or store
itself, or the top-level signals and stores of the returned object. Computeds and functions are
not sent; the factory runs again in the browser and the server values replace its signals and
stores before any island reads them, so hydration matches. Values go once per page, in the chunk
(shell or streamed boundary) where the state was first used, and must be plain data like island
props ([LUM4011](../errors/LUM4011.md)). States that only server code imports are never sent.
Everything a sent state holds is public: never put secrets in it.

Define states at module scope with `export const x = defineState(…)` (or export the binding):
`@lumiose/vite` names each one after its module and export, the way it names islands. States
created elsewhere (inside a function) are never sent.

```ts
import { computed, cookies, defineState, isServer, signal } from "lumiose";

export const prefs = defineState(() => {
  const theme = signal(isServer ? (cookies().get("theme") ?? "light") : "light");
  return { theme, dark: computed(() => theme() === "dark") };
});
// prefs().theme(), prefs().dark(), prefs().theme.set("dark")
```

## isServer

```ts
const isServer: boolean;
```

`true` in the server entry of `lumiose` (the `node` condition), `false` in the browser entry
(Solid's name). Use it to guard code that runs on both sides, such as a `defineState` factory that
reads request APIs: `signal(isServer ? locals().user : null)`. The guard stays explicit: request
APIs called in the browser still throw [LUM4003](../errors/LUM4003.md).

It is a constant, so production client builds fold it: `if (isServer) { … }` and
`isServer ? a : b` lose their server branch, and server-only strings in it never reach the
bundle. The server branch must still type-check and import only what client code may import;
server-only modules stay out of client graphs ([LUM4003](../errors/LUM4003.md)).

## isPending

```ts
function isPending(): boolean;
```

Inside an async component (its body or its UI): whether a **re-run** is in flight. The first load is
not a re-run (`<Suspense>` covers it). Reading it in the body does not re-run the component.
Always `false` on the server.

## isBusy

```ts
function isBusy(): boolean;
```

App-wide: whether anything is in flight: an async component run, a `<Suspense>` showing its
fallback, a form submission (`submit()`), an SPA navigation or a request of the async cache
(`fetchJSON`, `query`), background refetches included. Reactive. Always `false` on the
server.

## resource

```ts
function resource<T>(fetcher: (signal: AbortSignal) => T | PromiseLike<T>): Resource<T>;

interface Resource<T> {
  (): T | undefined; // latest value, tracked
  loading(): boolean;
  error(): unknown;
  refetch(): void; // aborts a load in flight and loads again
}
```

Low-level on-demand loading. `fetcher` runs now and whenever a signal it read synchronously
changes; its `AbortSignal` aborts when superseded or disposed. The first load counts as pending
for the nearest `<Suspense>`. Errors are not thrown: read `error()`. Browser only: on the server it
stays loading. Prefer [async components](../concepts/async.md).

## optimistic

```ts
function optimistic<T>(source: () => T): Optimistic<T>;

interface Optimistic<T> {
  (): T; // source() with the pending overlays applied in order, tracked
  set(value: T, promise: PromiseLike<unknown>): void;
  update(fn: (value: T) => T, promise: PromiseLike<unknown>): void;
}
```

A value that follows `source` (a getter such as `() => props.likes`, or a signal), plus overlays
held while their promises are pending. Each `set`/`update` applies at once and drops when its own
promise settles, either way: on success the (refreshed) source shows, on failure the value rolls
back. Concurrent overlays apply in call order over the latest source value, so an `update` is
re-applied when the source changes. A rejection is not re-thrown; await the promise itself to
handle it. Writes stop when the owner is disposed. On the server it reads `source()` and `set`/`update`
do nothing. See [optimistic updates](../concepts/data-and-actions.md) in Data and actions.

## Example

```tsx check
import { batch, effect, getAbortSignal, onCleanup, resource, signal, untrack } from "lumiose";

export function Clock() {
  const now = signal(new Date());
  const timer = setInterval(() => now.set(new Date()), 1000);
  onCleanup(() => clearInterval(timer));

  const first = signal("Ada");
  const last = signal("Lovelace");
  const rename = () =>
    batch(() => {
      first.set("Grace");
      last.set("Hopper");
    });

  effect(() => {
    console.log(`${first()} ${last()} at`, untrack(now).toISOString());
  });

  const user = resource((signal) =>
    fetch(`/api/users/${first()}`, { signal }).then((res) => res.json() as Promise<{ id: string }>),
  );

  return (
    <p onClick={rename}>
      {now().toLocaleTimeString()} · {user.loading() ? "…" : user()?.id}
      {String(getAbortSignal().aborted)}
    </p>
  );
}
```

<!-- source: reference/components.md -->

# `lumiose`: components

> Signatures of the built-in components, from Suspense and error boundaries to portals, head tags and view transitions.

All are exported by `lumiose` in the browser and on the server. Concepts:
[Components](../concepts/components.md), [Async components](../concepts/async.md),
[Head and document](../concepts/head.md).

## Suspense

```ts
function Suspense(props: SuspenseProps): JSX.Element;
interface SuspenseProps {
  /** Shown while new content below is pending. */
  fallback?: JSX.Element;
  children?: JSX.Element;
}
```

Shows `fallback` while **new** async content below it is pending: the first load, and async
components or resources that a branch mounts later. Re-runs of revealed content keep their stale UI
(`isPending()` tells them apart). Hidden content stays alive. A shown fallback counts for `isBusy()`.
On the server, a boundary marks content that streams after the shell; with prerendering it is
resolved inline.

## ErrorBoundary

```ts
function ErrorBoundary(props: ErrorBoundaryProps): JSX.Element;
interface ErrorBoundaryProps {
  /** Rendered instead of the children after an error. */
  fallback?: JSX.Element | ((error: unknown, reset: () => void) => JSX.Element);
  children?: JSX.Element;
}
```

Renders `fallback` when its children throw while rendering, an effect below throws, or an async
component below rejects. `reset()` disposes the fallback and renders the children again. On the
server, an error in a streamed boundary renders the nearest `ErrorBoundary` in place.

In production server rendering, a fallback receives a generic `Error` with a short `digest`
(`An error occurred while rendering this part of the page (digest 1a2b3c4d).`) instead of an
error that is not an `HttpError`, which could reveal a database message or a file path. The
original error goes to the server log (the request handler's `onError`) with the same `digest`
property, so a user's report can be matched to the log entry. `HttpError`s (`notFound()`,
`error(403, …)`) reach the fallback as they are, development keeps the raw error, and boundaries
that catch in the browser get the error itself (decision-29).

## Portal

```ts
function Portal(props: PortalProps): JSX.Element;
interface PortalProps {
  /** Where the content goes. Default: document.body. */
  mount?: Node;
  children?: JSX.Element;
}
```

Renders `children` into a `<div>` appended to `mount`, removed with the owner. Delegated events
from the portal's content continue at the portal's position in the component tree.

## Dynamic

```ts
function Dynamic(props: DynamicProps): JSX.Element;
interface DynamicProps {
  /** A component or an intrinsic tag name. Nothing renders while it is nullish or false. */
  component: Component | string | null | undefined | false;
  [prop: string]: unknown;
}
```

Renders `component` with the other props, re-creating it only when `component` changes.

## ref

```ts
function ref<T extends Element>(): JSX.Ref<T>;
```

A callback for the `ref` prop that can also be read like a signal: `input()` is `undefined` until
the element exists. Pass it as `ref={input}`.

## Title

```ts
function Title(props: { children?: JSX.Element }): JSX.Element;
```

Sets the document title. The deepest `<Title>` wins, so a page overrides its layouts. It replaces
the `<title>` that `src/document.stsx` writes in `<head>`, which comes back after an SPA navigation to
a page without a `<Title>` ([head defaults](../concepts/head.md)).

## Meta

```ts
function Meta(props: Record<string, unknown>): JSX.Element;
```

Adds or updates a `<meta>` in `<head>`, with the given attributes. Metas with the same `charset`,
`name`, `property`, `http-equiv` or `itemprop` dedupe: the deepest wins, and the previous one comes
back when it is removed. A `<Meta>` replaces the `<meta>` with the same key that the document writes
in `<head>` (`src/document.stsx`, or the default document's `charset` and `viewport`), which comes
back after an SPA navigation to a page without one.

## Head

```ts
function Head(props: { children?: JSX.Element }): JSX.Element;
```

Appends its children to `<head>` and removes them on disposal. Elements equal to one already in
`<head>` (for example rendered by the server) are skipped.

## viewTransition

```ts
function viewTransition(fn: () => void): Promise<void>;
```

Runs `fn`, a state update (signal and store writes), inside
[`document.startViewTransition`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Document/startViewTransition),
and flushes, so the DOM shows the new state when the browser captures it: the page cross-fades from
the old state to the new one, and named elements morph. The browser captures the old state first,
so `fn` runs a frame later. The promise resolves when the transition finished, and rejects when
`fn` throws. Without View Transitions support, or when the reader prefers reduced motion, it runs
`fn` and flushes at once. On the server it only runs `fn`.

With [`lumiose({ viewTransitions: true })`](vite.md#lumiose), SPA navigations to another page swap
the page inside `viewTransition()` ([Routing](../concepts/routing.md)).

## ViewTransition

```ts
function ViewTransition(props: ViewTransitionProps): JSX.Element;
interface ViewTransitionProps {
  /** The child's view-transition-name. Default: a useId() id, unique in the page. */
  name?: string;
  /** The child's view-transition-class while it enters in a viewTransition(). */
  enter?: string;
  /** The child's view-transition-class while it exits in a viewTransition(). */
  exit?: string;
  /** A single element. */
  children?: JSX.Element;
}
```

Gives its single child element a `view-transition-name`, so that in a `viewTransition()` it
animates on its own instead of with the page:

- **Moves.** In the old and the new state (a keyed list row that moved, a layout change), it morphs
  from its old position and size to the new ones.
- **Enters.** Rendered by the update (a conditional that turns on, a new row), it fades in, with
  `view-transition-class: <enter>` until the transition finished.
- **Exits.** Removed by the update, it fades out, with `view-transition-class: <exit>`. Every
  `<ViewTransition>` with `exit` gets that class before the browser captures the old state (it is
  not known yet which elements go); the ones that stay lose it again.

Style the animations in a global style block with the
[`::view-transition-*`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/CSS/::view-transition-new)
pseudo-elements, by name or by class: `::view-transition-new(.slide-in)` for entering elements,
`::view-transition-old(.slide-out)` for exiting ones. The name is set in the browser, when the
element is created or hydrated; for cross-document transitions between MPA pages, set
`view-transition-name` in CSS ([Routing](../concepts/routing.md)). Anything but one element child
renders unnamed, with a warning in development.

```tsx check
import { signal, viewTransition, ViewTransition } from "lumiose";

export function Notifications() {
  const items = signal([{ id: 1, text: "Welcome" }]);
  let next = 2;
  const add = () =>
    viewTransition(() => items.set([{ id: next, text: `Note ${next++}` }, ...items()]));
  const dismiss = (id: number) =>
    viewTransition(() => items.set(items().filter((item) => item.id !== id)));

  return (
    <section>
      <button onClick={add}>Add</button>
      <ul>
        {items().map((item) => (
          <ViewTransition key={item.id} enter="slide-in" exit="slide-out">
            <li>
              {item.text} <button onClick={() => dismiss(item.id)}>Dismiss</button>
            </li>
          </ViewTransition>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </section>
  );
}
```

```css
/* In a global style block */
::view-transition-new(.slide-in) {
  animation: slide-in 0.25s ease-out;
}
::view-transition-old(.slide-out) {
  animation: slide-out 0.2s ease-in forwards;
}
@keyframes slide-in {
  from {
    transform: translateX(-2rem);
    opacity: 0;
  }
}
@keyframes slide-out {
  to {
    transform: translateX(2rem);
    opacity: 0;
  }
}
```

## Example

```tsx check
import { Dynamic, ErrorBoundary, Portal, Suspense, ref, signal } from "lumiose";

function Info() {
  return <p>Info</p>;
}

export function Dialog() {
  const open = signal(false);
  const kind = signal<"h2" | "h3">("h2");
  const button = ref<HTMLButtonElement>();

  return (
    <ErrorBoundary fallback={(error, reset) => <button onClick={reset}>{String(error)}</button>}>
      <button ref={button} onClick={() => open.set(true)}>
        Open
      </button>
      {open() && (
        <Portal>
          <div role="dialog">
            <Dynamic component={kind()}>Title</Dynamic>
            <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading…</p>}>
              <Dynamic component={Info} />
            </Suspense>
            <button onClick={() => (open.set(false), button()?.focus())}>Close</button>
          </div>
        </Portal>
      )}
    </ErrorBoundary>
  );
}
```

<!-- source: reference/app.md -->

# `lumiose`: app layer

> Signatures of the app-layer exports: data fetching, form actions, routing helpers, request APIs, cookies and env.

`lumiose` exposes the same names in the browser and on the server. Server-only APIs exist in the
browser build as stubs that throw `LUM4003` with a hint; browser-only APIs reject on the server.
Concepts: [Data and actions](../concepts/data-and-actions.md), [Server](../concepts/server.md),
[Routing](../concepts/routing.md).

## Data

### fetchJSON

```ts
function fetchJSON<T = unknown>(input: string | URL, init?: RequestInit): Promise<T>;
```

Fetches and parses JSON (`Accept: application/json` unless `init` sets it); an empty body is
`undefined`. Non-2xx responses throw a `FetchError`. During SSR, same-origin URLs are served
in-process through the request handler, with the page request's cookies and headers. Returns plain
data, so awaited results stay serializable in islands.

Awaited in an async component, a GET is **cached by its absolute URL** (see [query](#query) for the
cache's behaviour): components awaiting the same URL share one request. The first caller's `init`
(headers, credentials) makes the request. Inside an async component the signal defaults to
`getAbortSignal()`: a superseded run stops waiting, and the request is cancelled once no component
waits for it. Elsewhere (event handlers, middleware, endpoints, actions) and for other methods it is
a plain request.

`fetchJSON(url, { cache: "no-store" })` opts a component-level GET out of the cache: a plain
request, not deduped with other components, not kept, and not sent with the page payload (inside an
island, its value is still recorded for hydration like any other await). Other `cache` values keep
the default behaviour; `init` always reaches `fetch` as given.

### query

```ts
function query<T, const TKey extends readonly unknown[]>(
  key: TKey,
  fn: (context: QueryFunctionContext<TKey>) => T | PromiseLike<T>,
): Promise<T>;

interface QueryFunctionContext<TKey extends readonly unknown[] = readonly unknown[]> {
  signal: AbortSignal; // the shared request's signal
  queryKey: TKey; // `key`
}
```

Awaited in an async component, caches what `fn` resolves to under `key`, an array of
JSON-serializable values hashed stably (object key order does not matter), as TanStack Query's
`queryKey`. Use it for data that does not come from `fetchJSON`: a database call in a server
component, a third-party SDK. `fn` receives `{ signal, queryKey }`, TanStack Query's
`QueryFunctionContext`: `fn` runs outside the component, so `signal` is the shared request's
(the same one `getAbortSignal()` returns inside `fn`), aborted once no component waits for it.
Pass it on to `fetch` or an SDK: `query(["user", id], ({ signal }) => sdk.getUser(id, { signal }))`.
Outside an async component it calls `fn` without caching, with the current owner's signal (one that
never aborts when there is no owner).

The cache behind `fetchJSON` and `query`:

- **Scope:** one per request on the server; one per page in the browser, shared by every island and
  the SPA tree and kept across client navigations.
- **Deduplication:** components awaiting the same entry share one request.
- **Stale-while-revalidate:** in the browser, an entry with data returns it at once (a new
  component shows it without a `<Suspense>` fallback) and refetches in the background; when the
  data changed, the components that awaited it re-run. Defaults follow TanStack Query: `staleTime`
  0, `gcTime` 5 minutes after the last component that awaited it is gone.
- **Invalidation:** [`invalidate(target)`](#invalidate) re-runs only the components that awaited the
  matching entries; their re-runs wait for the refetch, keeping their UI meanwhile.
- **Islands:** entries awaited inside an island (or an SPA page) during SSR are sent once with the
  page, so the browser cache starts with them and islands hydrate without fetching. Their values
  must be plain data (`LUM4007`); entries only server components awaited are never sent.
- **Errors** are never cached: the next await fetches again. A failed background refetch keeps the
  old data.
- Cached data is shared, not copied: treat it as read-only.

### FetchError, isFetchError

```ts
interface FetchError extends HttpError {
  readonly status: number; // 0 for network failures
  readonly url: string;
  /** Parsed JSON body for JSON responses, else text; undefined when empty. */
  readonly data: unknown;
}
function isFetchError(value: unknown): value is FetchError;
```

Thrown by `fetchJSON()` and by `submit()` for unexpected errors. An `HttpError`, so if a server
component lets it escape, the page renders the `error` (or `not-found`) page with the same status.

## Form actions

### submit

```ts
function submit(target: SubmitTarget, options?: SubmitOptions): Promise<ActionResult>;
// Typed by the action it posts to: submit<typeof actions.save>(event)
function submit<A extends ActionsExport>(
  target: SubmitTarget,
  options?: SubmitOptions,
): Promise<ActionResult<ActionSuccessData<A>, ActionFailureData<A>>>;

type SubmitTarget =
  | HTMLFormElement
  | Event // a submit event: onSubmit={submit}
  | FormData
  | URLSearchParams
  | Record<string, string | Blob | readonly (string | Blob)[]>;

interface SubmitOptions {
  /** A URL, or "?/name" for a named action. Default: the submitter's formaction, else the
   *  form's action, else the current URL. */
  action?: string;
  /** Default POST. A form must say method="post". */
  method?: string;
  signal?: AbortSignal;
  /** After a success: true (default) refreshes the whole page with invalidate() on client-routed
   *  (SPA) pages, false keeps the page, and a list of targets (URLs, query() keys) refetches only
   *  those, on SPA and MPA pages. MPA pages never refresh as a whole on their own. */
  invalidate?: boolean | readonly (string | readonly unknown[])[];
}

type ActionResult<Data = unknown, Failure = unknown> =
  | { type: "success"; status: number; data: Data }
  | { type: "failure"; status: number; data: Failure }
  | { type: "redirect"; status: number; location: string };
```

Posts without a page load. `success` and `failure` set `actionData()`; `redirect` navigates.
On client-routed (SPA) pages, after a `success`, `submit()` runs [`invalidate()`](#invalidate) and
resolves once the page's data is fresh (decision-20); `{ invalidate: false }` skips it, and
`{ invalidate: ["/api/books/1", ["stats"]] }` refetches only those targets instead, on SPA and MPA
pages alike. On MPA pages it never reloads: the island updates itself from the result, refetches
targets, or calls `invalidate()` explicitly.
Failures, redirects and errors do not invalidate. Rejects only for unexpected errors (the action throws, an error response, a network
failure) with a `FetchError`, and with a `TypeError` for a redirect to a URL that is not `http(s)`
(a `javascript:` location never runs). Browser only: rejects on the server.

### isSubmitting

```ts
function isSubmitting(name?: string): boolean;
```

Whether a `submit()` is in flight; with a name, one to that named action (`?/name`). Reactive.
`false` on the server. Submissions of `submission()` handles count too.

### submission

```ts
function submission(): Submission;
// Typed by the action it posts to: submission<typeof actions.toggle>()
function submission<A extends ActionsExport>(): Submission<
  ActionSuccessData<A>,
  ActionFailureData<A>
>;

interface Submission<Data = unknown, Failure = unknown> {
  /** submit() for this handle: aborts its submission in flight, returns submit()'s promise. */
  submit(target: SubmitTarget, options?: SubmitOptions): Promise<ActionResult<Data, Failure>>;
  isSubmitting(): boolean; // this handle's submission is in flight
  result():
    | { type: "success"; status: number; data: Data }
    | { type: "failure"; status: number; data: Failure }
    | undefined; // the last settled result
  error(): FetchError | undefined; // the last unexpected error
  abort(): void; // cancels the submission in flight; the handle is idle at once
  reset(): void; // clears result() and error()
}
```

The submissions of one component instance (decision-51, after Solid Router's `useSubmission` and
React Router's `useFetcher`). Call it during component setup: disposing the component aborts its
submission in flight. Its results never set `actionData()`, and [`isSubmitting(name)`](#issubmitting)
still counts them; invalidation and redirects behave as with `submit()`. The promise `submit()`
returns rejects for errors (also in `error()`) and aborts (`AbortError`, not an error of the
handle), but an unawaited one (`onSubmit={handle.submit}`) reports no unhandled rejection. On the
server the handle is idle and its `submit()` rejects.

### actionData

```ts
function actionData(): unknown;
// Typed by the page's actions: actionData<typeof actions>() or actionData<typeof action>()
function actionData<A extends ActionsExport>(): ActionData<A> | undefined;
type ActionData<A extends ActionsExport> =
  | ActionSuccessData<A> // what the actions return (not fail() or a Response); void → undefined
  | ActionFailureData<A>; // the data they pass to fail()
// typeof action, typeof actions or typeof actions.name
type ActionsExport =
  | ((ctx: never) => unknown)
  | { readonly [name: string]: (ctx: never) => unknown };
```

The data of the last action result: what the action returned, or its `fail()` data. The type
argument is the actions export itself, never a data type: the result types are inferred from it.
`ActionData<typeof actions>` names the same type, for the props of a component that receives it
(`failed: ActionData<typeof action> | undefined`). Success and failure data are told apart by
their shape, as with React Router's `useActionData` and SvelteKit's `form`. Reactive in
the browser; after a no-JS form post it starts with the data the page was rendered with. On the
server: the current request's action result while the page re-renders after a post.

### fail, ActionFailure

```ts
function fail(status: number): ActionFailure<undefined>;
function fail<Data>(status: number, data: Data): ActionFailure<Data>;
```

A failed action result, usually for validation errors: `return fail(400, { errors })`. Without
JavaScript the page re-renders with `status`; `submit()` resolves with `{ type: "failure" }`.

### invalidate

```ts
function invalidate(...targets: (string | readonly unknown[])[]): Promise<void>;
```

With targets, refetches only the matching [cache](#query) entries and re-runs the async components
that awaited them, on SPA and MPA pages alike; their UI stays until the new data arrives. A string
is a URL (resolved against the page) and matches the `fetchJSON()` entry of that exact URL; an
array matches the `query()` entries whose key starts with it, as TanStack Query's
`invalidateQueries`: `invalidate(["books"])` matches `["books"]`, `["books", 1]` and
`["books", { page: 2 }]`. In development, a string that does not look like a URL (`/…`, `./…`,
`../…`, `http(s):…`) logs a warning: `invalidate("stats")` was probably meant as
`invalidate(["stats"])`.

Without targets, refreshes the whole page after a mutation: re-runs the page's async components in
SPA routes, refetching every cache entry (their UI stays until the new data arrives), and reloads
the page otherwise (that promise never settles, as the page is going away). A successful `submit()`
calls it for you on SPA pages only; on MPA pages call it yourself when the page needs fresh server
HTML.

Resolves once nothing is in flight anymore (`isBusy()` is false). Browser only: rejects on the
server.

## Routing

### href

```ts
function href<P extends Routes>(pattern: P, ...args: HrefArgs<P>): string;
```

Builds a path from a route pattern, encoding each param; `params` is required when the pattern has
params. A `[...rest]` param keeps its `/` separators; an optional `[[param]]` or `[[...rest]]`
whose value is missing or empty leaves its segment out (`href("/docs/[[...path]]")` is `/docs`).
Throws on a missing or empty `[param]` or `[...rest]`.

The path is below Vite's `base` and follows `lumiose({ trailingSlash })`, on the server and in the
browser alike (`lumiose dev`, `lumiose build` and prerendering):

| `base`  | `trailingSlash` | `href("/")` | `href("/blog/[slug]", { slug: "a" })` | `href("/feed.xml")` |
| ------- | --------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `/`     | `"ignore"`      | `/`         | `/blog/a`                             | `/feed.xml`         |
| `/sub/` | `"never"`       | `/sub/`     | `/sub/blog/a`                         | `/sub/feed.xml`     |
| `/sub/` | `"always"`      | `/sub/`     | `/sub/blog/a/`                        | `/sub/feed.xml`     |

With `"always"`, a pattern whose last segment has a dot (an endpoint such as `/feed.xml`) gets no
trailing slash. A relative `base` (`./`) counts as `/`. Outside Vite (plain Node) the path is
root-relative.

With `lumiose({ i18n })`, the path is in the current locale: the request's on the server, the
page's URL in the browser (`/es/...` on a Spanish page). The `locale` key switches it and is no
route param: `href("/blog/[slug]", { slug, locale: "es" })` is `/es/blog/hello`, `{ locale: "en" }`
(the default locale) `/blog/hello`. An unknown locale throws. `href()` does not check that the
page declares the locale: `alternates()` lists the URLs that exist. See
[Internationalization](../concepts/i18n.md).

### Route types

```ts
interface RouteMap {}                  // augmented by .lumiose/types/routes.d.ts (typegen)
interface LayoutMap {}                 // the same, for layouts (by the URL scope of their folder)
interface LocaleMap {}                 // the same, for the locales of lumiose({ i18n })
type Locale = /* "en" | "es" | …, or string before typegen */;
type Routes = /* every route pattern, or string before typegen */;
type RouteParams<P extends Routes>;    // { slug: string } for "/blog/[slug]"
interface PageProps<P extends /* a page pattern */> { params: RouteParams<P> }
interface LayoutProps<P extends /* a layout pattern */> {
  params: /* the params of the layout's scope */;
  children: JSX.Element;
}
```

## Control flow

```ts
function redirect(location: string | URL, status?: 301 | 302 | 303 | 307 | 308): never;
function notFound(message?: string): never;
function error(status: number, message?: string): never; // 400-599
function isRedirect(value: unknown): value is Redirect;
function isHttpError(value: unknown): value is HttpError;
```

They throw; the framework renders a redirect, the nearest `not-found` page (404) or the nearest
`error` page.
Without a status, `redirect()` uses 302 for GET/HEAD and 303 otherwise. `HttpError` is an `Error`
with a `status`.

## Request APIs (server)

```ts
function request(): Request;
function url(): URL;
function params<P extends Routes = never>(): RouteParams<P>; // Record<string, string> without P
function route(): Routes | undefined; // the matched pattern, "/blog/[slug]"; undefined if none
function locals(): Locals;
function cookies(): Cookies;
function response(): ResponseContext;
function env(name: string): string | undefined;
function publicEnv(source?: ServerEnv): Record<string, string>;
function cspNonce(): string | undefined; // lumiose({ csp: "strict" }): the response's nonce
function locale(): Locale; // lumiose({ i18n }): the request's locale; string | undefined without it
function alternates(): { locale: Locale; href: string }[]; // the page in each declared locale
function alternates<P extends Routes>(
  pattern: P,
  params?: RouteParams<P>,
): { locale: Locale; href: string }[];
```

`locale()` is the locale of the request's URL prefix (`/es/about` → `"es"`), else the default
locale, also while prerendering (each locale renders separately); without `lumiose({ i18n })` it
is `undefined`, typed `string | undefined` (so is `ctx.locale`). `alternates()` lists the current
route's URL in every locale it declares, with `base` and the trailing-slash policy, for language
switchers; `[]` without `lumiose({ i18n })` or when no route matched. With a route pattern (and
params, required when the route has some, as for `href()`), it lists that route's URLs from its
`locales` list, a layout's or the default locale, to link a page translated into fewer locales:
`alternates("/about")`. It throws for an unknown pattern and for a route whose locales come from a
`locales({ params })` function. See [Internationalization](../concepts/i18n.md).

`cspNonce()` is `undefined` without strict CSP, outside a request and while prerendering (the
page's hash policy covers its inline elements); in the browser it reads
`<meta property="csp-nonce">`. See [Security](../concepts/security.md).

Available anywhere during a server render (also after `await`), scoped to the current request. In
the browser they throw `LUM4003`. `url()`, `params()` and `route()` also exist in
[`lumiose/router`](router.md): those are reactive, follow client navigations and also work during
server rendering, so use them in code that runs in the browser (SPA routes, islands). `env()` reads the adapter's env, else `process.env`;
`publicEnv()` returns the `PUBLIC_*` subset.

```ts
interface ResponseContext {
  readonly status: number;
  setStatus(status: number): void;
  getHeader(name: string): string | null;
  setHeader(name: string, value: string): void;
  setStreaming(streaming: boolean): void; // false: one fully resolved document
}
```

Writable until the shell is sent; later writes throw `LUM5004`. `setStreaming(false)` makes the
response wait for every `<Suspense>` boundary and send one complete document, without fallbacks
or swap scripts, as prerendering renders; call it in middleware, or in a page before its first
`<Suspense>`. It is meant for crawlers: see
[the middleware recipe](../concepts/server.md#crawlers-get-one-resolved-document). The response
still waits at most `lumiose({ streamTimeout })` ([`LUM5009`](../errors/LUM5009.md)).

## Cookies

```ts
interface Cookies {
  get(name: string): string | undefined;
  getAll(): Array<{ name: string; value: string }>;
  set(name: string, value: string, options?: CookieOptions): void;
  delete(name: string, options?: CookieDeleteOptions): void;
}
interface CookieOptions {
  path?: string; // default "/"
  domain?: string;
  maxAge?: number; // seconds
  expires?: Date;
  httpOnly?: boolean; // default true
  secure?: boolean; // default: true in production and on https
  sameSite?: "lax" | "strict" | "none"; // default "lax"; "none" forces secure
  partitioned?: boolean; // CHIPS; forces secure
}
type CookieDeleteOptions = Pick<CookieOptions, "path" | "domain" | "secure" | "sameSite">;

function signedCookie(name: string, options?: SignedCookieOptions): SignedCookie;
interface SignedCookieOptions extends CookieOptions {
  /** HMAC secret; an array rotates keys (the first signs). Default: env LUMIOSE_SECRET. */
  secret?: string | readonly string[];
  /** Accept secrets under 32 bytes (else they throw in production, warn in dev). */
  allowWeakSecret?: boolean;
}
interface SignedCookie {
  readonly name: string;
  get(cookies: Cookies): Promise<string | undefined>; // undefined when the signature is invalid
  set(cookies: Cookies, value: string, options?: CookieOptions): Promise<void>;
  delete(cookies: Cookies, options?: CookieDeleteOptions): void;
}
```

## Context types

```ts
// P is a route pattern ("/books/[isbn]"); without one, params is Record<string, string>.
interface RequestContext<P extends Routes = never> {
  request: Request;
  url: URL;
  params: RouteParams<P>;
  // The matched pattern (route()); undefined only in src/middleware.ts for a URL no route matches.
  route: Routes | undefined;
  locals: Locals;
  cookies: Cookies;
  env: ServerEnv; // Readonly<Record<string, string | undefined>>
  platform: Platform; // what the host adds: bindings, waitUntil, client address
  locale: Locale; // lumiose({ i18n }): the request's locale; undefined without it
}
interface Platform {
  readonly env: PlatformEnv; // the platform's bindings; {} where there are none
  waitUntil(promise: Promise<unknown>): void; // fallback: runs it, reports a rejection
  readonly clientAddress: string | undefined;
}
interface ActionContext<P extends /* a page pattern */ = never> extends RequestContext<P> {
  formData(): Promise<FormData>; // parsed once; 400 if the body is not a form
}
// src/middleware.ts, or a folder's middleware.ts with the folder's URL scope as P ("/admin"):
// then ctx.params holds the folder's params and ctx.route the patterns below it (decision-48).
type Middleware<P extends /* a layout or middleware folder's pattern */ = never> = (
  ctx: RequestContext,
  next: () => Promise<Response>,
) => Response | Promise<Response>;
type Endpoint<P extends /* an endpoint pattern */ = never> = (
  ctx: RequestContext<P>,
) => Response | Promise<Response>;
// Annotating with Action hides the result from actionData<typeof action>(): type the parameter
// with ActionContext<P> instead, or use `satisfies Action<P>`.
type Action<P extends /* a page pattern */ = never, Result = unknown> = (
  ctx: ActionContext<P>,
) => Result | Promise<Result>;
type HttpMethod = "GET" | "HEAD" | "POST" | "PUT" | "PATCH" | "DELETE" | "OPTIONS";
interface ErrorPageProps {
  status: number;
  error: Error & { status?: number };
}
interface DocumentProps {
  head: JSX.Element;
  body: JSX.Element;
}
interface Locals {} // augment: declare module "lumiose" { interface Locals { … } }
interface PlatformEnv {} // augment: declare module "lumiose" { interface PlatformEnv { … } }
```

### Instrumentation types

The exports of `src/instrumentation.server.ts` ([Server](../concepts/server.md#instrumentation)):
`register(): unknown`, `onRequestError(error: unknown, info: RequestErrorInfo): unknown` and
`instrumentations: ServerInstrumentation[]`.

```ts
interface RequestErrorInfo {
  request: Request;
  route: Routes | undefined; // the matched pattern; undefined when no route matched
  params: Record<string, string>;
  phase: "middleware" | "action" | "endpoint" | "render" | "stream" | "waitUntil";
  digest: string | undefined; // what an <ErrorBoundary> fallback shows outside dev
}
// Each wrapper: (call, info) => unknown. call() runs the phase (once) and never throws.
type Result = { status: "success" } | { status: "error"; error: unknown };
type Info = { request: Request; route: Routes | undefined; params: Record<string, string> };
interface ServerInstrumentation {
  request?(call: () => Promise<Result & { response?: { status: number } }>, info: Info): unknown;
  middleware?(call: () => Promise<Result>, info: Info & { file: string }): unknown;
  action?(call: () => Promise<Result>, info: Info & { name: string }): unknown; // "default" for `action`
  endpoint?(call: () => Promise<Result>, info: Info & { method: HttpMethod }): unknown;
  render?(call: () => Promise<Result>, info: Info): unknown; // until the shell is ready
  stream?(call: () => Promise<Result>, info: Info): unknown; // each streamed boundary
}
```

The exports of `src/instrumentation.client.ts` ([Islands](../concepts/islands.md#concept)):
`onError(error: unknown, info: ClientErrorInfo): unknown` and
`instrumentations: ClientInstrumentation[]`.

```ts
interface ClientErrorInfo {
  phase: "hydrate" | "render" | "effect" | "navigate" | "submit";
  route: Routes | undefined; // the SPA route; undefined on MPA pages
  island: string | undefined; // the island's module#export, for errors in an island
}
type ClientInfo = { route: Routes | undefined };
interface ClientInstrumentation {
  navigate?(
    call: () => Promise<Result>,
    info: ClientInfo & {
```
